the structural-equality → leadership node (Thread E · Gender & Respect). "You don't need a title or a megaphone
to lead: be the ally, set the example, lift others, and change the room you're in, whatever your gender." 84
researched, India-grounded, even-handed scenarios across the-gaps → what-allyship-is → lead-by-example →
lift-as-you-climb → call-in-not-out → your-leadership-style, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play actions
(reflect / branch / strike-rewrite / sort / role-play / match / spot): no binary "tap the right card". Lead:
branch (your move), strike-rewrite (bust the myth), reflect. Allyship is everyone's job and MEN LEADING ON
GENDER EQUALITY IS STRENGTH, NOT BETRAYAL (the key India reframe). Understands the real gaps (pay ~34% in
India, women's leadership gap, unpaid-care load) and turns understanding into quiet, everyday leadership: lead
by example, lift as you climb, call IN over call OUT, lead from your values. India: engaging boys/men as allies
is a top lever; respect families (persuasion over confrontation); Women's Reservation Act 2023; India's own
role models. Safety first: witnessing harm routes to a trusted adult/teacher, 181, 112, Childline 1098.
Builds on g26 (Equalize) & g27 (Stand Up); sets up g34 (Change Makers). gameId "lead-the-way".
title: Lead the Way
greet: Hey, I’m Lensy. 🧭 You don’t need a title to lead. Be the ally, set the example, lift others, change the room. Leading on equality is strength. Let’s go.

badge.title: Lead the Way 🧭
badge.blurb: You know the real gaps and that allyship is everyone’s job, and you can lead quietly and powerfully: lead by example, lift as you climb, call in not out. 🤝

helpLine: If you witness harm or danger, safety comes first: get a trusted adult or teacher, or call Women Helpline 181, emergency 112, or Childline 1098.
reassure: You don’t have to fix everything alone, and safety comes first. If calling out feels unsafe, bring others in: a trusted adult, 181, 112, or Childline 1098. 🤝

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real, measured gap, or a comforting myth?

items.text: Women earn notably less for similar work
Women do far more unpaid care
Few women reach top leadership roles

scenarios.relearn: The pay, care and leadership gaps are real and measured; denying them is a myth.

scenarios.hook: Match each gap to a true fact about it.

pairs.right: Women earn far less for similar work
Women do far more of it
Under a quarter of women take part
A third of seats kept for women

scenarios.relearn: Pay, care, leadership and participation gaps are real and measured.

scenarios.hook: "The pay gap is just because women choose easier jobs."

myth.un: The pay gap is just women choosing easier jobs.
myth.re: Much of it is bias and the unpaid-care load women carry, not 'choice'.
myth.why: Women earn less even for similar work.

scenarios.relearn: Much of the pay gap is bias and the care load, not 'easier choices'.

scenarios.hook: "Unpaid housework and care aren't real work."

myth.un: Unpaid housework and care aren't real work.
myth.re: It's enormous, essential work, in India women average around 283 minutes a day of it.
myth.why: It's invisible in GDP but it holds families and economies up.

scenarios.relearn: Unpaid care is huge, essential work, and women do most of it.

scenarios.hook: "Women just aren't interested in leadership."

myth.un: Women just aren't interested in leadership.
myth.re: Barriers and bias, not interest, keep women out of top roles.
myth.why: Where barriers fall, women lead in every field.

scenarios.relearn: It's barriers and bias, not lack of interest, behind the leadership gap.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: India passed a law reserving a third of legislative seats for women. Step toward closing the leadership gap?
scenarios.affirm: The Women's Reservation Act is a concrete move toward more women in leadership.
scenarios.relearn: India's Women's Reservation Act reserves a third of legislative seats for women.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps close a gap, or widens it?

items.text: Assuming only women should cook and clean
Paying women less for the same job

scenarios.relearn: Sharing care and backing women closes gaps; bias and steering widen them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: when care work is shared fairly, women have more time for paid work and leadership. See the link?
scenarios.affirm: The unpaid-care load and the pay/leadership gaps are linked; sharing care helps close all of them.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing unpaid care frees women's time for paid work and leadership.

scenarios.hook: "Equality just means men losing out."

myth.un: Closing these gaps just means men lose out.
myth.re: Equality isn't zero-sum; it lifts everyone, men included.
myth.why: Fairer homes and stronger economies benefit all.

scenarios.relearn: Closing the gaps isn't men losing; equality lifts everyone.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a structural cause of the gap, or victim-blaming?
scenarios.relearn: Bias, the care load and steering are structural; 'they don't try' is victim-blaming.

scenarios.hook: Match the lever to the gap it helps close.
scenarios.relearn: Shared care, fair pay, backing leaders, reserved seats and STEM access each close a gap.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing the gaps are real and fixable, do you feel like you could be part of the fix?
scenarios.affirm: The gaps are made by choices and systems, which means people, including you, can help change them.
scenarios.relearn: The gaps are real and fixable, and you can be part of closing them.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: this game is about turning that understanding into leadership. Ready to lead on it?
scenarios.affirm: Understanding the gaps is step one; leading to close them is what's next.
scenarios.relearn: Understanding the gaps becomes leadership when you act to close them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an accurate picture, or a comforting myth?

items.text: The gaps are measured, not invented

scenarios.relearn: Gaps remain but change is real; 'all equal', 'never changes' and 'made up' are myths.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which gap do you most want to help close?
scenarios.affirm: Whichever you choose, leading on it makes a real difference.
scenarios.relearn: Pay, leadership and care gaps are all real places to lead change.

scenarios.hook: "You need a title or a stage to lead."

myth.un: You need a title or a stage to lead.
myth.re: Quiet, everyday leadership, modelling respect and lifting others, is real leadership.
myth.why: Most change comes from ordinary people, not megaphones.

scenarios.relearn: You don't need a title or a stage; quiet everyday leadership is real.

scenarios.hook: "Gender equality is women's job, not boys' problem."

myth.un: Gender equality is women's job, not boys' problem.
myth.re: It's everyone's job; engaging men and boys as allies is one of the strongest levers.
myth.why: Change is faster and fairer when everyone leads.

scenarios.relearn: Equality is everyone's job; men and boys leading is a powerful lever.

scenarios.hook: "A boy who supports equality is betraying his side or is weak."

myth.un: A boy supporting equality is betraying his side or is weak.
myth.re: Leading on equality is a sign of strength and maturity, and it frees boys too.
myth.why: There are no 'sides' in fairness; everyone gains.

scenarios.relearn: A boy leading on equality shows strength and maturity, not betrayal.

scenarios.hook: "Allyship is just posting a hashtag."

myth.un: Allyship is just posting a hashtag.
myth.re: Real allyship is listening, amplifying, and showing up consistently, not a performance.
myth.why: Actions over time, not slogans, are what help.

scenarios.relearn: Active allyship is listening, amplifying and showing up, not a hashtag.

scenarios.hook: Sort: active allyship, or just performance?
scenarios.relearn: Listening, amplifying and showing up are active allyship; posts-for-likes are performance.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: allyship is using whatever influence you have, however small, for others. Feel able to do that?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever influence you have, used for others, is exactly what allyship means.
scenarios.relearn: Allyship is using your influence, however small, for others.

scenarios.hook: Match the ally action to what it is.
scenarios.relearn: Listen, amplify, show up, credit and step back are the core ally moves.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: men leading on equality being seen as strength, why does that matter so much here?
scenarios.affirm: When male allyship is seen as strength, half the population joins the work, that's huge.
scenarios.relearn: Framing male allyship as strength brings everyone into the work.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real ally, or a bystander?

items.text: Waits for someone else to act
Names who really had the idea

scenarios.relearn: Backing people, sharing the mic and crediting ideas is allyship; silence and waiting is bystanding.

scenarios.hook: "Helping others get ahead means you fall behind."

myth.un: Helping others get ahead means you fall behind.
myth.re: Lifting others builds trust, teams and respect; leadership isn't a fixed pie.
myth.why: Good leaders are measured by who rises with them.

scenarios.relearn: Lifting others doesn't hold you back; it's what real leadership is.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: allyship isn't about being a hero for people, it's standing with them. Feel the difference?
scenarios.affirm: Standing with people, led by them, is allyship; 'saving' them isn't.
scenarios.relearn: Allyship is standing with people, led by them, not 'saving' them.

scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 moves that aren't real allyship.

scene.text: Crediting whose idea it was
Speaking over them to 'help'
Making space for them to speak
Taking credit for their idea
Asking what would help first

scenarios.why: Speaking over someone and taking their credit aren't allyship, even when they feel helpful.
scenarios.relearn: Crediting and making space is allyship; speaking over or taking credit isn't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: what kind of ally do you want to be?
scenarios.affirm: Listening, amplifying and showing up, that's an ally the world needs.
scenarios.relearn: You can be an ally who listens, amplifies and shows up.

scenarios.hook: "One person can't change anything."

myth.un: One person can't change anything.
myth.re: One person leading by example and lifting one other shifts the whole room.
myth.why: Norms change one steady example at a time.

scenarios.relearn: One person, leading and lifting one other, can shift the room.

scenarios.hook: At home, the women do all the chores while the men relax, and you want to lead.

steps.prompt: After lunch, plates pile up while the men sit. What do you do?

options.text: Start clearing the plates yourself, unasked
options.then: Your sister looks up in surprise. Your father watches but says nothing.

options.text: Complain loudly that it's all unfair
options.then: The room goes quiet. The plates stay where they are.

options.text: Help only when your mother asks
options.then: Your mother sighs, but asks. You help, once.

options.text: Tell your sister she should refuse to clear
options.then: Your sister frowns. "You tell them, then," she says.

steps.why: Sharing the load yourself, visibly and unasked, shifts the family norm.

steps.prompt: Later, your father asks what this new interest in chores is about. What do you say?

options.text: Say sharing feels fair, and ask him to join
options.then: He grunts, then picks up a cloth. "Show me where things go."

options.text: Say it's nothing and you were just bored
options.then: He nods, and nothing about the house changes.

options.text: Say he's been unfair to Mum all these years
options.then: He stiffens. "Don't talk to me like that."

options.text: Say you'd rather it was done quietly, unnoticed
options.then: He nods. The others never learn it was a choice.

steps.why: Showing that sharing feels fair, and inviting him in, works better than blaming.

steps.prompt: Your younger cousin walks in on you in the kitchen and teases you about women's work. What do you do?

options.text: Say "It's just housework" and hand him a cloth
options.then: He laughs but takes it. "Fine. Only today."

options.text: Drop the subject so there's no teasing
options.then: The teasing stops. So does the example.

options.text: Lecture him on gender roles
options.then: His eyes glaze over. He doesn't pick up the cloth.

options.text: Tease him back for being lazy
options.then: The two of you laugh. The point is lost.

steps.why: A calm shrug with action beats a lecture.

scenarios.debrief: Doing your fair share, visibly, sets a norm others follow.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by example: share the load yourself, without being asked.

scenarios.hook: A demeaning joke about girls lands in your group, and laughter starts.

steps.prompt: They look around to see who's laughing. What do you do?

options.text: Don't laugh, and keep a calm face
options.then: The laughter fades a little sooner. Someone glances at you.

options.text: Laugh along to fit in
options.then: The group relaxes. The joke counts as normal now.

options.text: Laugh a little, then tell a friend it was wrong later
options.then: Your friend agrees later. In the moment, you laughed.

options.text: Loudly call the joker sexist
options.then: He defends himself, and the others side with him.

steps.why: Not laughing sets a different tone without a scene.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend asks what you really thought of the joke. What do you say?

options.text: Say it wasn't funny to you, and leave it
options.then: He shrugs. "Fair." He seems to be thinking it over.

options.text: Say you didn't really think about it
options.then: He nods. Nothing changes, and he has no idea where you stand.

options.text: Say you're better than them
options.then: He bristles. "Oh, so now you're a saint?"

options.text: Say you'll laugh next time so it isn't awkward
options.then: He grins. You've just promised to go along.

steps.why: A plain, honest answer shows where you stand without a lecture.

steps.prompt: A week later, the same friend tells a similar joke and glances at you first. What do you do?

options.text: Don't laugh, and say "Got a better one?"
options.then: He grins sheepishly and tells a different joke.

options.text: Laugh this time so he doesn't feel judged
options.then: He's pleased. The joke has a licence now.

options.text: Give him a speech on respect
options.then: The table groans. He stops talking to you for the day.

options.text: Tell the others he's a creep
options.then: The table goes quiet. He feels humiliated and angry.

steps.why: A light refusal keeps the friendship and the norm.

scenarios.debrief: Refusing to laugh is a small, powerful act of leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Not laughing at a demeaning joke quietly sets a better norm.

scenarios.hook: In a group project, people assume the girls will take notes and the boys will present.

steps.prompt: The group starts dividing roles. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest roles by skill and interest
options.then: The group blinks, then starts listing who's good at what.

options.text: Go along with the split to keep the peace
options.then: The split stays. The girls do the notes again.

options.text: Announce that the split is sexist
options.then: Voices rise. Two boys say you're making it complicated.

options.text: Grab the role you want without telling the group
options.then: You get it, but the rest of the split stays as it was.

steps.why: Suggesting roles by skill and interest breaks the default calmly.

steps.prompt: A boy, Aarav, says he'd rather take notes, and the others tease him. What do you do?

options.text: Say roles go by skill, and he's good at it
options.then: Aarav smiles. The teasing stops when someone asks who has the neatest writing.

options.text: Laugh along with the teasing
options.then: Aarav looks down. He says he'll present after all.

options.text: Tell him to present like the others
options.then: He agrees, though he's clearly unhappy.

options.text: Say nothing and let the group sort it out
options.then: The teasing carries on until Aarav gives in.

steps.why: Backing a skill-based choice shows the new norm applies to everyone.

steps.prompt: The teacher praises the project and thanks only the presenters. What do you do?

options.text: Say everyone's work counted, and name the note-takers
options.then: The teacher smiles. "Of course. Thank you all."

options.text: Stay quiet, since the roles were the group's idea
options.then: The note-takers go unthanked. Someone shrugs.

options.text: Say you're proud of the presenters, and leave it
options.then: The presenters beam. The rest of the team stays unnamed.

options.text: Complain afterwards that the teacher was unfair
options.then: Your friends nod, but the teacher never hears it.

steps.why: Naming everyone's work is how credit gets shared.

scenarios.debrief: Quietly assigning roles fairly resets the group's assumptions.
scenarios.relearn: Assign roles by skill, not gender, and model the fairer way.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: your everyday behaviour is the norm others quietly copy. Powerful, isn't it?
scenarios.affirm: People copy what they see; your consistent example is real influence.
scenarios.relearn: Your everyday behaviour sets a norm others quietly follow.
Real example is consistent respect, not a show put on only when watched.
scenarios.hook: Spot the two moves that only look like leadership but aren't.

scene.text: Speaking respectfully to everyone, every day
Only sharing chores when a relative visits
Sharing the load at home without being asked
Acting fair on camera, unfair off it
Same respect for juniors and seniors

scenarios.why: Being fair only when watched or filmed is a show, not leadership; real example is consistent.

scenarios.hook: You notice that your friends copy what you say and do.

steps.prompt: A friend wants everyone to mock a girl's looks in the group chat. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'd rather talk about something else
options.then: The friend shrugs. Two others quietly shift the topic too.

options.text: Join in lightly so you don't stand out
options.then: The chat gets nastier, and you feel it was partly you.

options.text: Ignore it, since you're no leader
options.then: Your silence reads as a yes. The mocking carries on.

options.text: Lecture them all for being shallow
options.then: The chat goes cold. The mocking moves to a new group.

steps.why: Using the influence you already have to set a calm tone lifts the group.

steps.prompt: A younger friend asks what you think of how the group treats girls. What do you say?

options.text: Say honestly what you think, and what you try to do
options.then: He nods. "I never thought about it. I'll try."

options.text: Say it's not your job to tell others how to behave
options.then: He shrugs and drifts back to the group's default.

options.text: Say you just do whatever the group does
options.then: He decides that's the way to be.

options.text: Say the group is hopeless
options.then: He frowns. He's one of the group.

steps.why: Sharing honestly what you think and do is an example he can use.

steps.prompt: Your friends start asking you to decide the group's plans. How do you use that?

options.text: Share decisions, and ask the quieter ones first
options.then: The quieter members start offering ideas.

options.text: Decide everything yourself, quickly
options.then: Plans are quick, but others stop offering ideas.

options.text: Let the loudest friend decide
options.then: Plans suit him. The quieter ones stop coming.

options.text: Refuse to decide so you aren't the boss
options.then: The group drifts. Nobody knows who to ask.

steps.why: Sharing decisions and hearing quieter voices turns influence into trust.

scenarios.debrief: Influence you already have, used well, is leadership.
scenarios.relearn: If people look to you, model respect: your example leads.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: integrity, doing the fair thing even when no one's watching, is the heart of leading by example. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Doing right unwatched is exactly the integrity that makes an example worth following.
scenarios.relearn: Integrity, fairness even when unwatched, is the heart of leading by example.

scenarios.hook: Your younger brother Ayaan watches how you treat people and copies you.

steps.prompt: Ayaan saw you snap at your mother over dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise to her, where he can see
options.then: Your mother softens. Ayaan watches closely.

options.text: Say nothing, since it was just a bad day
options.then: Ayaan notes that snapping is allowed.

options.text: Tell Ayaan not to copy you
options.then: He looks confused. "Then what should I do?"

options.text: Say she was being annoying
options.then: Ayaan nods. He files it away for later.

steps.why: Making things right where he can see teaches more than any lecture.

steps.prompt: Ayaan mentions he teased a classmate for crying at school. What do you do?

options.text: Say you cry too, and ask how the classmate felt
options.then: Ayaan looks surprised. "Really? You?" Then, slowly: "He probably felt bad."

options.text: Scold him sharply and send him to his room
options.then: He sulks and hides things from you next time.

options.text: Laugh and say kids will be kids
options.then: Ayaan relaxes. The classmate is teased again.

options.text: Tell him boys shouldn't cry anyway
options.then: Ayaan nods. He decides tears are something to hide.

steps.why: Sharing your own feelings and asking about the classmate teaches kindness.

steps.prompt: Your uncle teases Ayaan for helping with the dishes. What do you do?

options.text: Join in washing too, and say "We both help here."
options.then: Your uncle chuckles. Ayaan stands a little taller.

options.text: Say nothing and let Ayaan handle it
options.then: Ayaan looks at the floor and stops drying the plates.

options.text: Argue with your uncle about gender roles
options.then: Your uncle gets defensive. Dinner turns chilly.

options.text: Tell Ayaan to stop helping when uncle visits
options.then: Ayaan nods. He learns to hide what he does.

steps.why: Doing the job alongside him says it's normal, with no fight.

steps.prompt: That night, Ayaan wonders aloud whether being fair matters when nobody's watching. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's who you want to be, watched or not
options.then: Ayaan nods slowly. "Okay. I want that too."

options.text: Say you do it so he learns from you
options.then: Ayaan frowns. "So you'd stop if I weren't there?"

options.text: Say he'll understand when he's older
options.then: Ayaan shrugs. The question stays with him.

options.text: Say it's because Mum told you to
options.then: Ayaan decides fairness is something you do only when told.

steps.why: Fairness that stays the same without an audience is the kind he'll copy.

scenarios.debrief: You're already teaching by example. Choose what you teach.
scenarios.relearn: Model for younger ones the respect and fairness you want them to learn.
A consistent, humble example lands; one-off gestures and credit-seeking don't.
scenarios.hook: Spot the two things that stop an example from actually landing.

scene.text: Doing the fair thing consistently over time
One big gesture, then back to old habits
Quietly leading without seeking credit
Loudly announcing how fair you are
Owning your slip-ups and correcting them

scenarios.why: A one-off gesture and loud credit-seeking undercut the example; steady, humble action lands.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: small, steady acts of respect, do they really add up to leadership?
scenarios.affirm: Small steady acts, repeated, are how norms, and leaders, are actually made.
scenarios.relearn: Small, steady acts of respect add up to real leadership.

scenarios.hook: In your friend group, only the girls are ever asked to organise the snacks.

steps.prompt: Planning the party, they turn to the girls again. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest a snack rota and sign up first
options.then: A couple of friends look surprised. One girl smiles. "Thanks."

options.text: Stay quiet to avoid standing out
options.then: The girls organise the snacks again, as usual. A friend notices your frown.

options.text: Say it's unfair, and then do nothing
options.then: The group groans. The snacks fall on the girls anyway.

options.text: Let it be, since people won't change
options.then: The pattern carries on, and you feel stuck. A friend notices your mood.

steps.why: Doing the fair thing yourself, even if people notice, leads best.

steps.prompt: Later, a friend asks what's bothering you about the snacks. What do you do?

options.text: Smile and say it's just about being fair
options.then: He rolls his eyes but lets it go.

options.text: Say it's nothing and change the subject
options.then: The questions stop, and so does any change.

options.text: Snap back that he's just lazy
options.then: He snaps back, and the party starts tense.

options.text: Explain at length why you're right
options.then: He nods politely and is thinking about something else.

steps.why: A light, steady answer keeps your example from becoming a fight.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a boy offers to organise the snacks unasked. What do you do?

options.text: Thank him, and offer to share the job
options.then: He grins. "Okay, you and me."

options.text: Say "I told you so"
options.then: He laughs, but it stings a bit.

options.text: Take over so it's done properly
options.then: He backs off, and the offer is forgotten.

options.text: Say nothing and let him get on with it
options.then: He does it alone, and wonders if it mattered.

steps.why: Sharing the job turns one example into a habit for two.

scenarios.debrief: Standing slightly apart to do right is what leaders do.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by example even if it means briefly standing out.

scenarios.hook: In your study group, the same two people do all the talking.
scenarios.setup: Today you want to model fairer talk.

steps.prompt: Karan says: "Let's finish quickly. Same plan as last time?"

options.text: "Quick check first. Let's hear from everyone."
options.then: Karan blinks. "Oh. Sure. Meera, you were saying something?"

options.text: "Sure, same plan."
options.then: Karan nods. "Great. Moving on."

options.text: "You two decide. I'm easy."
options.then: "Okay, we will." The two of them start planning.

options.text: "Can you stop dominating the group, please?"
options.then: Karan bristles. "Dominating? We're just being efficient."

steps.why: An open invitation lets quieter voices in without blaming anyone.

steps.prompt: Meera says hesitantly: "I had a different idea, but it's probably not important."

options.text: "I'd like to hear it. Go ahead."
options.then: She lights up. "Okay. What if we split the topic in two?"

options.text: "If it's not important, maybe skip it."
options.then: She nods and closes her notebook.

options.text: "I'll tell them your idea for you."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay. It was my idea, though."

options.text: "Don't be shy. Everyone's waiting."
options.then: Meera flushes. "Now I feel worse."

steps.why: Asking for her idea plainly tells her it matters.

steps.prompt: Karan says: "We're running late. Can we just lock the plan now?"

options.text: "Five minutes on Meera's idea now saves us redoing it."
options.then: Karan sighs. "Fair. Go on, Meera."

options.text: "You're right. Let's wrap up."
options.then: "Great." Meera's idea goes unheard.

options.text: "Fine. Meera can send her idea later."
options.then: Karan nods. By tonight, nobody has read it.

options.text: "You never listen to anyone."
options.then: Karan snaps. "Excuse me?"

steps.why: A calm, practical reason lets him say yes without feeling blamed.

steps.prompt: Karan asks: "So how do we run next week? Same as today?"

options.text: "Let's rotate who starts each week."
options.then: Karan nods. "Okay. I'll go second."

options.text: "Sure. Meera leads from now on."
options.then: Meera looks alarmed. "Always me?"

options.text: "Let's go back to how we did it."
options.then: Karan grins. "Fine by me." The old pattern returns.

options.text: "Whatever you two want."
options.then: Karan shrugs. "Then Meera, I guess." Nobody asked Meera.

steps.why: Rotating who starts keeps every voice in play, week after week.

scenarios.relearn: Modelling inclusive language, like inviting quieter voices, leads gently.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: people remember how you made them feel. What example do you want to leave?
scenarios.affirm: Leaving people feeling respected, included and encouraged is leadership at its best.
scenarios.relearn: The example worth leaving makes people feel respected and included.
Equal treatment and fair sharing set the example; mocking and credit-taking undercut it.

scenarios.hook: A capable but shy classmate keeps getting overlooked.

steps.prompt: A school quiz team is picking members this week. What do you do?

options.text: Encourage her to try, and offer to practise
options.then: She hesitates, then nods. You set up a first practice for Saturday.

options.text: Focus on your own try-out
options.then: Your try-out goes well. She doesn't turn up.

options.text: Put her name forward without asking her
options.then: She's startled and says she can't. She's upset you didn't ask.

options.text: Tell her to just be braver about it
options.then: She nods and stares at her shoes. She's still unsure.

steps.why: Encouraging her and practising together gives a push without taking over.

steps.prompt: She says she'd like to join something but fears being laughed at. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to go with her, and ask what helps
options.then: She breathes out. "Just sit near me at first."

options.text: Tell her no one will laugh
options.then: She nods, unconvinced. You can't promise that.

options.text: Tell her to ignore what others think
options.then: She smiles weakly. It's easier said than done.

options.text: Offer to join and do the talking for her
options.then: She's relieved at first, then quiet. Everyone hears your voice, not hers.

steps.why: Offering company and asking what helps lifts her without speaking for her.

steps.prompt: She gets a chance to speak at a meeting and looks to you. What do you do?

options.text: Nod to her, and let her say it herself
options.then: She takes a breath and begins. The room listens.

options.text: Say it for her to save time
options.then: You say it well. She sits back, feeling it wasn't hers.

options.text: Tell the others to be quiet for her
options.then: The room goes silent and stares at her. It makes things harder.

options.text: Look away so she doesn't feel watched
options.then: She waits for a sign. The moment passes.

steps.why: Letting her speak in her own words builds her confidence.

scenarios.debrief: Mentoring someone with less confidence is leadership in action.
scenarios.relearn: Lift as you climb: mentor and encourage those who get overlooked.

scenarios.hook: At a club meeting, Hema's idea is ignored and then another member repeats it.

steps.prompt: The president praises the second speaker. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Nice. That was Hema's idea earlier."
options.then: The president turns to Hema. "Oh, I missed that. Go on."

options.text: Say nothing, to avoid causing a scene
options.then: The praise stands. Hema's face falls.

options.text: Message Hema later to say you're sorry
options.then: She appreciates it. The meeting still credits someone else.

options.text: Say loudly that he copied Hema's idea
options.then: The room freezes. He protests it was an honest mistake.

steps.why: Crediting the original voice is a simple, powerful lift.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, he asks if that idea was Hema's, saying he honestly didn't hear it earlier. What do you say?

options.text: Say it happens, and ask him to credit others
options.then: He nods. "Fair. I'll check who said it first."

options.text: Tell him he did it on purpose
options.then: He bristles. "I didn't!"

options.text: Say it's fine and drop it
options.then: He relaxes. The habit stays.

options.text: Tell him to apologise to Hema before everyone
options.then: He mumbles it in front of the club. Hema looks mortified.

steps.why: Assuming good faith and naming the habit helps him do better.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, Hema has a new idea but hesitates. What do you do?

options.text: Invite her to share it, and listen
options.then: She shares. People nod and the president notes her name.

options.text: Wait to see if she speaks up on her own
options.then: She stays silent. The meeting moves on.

options.text: Present her idea yourself so she's spared
options.then: It goes down well. Hema smiles, but feels she has vanished from it.

options.text: Tell her to speak louder so people hear
options.then: She nods and shrinks further.

steps.why: Opening space for her turns one-off credit into a lasting habit.

scenarios.debrief: Amplifying and crediting a talked-over voice is everyday leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Credit the person whose idea it was; amplify talked-over voices.

scenarios.hook: A girl in your group was steered away from a subject she's great at.

steps.prompt: She says she'll drop physics because a teacher called it tough for girls. What do you do?

options.text: Encourage her to stay and offer to study together
options.then: She thinks it over. "Maybe. Let's try one chapter."

options.text: Assume she's made her choice
options.then: She hands in the form. You wonder if she'll miss it.

options.text: Tell the teacher in front of everyone that he's wrong
options.then: The class tenses. She's mortified to be the centre of it.

options.text: Say she can always return to it later
options.then: She smiles. Later rarely comes.

steps.why: Backing her and studying together keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Her parents ask you whether physics is a good idea for her. What do you say?

options.text: Say you've seen her work and it's strong
options.then: They look surprised, then thoughtful. "We didn't know."

options.text: Say it's their decision
options.then: They nod. The conversation ends there.

options.text: Say it's a hard subject for anyone
options.then: They exchange a look. "Then maybe not."

options.text: Tell them they're being old-fashioned
options.then: They stiffen. The conversation ends coldly.

steps.why: Sharing what you've seen of her work respects the family and informs the choice.

steps.prompt: In your study group, she asks a physics question out of curiosity, and a boy snickers. What do you do?

options.text: Answer her question and say it's fair
options.then: She relaxes. The snickering boy looks down at his book.

options.text: Ignore it so it doesn't escalate
options.then: She goes quiet. She asks fewer questions.

options.text: Tell the boy off in front of the group
options.then: He mutters. The group turns uncomfortable.

options.text: Tell her to ask you privately instead
options.then: She nods. She stops asking in the group.

steps.why: Treating her question as normal makes asking safe for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Opening a door someone was pushed from is real leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Encourage people toward roles and subjects they were steered from.

scenarios.hook: In a team meeting, a quieter teammate, Priya, made a point that nobody picked up.
scenarios.setup: The meeting is nearly over.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "Any other ideas before we decide?"

options.text: "Priya raised something earlier. Priya, say more?"
options.then: The teacher turns. "Priya? Please go on."

options.text: "No, I think we've covered it. Shall we vote?"
options.then: The teacher nods and starts closing the meeting.

options.text: "I'll explain Priya's idea to save us some time."
options.then: The teacher nods. Priya sits quietly while you explain it.

options.text: "Maybe someone should ask Priya what she meant."
options.then: The teacher looks around. Nobody moves.

steps.why: Handing the floor to Priya lets her own her idea.

steps.prompt: The next day, Priya says: "I have ideas, but I never know how to jump in."

options.text: "Let's agree a signal. I'll pass you the floor."
options.then: Priya smiles. "A signal. Okay, that might work."

options.text: "Just say it louder next time."
options.then: She shrugs. "Easy for you to say."

options.text: "I'll just say your ideas for you from now on."
options.then: Priya hesitates. "But then they'd be coming from you."

options.text: "It's fine. Good ideas always get heard."
options.then: She nods, but doesn't look convinced.

steps.why: A shared signal gives her control over when she speaks.

steps.prompt: With Priya beside you, another teammate asks: "Does it matter who gets heard in meetings? People can speak for themselves."

options.text: "Good ideas get lost in loud rooms. It could be anyone."
options.then: He pauses. "Fair. I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Fine. Maybe it doesn't matter."
options.then: He shrugs. The next time a quiet voice goes unheard, nobody says a word.

options.text: "Priya, can you explain to him why this matters?"
options.then: Priya looks mortified. He rolls his eyes.

options.text: "Mind your own business."
options.then: He holds up his hands and goes cold on the project.

steps.why: Explaining why you amplify others shows it's about fairness, not favour.

scenarios.relearn: Handing the mic back to a quieter voice amplifies them.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Rhea is hesitant about a chance that has come her way.
scenarios.setup: Before class, she hesitates beside you.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "They asked me to lead the club. I'm not really the type."

options.text: "You'd be great. I'll back you if you go for it."
options.then: Rhea smiles nervously. "Really? You'd back me?"

options.text: "Maybe it's not for you, honestly. It's a lot of work."
options.then: Her face falls. "Yeah. That's what I thought."

options.text: "Everyone says that at first. Just say yes already."
options.then: She frowns. "It's not that simple."

options.text: "I'll lead it for now, and you can join in later."
options.then: Rhea shrugs. "Okay. That's easier, I guess. But they asked me."

steps.why: Honest belief plus an offer of backing helps her step up.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Rhea asks: "What if I say yes and mess up in front of everyone?"

options.text: "Then we fix it together. Everyone fumbles at first."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "Okay. Together sounds better."

options.text: "You won't mess up. Trust me. You'll be perfect."
options.then: She winces. "That's a lot of pressure."

options.text: "Then someone else can step in and take over."
options.then: Rhea nods slowly. "So I should have a backup plan to quit."

options.text: "Just act confident and nobody will ever notice."
options.then: She laughs, unconvinced. "I can't fake that."

steps.why: Sharing the risk makes a first try feel safe.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "My uncle thinks clubs like this are for boys."

options.text: "Invite him to a club session. Let him see it."
options.then: Rhea laughs. "He'd hate to admit it, but he'd come."

options.text: "Your uncle is wrong. Just ignore what he says."
options.then: Rhea sighs. "He's family. I can't just ignore him."

options.text: "Maybe skip it, to keep things calm at home."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Maybe you're right. Maybe it's not worth it."

options.text: "Tell him that's old-fashioned and walk off."
options.then: Rhea winces. "That would only make things worse at home."

steps.why: Showing the work persuades family better than arguing.

scenarios.relearn: Genuine encouragement plus backing helps someone step up.

scenarios.hook: Your team wins the inter-school quiz, and you're the one being praised.
scenarios.setup: In the staff room, your teacher lines up the photo.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Well done. You did all the work, didn't you?"

options.text: "It was a team effort, especially Anil and Meena."
options.then: The teacher blinks. "Anil, Meena, come here, both of you."

options.text: "Thanks. I did prepare the most, honestly."
options.then: The teacher beams. "I knew it. Smile for the photo."

options.text: "Thank you. I couldn't have done it without the team."
options.then: The teacher nods and moves on. Nobody else is named.

options.text: "Thanks. Let's not make a fuss in front of everyone."
options.then: The teacher laughs. "Modest too. Come, the photo."

steps.why: Naming the people who helped makes the credit real.

steps.prompt: The newsletter editor asks: "Who should I list as the team?"

options.text: "All four of us. I'll send the names and roles."
options.then: She types it in. "Send them by tonight, please."

options.text: "Just put my name, and I'll mention the rest."
options.then: She writes your name. "Easy. I'll add them if there's space."

options.text: "The whole class. It's simpler that way."
options.then: She shrugs. "Fine. The whole class it is."

options.text: "List whoever you think. I don't mind."
options.then: She nods and lists the three people she remembers.

steps.why: A full list with roles lets everyone's work be seen.

steps.prompt: A junior says: "Could I join the quiz team next year? I'm not a topper."

options.text: "Yes. Come to practice, and we'll show you how."
options.then: Her face brightens. "Really? When do you meet?"

options.text: "Maybe. Usually only the toppers make it."
options.then: Her face falls. "Oh. Then I won't bother."

options.text: "Ask the teacher. I don't pick the team."
options.then: She nods, unsure she should ask a teacher. She doesn't.

options.text: "We already have enough people for next year."
options.then: She says okay and walks away quietly.

steps.why: Opening the team to a newcomer passes on the chance you had.

scenarios.relearn: Sharing credit lifts others and builds trust.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: real leadership is measured by who rises with you. Sit with that.
scenarios.affirm: Lifting others as you go, that's the truest measure of a leader.
scenarios.relearn: Real leadership is measured by who rises with you.

scenarios.hook: You hear of a school magazine spot, and a talented friend hasn't heard.

steps.prompt: You're free to apply this week. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her about it and suggest she applies too
options.then: She looks startled. "Me? Maybe." She asks for the form.

options.text: Apply and keep quiet about it
options.then: You get a place. She finds out later and says nothing.

options.text: Apply and tell her after the results
options.then: She's pleased for you. The form closed days ago.

options.text: Tell her it's very competitive so she needn't try
options.then: She nods and gives up on the idea.

steps.why: Telling her in time hands over a real chance, not just good news.

steps.prompt: The teacher says there's one more place and asks for suggestions. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest your friend and say why her writing fits
options.then: The teacher notes her name and asks to see her work.

options.text: Say it should go to whoever applied first
options.then: The teacher agrees. Your friend isn't mentioned.

options.text: Say you can't decide and leave it
options.then: The teacher picks someone else without much thought.

options.text: Suggest someone popular who would draw readers
options.then: The teacher likes it. A louder student gets the place.

steps.why: Naming her with a reason gives the teacher something real to act on.

steps.prompt: Months later, a younger student asks how to get a spot in the school magazine. What do you say?

options.text: Share what you know about applying and read their draft
options.then: They light up. "Really? Can I show you on Friday?"

options.text: Say it's mostly luck
options.then: They look discouraged. They don't try.

options.text: Say they should find their own way
options.then: They shrug. They've no idea where to start.

options.text: Send them to the teacher with no more help
options.then: The teacher is busy. They give up after one try.

steps.why: Sharing how it works makes the platform bigger than just you.

scenarios.debrief: Deliberately shared opportunity is exactly how gaps actually close.
scenarios.relearn: Share opportunity and platforms with those who'd benefit.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: who lifted you, and could you do that for someone else?
scenarios.affirm: Passing on the lift you got is how leadership multiplies.
scenarios.relearn: You can pass on the lift others gave you to someone else.

scenarios.hook: A talented friend won't apply for something, sure she'll be rejected.

steps.prompt: She says she's not even going to try. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what worries her, then help her prepare
options.then: She admits she fears being judged. You jot down what to practise.

options.text: Agree it's a long shot, so she isn't hurt
options.then: She nods, relieved. A few days on, she's still thinking about it.

options.text: Promise her she'll definitely get in
options.then: She smiles, but she's more scared now. She still keeps thinking about it.

options.text: Fill out the form for her
options.then: She's shocked and feels pushed. She asks you to give it back.

steps.why: Asking what worries her and helping her prepare makes trying feel possible.

steps.prompt: A few days later, she says she might apply but fears the interview. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to run a practice interview with her
options.then: She laughs nervously, then agrees. You pick a Saturday.

options.text: Tell her interviews are easy
options.then: She frowns. If it's easy, why is she so scared?

options.text: Send her tip videos and leave it there
options.then: She watches one, then freezes at the next. She applies anyway, shakily.

options.text: Say she can skip it and apply next year
options.then: She sighs, relieved. Then the deadline is extended, and the question returns.

steps.why: A practice run turns fear into something she can rehearse.

steps.prompt: She's offered a place and says she isn't sure she deserves it. What do you do?

options.text: Name two things she did that earned it
options.then: She goes quiet, then nods. "I did do those."

options.text: Tell her not to be silly
options.then: She laughs weakly. The doubt stays.

options.text: Tell her she can always say no
options.then: She nods. The place hangs in the air.

options.text: Say she's lucky to have been picked
options.then: Her face falls. It makes her feel more like a fluke.

steps.why: Naming what she actually did helps her believe it was earned.

scenarios.debrief: A nudge and some help can change whether someone even tries.
scenarios.relearn: Encourage a doubting friend to try, and help them prepare.

scenarios.hook: You notice a teammate, Karthik, is always given the background tasks.
scenarios.setup: During planning, the group is handing out parts.

steps.prompt: Your group leader asks: "Okay, who wants to lead the next section?"

options.text: "Karthik should lead it. He's earned a turn."
options.then: The leader looks at him. "Karthik? Are you up for it?"

options.text: "I'll take it. Karthik can do the slides again."
options.then: The leader nods. Karthik opens his laptop without a word.

options.text: "Whoever wants it. I don't mind either way."
options.then: A louder teammate says yes. Karthik stays quiet.

options.text: "Let's draw lots, so nobody can complain."
options.then: Names go into a bag. The draw is fair, but the pattern is untouched.

steps.why: Naming him for a bigger role breaks the pattern.

steps.prompt: Later, Karthik says quietly: "I've only done the small tasks. I wouldn't know how to lead."

options.text: "You've held this together. I'll help you plan."
options.then: He looks up. "Okay. Maybe I can try."

options.text: "Then I'll lead it myself. No pressure."
options.then: He relaxes, but the tasks stay where they were.

options.text: "You can't stay in the background forever."
options.then: He stiffens. "I didn't say I wanted to."

options.text: "It's fine. Do the slides again. Nobody minds."
options.then: He nods. "Sure." He doesn't look happy.

steps.why: Naming his real contribution and offering help builds his confidence.

steps.prompt: The leader says: "Maybe it's easier if we keep roles as they were."

options.text: "Easier isn't fair. Let's rotate roles."
options.then: The leader thinks. "A rotation. Okay, let's try it."

options.text: "Okay, easier works. Let's just finish."
options.then: The leader smiles. The old roles are back, and Karthik is too.

options.text: "Fine, but I'll do the hard parts myself."
options.then: The leader nods. "Good. Less arguing."

options.text: "Let's ask the teacher to decide."
options.then: The leader shrugs. The teacher says, "Work it out yourselves."

steps.why: A rotation shares chances fairly instead of freezing old roles.

scenarios.relearn: Offering someone a bigger role breaks a limiting pattern.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: lifting one person well can ripple out to many. Believe it?
scenarios.affirm: Lift one person, and they often go on to lift others, that's how it spreads.
scenarios.relearn: Lifting one person well can ripple out to many.
Mentoring, amplifying, sharing opportunity, crediting and encouraging each lift someone concretely.
scenarios.hook: Match the lift to what it does.
Your group's project is a success, and you did the final polish.

steps.prompt: The head asks who made it happen. What do you say?

options.text: Name everyone and what each of them did
options.then: Teammates sit up as their names are read out.

options.text: Say it was mostly you, since you finished it
options.then: She writes down your name alone.

options.text: Say it was a team effort, with no names
options.then: She smiles and moves on. Nobody's name is written.

options.text: Name only the people the head already knows
options.then: Her list is short. The quieter members aren't on it.

steps.why: Naming each person lets them be seen, and builds trust in you.

steps.prompt: A teammate says she'd like to put the project in her portfolio. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and offer a line on what she did
options.then: She grins. "Please. Mention the survey part."

options.text: Say it's mostly your work, so be careful
options.then: She goes red and says no more.

options.text: Say yes, and add that you led it
options.then: She nods slowly. The line makes her part look smaller.

options.text: Say you'll check with the others first
options.then: She waits. Nobody answers for days.

steps.why: A specific line of credit helps her get recognised by others too.

steps.prompt: A teacher asks you to lead the next project and choose your team. What do you do?

options.text: Pick people by skill, and give each a clear role
options.then: Each person gets a title and a task. They look pleased.

options.text: Pick your best friends so it's easy
options.then: It runs smoothly. Two strong classmates feel left out.

options.text: Pick the people who made you look good
options.then: The team is loyal but uneven. Weak spots go unnoticed.

options.text: Let the teacher choose to avoid hurt feelings
options.then: The teacher picks quickly. You lead a team you didn't shape.

steps.why: Visible roles let each person be seen, which keeps teams strong.

scenarios.debrief: Generosity with credit is a quiet superpower of good leaders.
scenarios.relearn: Name everyone who helped; generous credit lifts people.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'lift as you climb', could that be your leadership motto?
scenarios.affirm: Lift as you climb, a motto that makes everyone, including you, rise.
scenarios.relearn: 'Lift as you climb' is leadership that makes everyone rise.

scenarios.hook: "Publicly shaming someone is the best way to change them."

myth.un: Publicly shaming someone is the best way to change them.
myth.re: A respectful 'call-in', often private and good-faith, changes minds better than a shaming 'call-out'.
myth.why: Shame usually makes people defensive and dig in.

scenarios.relearn: A respectful call-in changes minds better than public shaming.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Karan says girls are too emotional to lead, probably without thinking.

steps.prompt: The others nod along. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him privately it didn't sit right
options.then: Karan frowns, then shrugs. "Oh. I just repeat what I hear."

options.text: Call him sexist in front of everyone
options.then: Karan's face hardens. He says you're overreacting, and the others go quiet.

options.text: Laugh it off and say nothing
options.then: The talk moves on. Karan takes your silence as agreement.

options.text: Complain about him to a mutual friend
options.then: Your friend agrees he's a bit much. Karan never hears a word of it.

steps.why: A private word gives him room to rethink without losing face.

steps.prompt: Days later, Karan says again that girls are too emotional to lead. What do you do?

options.text: Say you know he means well, but it lands badly
options.then: He pauses. "Lands badly how?" It's the first real question he's asked.

options.text: Roll your eyes and let it pass
options.then: Karan keeps going and gets a few more laughs, but he notices your face.

options.text: Tell him he's hopeless and walk off
options.then: Karan shouts after you that you can't take a joke.

options.text: Warn him you'll drop the friendship if he repeats it
options.then: Karan goes stiff. "Over one comment?" He stays wary of you.

steps.why: Assuming good faith while naming the impact keeps him listening.

steps.prompt: Later, Karan asks what bothers you so much about it. What do you say?

options.text: Say remarks like that put down girls who lead well
options.then: Karan thinks of Meera running the fest. "Yeah. She does," he admits.

options.text: Say everyone says so these days, so he should too
options.then: Karan shrugs. A reason borrowed from others doesn't move him.

options.text: Say it doesn't matter and drop the whole thing
options.then: He nods, relieved. The talk ends where it began.

options.text: Hand him an article and tell him to go read it
options.then: He takes it. It ends up unread at the bottom of his bag.

steps.why: Your own reason is something he can think about, not argue with.

scenarios.debrief: Assuming good faith and talking privately is the persuasive route.
scenarios.relearn: Call a friend in privately and in good faith, not out publicly.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Yash cracks a sexist joke at the canteen table.
scenarios.setup: Everyone laughs except Tanvi, and then he looks at you.

steps.prompt: Yash grins and asks: "That was funny, right?"

options.text: "Hey, that one didn't sit right with me. Can we not?"
options.then: Yash's grin slips. "Oh. Okay. I didn't mean anything by it."

options.text: "Ha, yeah. Good one, Yash. You're too much."
options.then: Yash beams and looks for the next laugh.

options.text: "Wow, you're such a sexist. Everyone, listen up."
options.then: The table goes silent. Yash snaps, "Chill out, I was joking."

options.text: "Ha. Whatever. Dev would never laugh at that."
options.then: Yash laughs, unbothered. "Dev is no fun anyway."

steps.why: A short, low-drama line is clear without starting a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, Yash says: "Tanvi's been quiet with me since lunch. Was the joke that bad?"

options.text: "I know you didn't mean harm. It just lands badly."
options.then: He frowns, thinking. "Lands badly on who?"

options.text: "Honestly, it doesn't matter. Forget it."
options.then: Yash relaxes. The joke stays as it was.

options.text: "Honestly? You're being a jerk."
options.then: Yash's face closes. "Okay, relax."

options.text: "It was bad. Say it again and I'm done with you."
options.then: Yash stares. "Wow. Okay, then." He backs off, and he's wary of you now.

steps.why: Assuming good faith while naming the impact keeps him listening.

steps.prompt: Yash adds: "Anyway, my other friends joke like this all the time."

options.text: "Maybe. I'd still like us to be better than that."
options.then: He laughs awkwardly. "Better than that. Okay."

options.text: "Then they're all sexist, and so are you."
options.then: Yash stiffens. "Forget it."

options.text: "Okay, then I guess it's fine."
options.then: Yash nods. The joke counts as normal.

options.text: "I'll tell them that too, at lunch tomorrow."
options.then: Yash's face drops. "Please don't make a scene."

steps.why: Setting your own bar, kindly, doesn't need anyone else to agree.

steps.prompt: Later that day, Yash texts: "Are we cool?"

options.text: "Yes, we're cool. I'd just rather we skipped jokes like that."
options.then: He sends a thumbs up. "Cool. See you at lunch."

options.text: "We'll see. Prove you've changed."
options.then: He sends a flat "ok". It's hard to read.

options.text: "Whatever. I'm busy right now."
options.then: He doesn't reply. The silence stays.

options.text: "No. I'm telling everyone how you reacted."
options.then: He sends three question marks. Then nothing.

steps.why: A warm, honest reply keeps the friendship and the point together.

scenarios.relearn: A short 'That didn't sit right. Can we not?' is a clear, low-drama call-in.

scenarios.hook: In your study group, Rahul keeps interrupting the girls.
scenarios.setup: Sana is mid-answer when he cuts in.

steps.prompt: Rahul talks over her: "What Sana means is..."

options.text: "Let's let her finish. I want to hear the whole point."
options.then: Rahul blinks. "Oh. Sure. Go ahead, Sana." Sana picks up her point.

options.text: "Ha, Rahul can't help himself, can he?"
options.then: The group laughs. Rahul smiles stiffly, and Sana never gets back to her point.

options.text: "It's fine, Rahul. Sana's idea is basically yours anyway."
options.then: Rahul nods, satisfied. Sana's idea is now his.

options.text: "Rahul, shut up and let people talk."
options.then: Rahul flushes. The group goes quiet, and nobody finishes a thought.

steps.why: Handing the floor back is calm, clear and doesn't shame him.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, Sana says quietly: "He does that to me a lot."

options.text: "That sounds frustrating. How can I help?"
options.then: She thinks. "Keep doing that. Maybe have a word with him."

options.text: "He doesn't mean it. He's just excited."
options.then: Sana nods and says no more.

options.text: "You should just speak louder."
options.then: Sana's face falls. "I do. He's louder."

options.text: "Ignore him. He's not worth it."
options.then: Sana gives a thin smile. It doesn't change the next meeting.

steps.why: Listening, and asking how she wants help, keeps the choice hers.

steps.prompt: After class, Rahul catches up with you: "Did I do something wrong back there?"

options.text: "You cut Sana off a few times. I'd like to hear her."
options.then: He rubs his neck. "Didn't notice. I'll watch it."

options.text: "No, nothing at all. It's fine."
options.then: Rahul shrugs and heads off, though he looks like he's turning it over.

options.text: "Yes. You're a bully, honestly. Everyone sees it."
options.then: Rahul's jaw tightens. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "Sana's upset with you. Go and fix it right now."
options.then: He goes off stiffly and apologises without knowing why.

steps.why: A specific, kind answer lets him fix it.

steps.prompt: A week later, Rahul finds you and says: "I keep thinking about it. I talk over everyone, don't I? Any tips?"

options.text: "Count to three before jumping in. I'll help."
options.then: He laughs. "Okay. Three. Deal."

options.text: "Just stop being so loud all the time."
options.then: He nods, but looks lost about how to do that.

options.text: "Don't worry. You'll grow out of it one day."
options.then: Rahul shrugs. Nothing about the next meeting changes.

options.text: "Nope, you're hopeless. Forget the tips."
options.then: Rahul laughs, but he's hurt.

steps.why: Offering a small, practical tool turns good intentions into a habit.

scenarios.relearn: A calm 'let her finish' redirects without shaming.

scenarios.hook: You spoke up about Ishaan's remark in the club meeting, and now he digs in.

steps.prompt: He says you're making a scene. What do you do?

options.text: Drop it for now and offer to talk later
options.then: Ishaan relaxes a little. "Fine, later," he mutters.

options.text: Push harder so the club sees he's wrong
options.then: The club watches in silence. Ishaan crosses his arms and won't budge.

options.text: Apologise for speaking up and call it nothing
options.then: Ishaan nods, satisfied. The remark stays, and so does the knot in your stomach.

options.text: Ask the other members to say what they think
options.then: Two members mumble. Ishaan feels ganged up on.

steps.why: Letting him save face in public keeps change possible.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, Ishaan packs up alone. What do you do?

options.text: Say you didn't mean to shame him, and ask to explain
options.then: He hesitates, then nods. "Okay. Go on."

options.text: Pretend nothing happened and talk about the fest
options.then: He's relieved. Neither of you mentions the remark that day.

options.text: Post in the club group that he was wrong
options.then: Ishaan's phone buzzes. He reads it and says nothing in the group.

options.text: Tell him he was out of line and must apologise
options.then: He bristles. "I'm not apologising to you."

steps.why: A calm, private opening lets him listen without an audience.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Ishaan tells you the remark didn't seem like a big deal. What do you say?

options.text: "I get that. For some girls here it adds up."
options.then: Ishaan goes quiet. "I hadn't thought about it adding up."

options.text: "Then you're not very thoughtful."
options.then: Ishaan's jaw sets. The conversation ends right there.

options.text: "Okay, whatever you think."
options.then: He nods and leaves. The remark goes unquestioned.

options.text: "Just say sorry to the girls and we're done."
options.then: He agrees stiffly. He will apologise without knowing why.

steps.why: Explaining how it adds up gives him something real to think about.

scenarios.debrief: Letting someone save face in private makes change possible.
scenarios.relearn: If someone digs in publicly, follow up privately and in good faith.

scenarios.hook: "Calling in is just being soft and letting things slide."

myth.un: Calling in is just being soft and letting it slide.
myth.re: It's firm about the issue and kind to the person; it still names the problem clearly.
myth.why: You can be clear and respectful at once.

scenarios.relearn: Calling in is firm on the issue and kind to the person, not soft.

scenarios.hook: You hear Dev say something harmful about girls in your hostel. It is more than clumsy.

steps.prompt: A few people look away uneasily. What do you do?

options.text: Say clearly that this isn't okay and you won't join in
options.then: Dev goes red. The room is silent, and nobody laughs.

options.text: Smile and stay gentle so there's no friction

options.text: Joke back lightly so it feels like banter

options.text: Wait and mention it to a friend afterwards

steps.prompt: That evening Dev tells you it was only a joke and nobody minds. What do you do?

options.text: Say calmly that it's not okay, and say why
options.then: Dev scoffs, but he doesn't say it again.

options.text: Say "Fine, forget it" to end the tension

options.text: Shout at him until he backs down

options.text: Say it's fine and ask him to just be careful

steps.prompt: The next day, you see Dev alone in the corridor. What do you do?

options.text: Go over, stay friendly, and say plainly why it mattered
options.then: Dev relaxes. "I didn't realise how it sounded," he says.

options.text: Ignore him until he comes to you

scenarios.hook: Someone in your circle often says harsh things about girls, and he gets angry when challenged.

steps.prompt: He's making another remark right now, and you feel uneasy. What do you do?

options.text: Step away, and tell a trusted adult later

options.text: Post about his remarks in the class chat

options.text: Mock him back so the others laugh at him

options.text: Keep it short and calm, then walk toward friends

options.text: Tell him he's a bully and needs to change

options.text: Laugh in his face and turn your back on him

options.text: Tell her what's been happening and ask for help

scenarios.debrief: Challenging is for safe moments. When it isn't safe, step away and get help, and it is never your fault.

scenarios.hook: Your cousin Nitin forwards a sexist joke to the family group.
scenarios.setup: You call him that evening, hoping to keep it friendly.

steps.prompt: Nitin answers: "Hey, what's up? You sounded annoyed in the chat."

options.text: "I don't think you meant it badly. Here's how it landed."
options.then: Nitin goes quiet. "How did it land? Tell me."

options.text: "You're a sexist, and I'm going to tell the whole family."
options.then: Nitin goes cold. "Don't call me that."

options.text: "Nothing. I just wanted to say hi."
options.then: Nitin chats happily, then pauses. "Wait, is this about that forward?"

options.text: "Your jokes embarrass the whole family."
options.then: Nitin gets defensive. "Okay, wow, thanks."

steps.prompt: Nitin says: "It's only a forward. I didn't even write it."

options.text: "I know. But when we forward it, we spread it too."
options.then: He sighs. "Hmm. Fair. I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Right, so it's not your fault. Sorry I called."
options.then: Nitin relaxes, then pauses. "Wait, did the family actually mind it?"

options.text: "That's a weak excuse, Nitin."
options.then: Nitin stiffens. "Why are you attacking me?"

options.text: "Then tell whoever sent it to stop."
options.then: Nitin shrugs. "I'd have to find who sent it first."

steps.why: Showing that forwarding spreads it helps him see his part.

steps.prompt: Nitin says: "The aunties laughed at it, though."

options.text: "Some just laugh to be polite. Let's be kind."
options.then: He gives a soft laugh. "Kind. Okay, I can do kind."

options.text: "Then the aunties are wrong too, all of them."
options.then: Nitin gasps. "You can't say that about Aunty!"

options.text: "Okay, then I guess it's fine."
options.then: He nods, and his next forward is worse.

options.text: "Then tell the aunties yourself."
options.then: Nitin groans. "Me? Why me?"

steps.why: Setting a kinder standard doesn't need to blame anyone else.

scenarios.relearn: Assuming good faith and explaining the impact invites change.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: calling in takes more patience than calling out, but works better. Worth it?

scenarios.hook: You want to lead on equality but aren't sure where to start.

steps.prompt: It's Sunday evening and you're planning your week. What do you do?

options.text: Pick one small, specific action to do this week

options.text: Wait until you feel fully ready
options.then: Sunday turns into Monday. The idea slides down your to-do list.

options.text: Make a long list of everything you'll change

options.text: Tell your friends you're going to change the school

steps.prompt: Midweek, a friend asks what you're actually doing about equality. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're still working out the big picture

options.text: Share a post about equality to show you care

options.text: Say you don't want to make a fuss about it
options.then: She shrugs and lets it go.

steps.prompt: It's Friday and the week is almost over. What do you do?

options.text: Do one small action tonight, even a tiny one

options.text: Wait for next week and start fresh
options.then: Next week arrives with its own list. The idea waits again.

options.text: Decide leading probably isn't for you

options.text: Do five big things tonight to make up for it

steps.prompt: Next Sunday you plan the week again. What do you do?

scenarios.hook: You want to lead on equality this term and aren't sure where to put your energy.

options.text: Wait for a big public stage
options.then: Weeks pass. No stage appears, and nothing starts.

options.text: Say you'll lead the whole school

scenarios.hook: You want your friend Tanvi to lead a fair-roles project alongside you.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Lead the project? I'm not sure I'm the leader type."

options.text: "Let's set the tone together. It's better with two."
options.then: Tanvi smiles. "With you? Okay, maybe."

options.text: "Then I'll just do the whole thing myself, no problem."
options.then: Tanvi nods, relieved, and looks a bit guilty. You feel the weight of it alone.

options.text: "You're right. Leaders have to be loud, and you're not."
options.then: Tanvi's face falls. "I know. That's what I thought." She goes quiet, then looks up.

options.text: "You have to do it. Nobody else will step up."
options.then: Tanvi stiffens. "That's not a reason I want."

steps.prompt: Tanvi asks: "If I did lead, what would I even do?"

options.text: "What do you enjoy most? Let's build from that."
options.then: Tanvi thinks. "I like organising the schedule."

options.text: "Mostly just agree with whatever I say."
options.then: Tanvi shrugs. "Then I'm not really leading."

options.text: "Everything. I'll tell you the details later."
options.then: Tanvi looks uneasy. "That sounds like a lot."

options.text: "Nothing much. I only need your name on it."
options.then: Tanvi frowns. "I'd want it to be real."

steps.why: Starting from her strengths makes her role real.

steps.prompt: Tanvi says: "Okay. But what if people ignore us?"

options.text: "Then we start small and bring in one more."
options.then: Tanvi relaxes. "Small I can do."

options.text: "Then we push harder until they listen."
options.then: Tanvi winces. "That sounds exhausting."

options.text: "They won't. Everyone likes us."
options.then: Tanvi laughs, but she's not sure.

options.text: "Then I'll tell everyone exactly how it should be."

scenarios.hook: Lensy: which part of leading do you most want to grow?
