scenarios.relearn: Name the harm to a friend quietly instead of mocking them back.

scenarios.hook: Your teammate Ishan keeps needling you about backing the girls on the team.
scenarios.setup: He starts in again after practice, with the whole team listening.

steps.prompt: Ishan smirks: "Admit it. You only do this to impress the girls."

options.text: "Nah. It's basic fairness. Costs me nothing."
options.then: Ishan shrugs, a bit less sure. "Okay. It just seems weird."

options.text: "That's not true. Look at all the things I've done!"
options.then: Ishan grins. You sound defensive, and he knows it.

options.text: "Maybe a bit. Does it matter?"
options.then: Ishan laughs. He feels proved right.

options.text: "At least I do something, unlike you."
options.then: Ishan's face tightens. "Wow. Okay."

steps.why: A calm, simple answer needs no proof.

steps.prompt: Ishan says: "Boys who back equality are just soft."

options.text: "I'd say it takes more spine than going along."
options.then: Ishan snorts, then grins. "Spine. Okay, I'll give you that."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Forget I said it."
options.then: Ishan smirks. He feels he's won.

options.text: "You're the soft one, always scared of girls."
options.then: Ishan snaps back, and the talk dissolves into trading digs.

options.text: "I don't care what you think."
options.then: Ishan shrugs and walks off.

steps.why: Backing someone's fair shot takes more spine than going along.

steps.prompt: Another day, Ishan catches you alone and asks: "Seriously, what do you get out of it?"

options.text: "A better team, where everyone gets a fair shot."
options.then: Ishan thinks. "Our relay did get better after Priya joined."

options.text: "Nothing. I'm just trying to be a good person."
options.then: Ishan rolls his eyes. "Okay, saint."

options.text: "Friends. Girls like guys who are like me."
options.then: Ishan grins. He thinks he's been right all along.

options.text: "You'll never get it, so why would I explain?"
options.then: Ishan shrugs. He keeps his view.

steps.why: A fairer team is something he can see for himself.

steps.prompt: Ishan says: "My sister wants to try out for the team. Would they let her?"

options.text: "She should try. I'll cheer, and I'll practise with her."
options.then: Ishan's face softens. "She'd love that."

options.text: "If she can keep up with the boys, sure."
options.then: Ishan nods. The bar for his sister is now higher.

options.text: "Let her try. The team might not like it, though."
options.then: Ishan frowns. "Then why bother?"

options.text: "Tell her to ask the coach herself."
options.then: Ishan nods slowly. She faces it alone.

steps.why: Offering real backing shows what you stand for.

scenarios.relearn: A calm 'it's just fairness' answers the dig without getting defensive.

scenarios.hook: At home, only your sister is expected to clear the dishes after dinner.

steps.prompt: Dinner ends, and everyone leaves the table. What do you do?

options.text: Quietly start clearing the dishes yourself
options.then: Your sister looks up in surprise. Your mother says nothing but watches.

options.text: Announce that chores should be equal, then do none
options.then: Your family stares. Your sister clears the dishes as before.

options.text: Wait for your parents to fix it
options.then: They don't notice. The dishes stay with your sister.

options.text: Offer to help only if your sister asks
options.then: She doesn't ask. She's used to doing it alone.

steps.why: Quietly doing your share teaches more than any speech.

steps.prompt: The next evening you offer to help. Your sister says she's used to it and doesn't need you. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want to do your share, and start anyway
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay. Dry, then." She hands you a cloth.

options.text: Say fine and step back
options.then: She goes back to doing it alone. The habit stays.

options.text: Say you're only helping her out this once
options.then: She smiles tightly. It still sounds like a favour.

options.text: Tell her she should refuse to do them
options.then: Your sister frowns. "Tell Mum that, then."

steps.why: Doing your share anyway shows it isn't a favour.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your father says dishes aren't a boy's job. What do you say?

options.text: Say they're everyone's job, and do your share
options.then: He grunts. "Hmm." Your mother hides a smile.

options.text: Say you'll leave them to your sister, then
options.then: He nods, satisfied. The old split stays.

options.text: Say he should wash up himself for once
options.then: He stiffens. "Watch your tone."

options.text: Argue about whose job it is until the kitchen goes tense
options.then: Everyone goes quiet. The dishes wait for your sister.

steps.why: Calmly saying it's everyone's job, and doing your share, changes the norm.

scenarios.debrief: Sharing a chore visibly and unasked teaches more than any lecture about fairness.
scenarios.relearn: Picking up a 'girls' chore yourself, unasked, shifts the home norm more than a speech.

scenarios.hook: The teacher steps out, and a few classmates start mocking a shy boy.

steps.prompt: The laughing grows louder and he goes red. What do you do?

options.text: Treat him exactly as you did before the teacher left
options.then: He looks up, surprised. A couple of classmates stop laughing and look away.

options.text: Join in a little so you fit in
options.then: The group grins at you. He stares at his desk and says nothing.

options.text: Stay silent and look at your notebook
options.then: The mocking carries on. He keeps his head down until the teacher returns.

options.text: Tell the loudest boy, so everyone hears, to stop
options.then: The boy snaps back, and the whole room watches. By break he is grinning again as if nothing happened.

steps.why: Your conduct should match your values whether or not an adult is watching.

steps.prompt: At break, the same boys plan a prank on him tomorrow and ask if you're in. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's not for you and suggest a game instead
options.then: They groan. One says, "Fine, cricket then."

options.text: Say yes, but promise yourself to go easy
options.then: They cheer. Tomorrow you are standing there while it happens.

options.text: Say you're busy and walk off
options.then: They shrug and plan it without you. You hear about it next day.

options.text: Warn him quietly, but say nothing to the group
options.then: He thanks you under his breath. The plan still goes ahead.

steps.why: A calm no with another idea shows the group a different way to be.

steps.prompt: Days later, the teacher is out again and the boy answers wrongly. Someone snickers. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Nice try. I got that one wrong last week."
options.then: He gives a small smile. The snicker dies and the class carries on.

options.text: Smile at him and say nothing to the class
options.then: He sees your smile. The snickering goes on a while longer.

options.text: Roll your eyes at the snicker
options.then: He catches your eye and looks away, unsure whose side you're on.

options.text: Tell the class they should feel ashamed
options.then: The room goes sour. Later a few mutter that you act like a teacher.

steps.why: Being the same person with no teacher in the room is what earns trust.

steps.prompt: The next morning, the teacher says she heard the class got loud while she was out. What do you do?

options.text: Say what happened plainly, without blaming anyone
options.then: The teacher nods. "Thank you. We'll talk about respect tomorrow."

options.text: Say it was nothing and everyone was fine
options.then: The teacher frowns but lets it go. The boy hears you say it.

options.text: Call out the loudest boys in front of the whole class
options.then: The boys glare at you. The room goes tense and the shy boy shrinks in his seat.

options.text: Say you weren't paying attention
options.then: The teacher moves on. Nothing is said about the shy boy.

steps.why: Plain truth without blame keeps your standard, and none of this is his fault.

scenarios.debrief: Integrity means your conduct matches your values even when no adult is in the room.
scenarios.relearn: Behaving the same way whether or not seniors watch is the integrity that earns trust.

scenarios.hook: Friends tease you for learning to cook and call it women's work.

steps.prompt: They bring it up again at the canteen. What do you do?

options.text: Keep cooking, and bring them something you made
options.then: One of them tries it and grudgingly asks what's in it. The teasing softens.

options.text: Hide that you cook so they drop it
options.then: The teasing stops. You feel a small knot each time cooking comes up.

options.text: Tease them back about what they can't do
options.then: They laugh, but it turns into a contest of jibes and nothing changes.

options.text: Explain at length why cooking isn't gendered
options.then: Their eyes glaze. Someone says, "Okay, professor," and the teasing carries on.

steps.why: Doing it openly shows cooking is a skill, and you need no speech.

steps.prompt: Your younger cousin watches you chop onions and asks if boys are allowed to cook. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's a useful skill and hand him the peeler
options.then: He grins and grabs it. You show him how to hold it.

options.text: Say yes, but keep it quiet outside the house
options.then: He nods. He learns it's fine at home and something to hide outside.

options.text: Tell him to ask his father
options.then: He shrugs and wanders off, still unsure.

options.text: Say it'll impress girls someday
options.then: He looks puzzled. Cooking has become a trick, not a skill.

steps.why: Offering a hands-on go shows cooking is for anyone, with no lecture.

steps.prompt: Before the school picnic, the teacher asks who will handle food. Your friends nudge you, half joking. What do you do?

options.text: Volunteer, and ask a few of them to join you
options.then: Two friends groan, then sign up. The food turns out to be the best part of the day.

options.text: Volunteer and do it all yourself
options.then: You cook for everyone and end up exhausted. Nobody else learns a thing.

options.text: Say someone else should do it
options.then: Another student gets it, and the joke stays on you.

options.text: Volunteer, but only if the girls help
options.then: The girls glance at each other. Nobody asked them.

steps.why: Inviting others in shares the skill and spreads the new norm.

scenarios.debrief: Doing a skill openly, unbothered by 'that's women's work', leads and frees others too.
scenarios.relearn: A boy doing a skill openly shows it's a useful skill, not shame, and resets what's 'manly'.

scenarios.hook: A teammate's idea gets ignored in your group, and then someone louder repeats it.

steps.prompt: The teacher calls the louder student's idea great. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Glad we're going with it. That was Meena's idea."
options.then: The teacher turns to Meena and asks her to say more. The louder student nods.

options.text: Stay quiet, because it's awkward to correct people
options.then: The praise stands. Meena looks at her notebook.

options.text: Whisper to Meena that she should speak up
options.then: Meena shrugs and says it's too late now. The moment passes.

options.text: Tell the class the louder student stole it
options.then: The room stiffens. He says he didn't mean it, and it becomes an argument.

steps.why: A light, specific credit puts the idea back with its owner without a fight.

steps.prompt: In the next group session, Meena has another idea but hesitates. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Meena, you had a plan. Let's hear it."
options.then: She shares it. The group listens and two people build on it.

options.text: Share her idea yourself so she needn't
options.then: The group likes it. Meena sinks back, and it is now yours.

options.text: Wait to see if someone else asks
options.then: The pause stretches, and the group moves on to another topic.

options.text: Tell her to speak up louder next time
options.then: She nods stiffly and stays quiet for the rest of the session.

steps.why: Opening the floor to her gives her the credit and the practice.

steps.prompt: The teacher asks who came up with the final plan, and the group looks at you. What do you say?

options.text: Say who proposed each part, Meena's included
options.then: Heads nod. Meena smiles, and others add what they did.

options.text: Say it was a group thing and leave it there
options.then: The teacher nods. No one's name goes on anything.

options.text: Say it was mostly your doing
options.then: The teacher praises you. Meena studies the table.

options.text: Let the louder student answer, since he speaks well
options.then: He gives a polished summary. Names get left out.

steps.why: Naming each contribution out loud turns fair credit into the group's habit.

steps.prompt: A newcomer joins the group and sits quietly while the louder students dominate. What do you do?

options.text: Ask the newcomer a question and wait for the answer
options.then: He says something shyly. Meena adds to it, and the group listens.

options.text: Tell the newcomer to speak up when he's ready
options.then: He nods. He's still waiting for a gap.

options.text: Leave him to settle in by himself
options.then: The louder students keep going. He stays silent all session.

options.text: Answer for him so the group can move on
options.then: You say it well. He feels he has no part in it.

steps.why: Asking and then waiting shows the newcomer that the group wants to listen.

scenarios.debrief: Pointing credit back to its source, lightly, sets a norm of fairness others copy.
scenarios.relearn: Crediting the person whose idea it was, out loud, models fairness better than the spotlight.

scenarios.hook: You've quietly made your group fairer for weeks, and someone calls you a show-off.

steps.prompt: A classmate says it with a smirk at lunch. What do you do?

options.text: Carry on as before, with no big defence
options.then: The smirk fades when nothing happens. The group keeps using the fair rota.

options.text: List every fair thing you've done
options.then: You count the deeds aloud. The classmate says, "See? Show-off."

options.text: Stop the changes so no one says it again
options.then: The comment stops. So does the rota, and old habits drift back in.

options.text: Complain about the classmate to your friends
options.then: Your friends sympathise. The group splits into sides.

steps.why: Steady action shows it was never about credit, so there's nothing to defend.

steps.prompt: A new member of the group heard the show-off remark and asks why you care so much about fairness. What do you say?

options.text: Say it makes the group work better for everyone
options.then: She nods slowly. "Huh. I'd like that too."

options.text: Say you want people to notice how fair you are
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. It sounds a lot like the show-off line.

options.text: Shrug and say it's nothing
options.then: She drops it, none the wiser about why it matters.

options.text: Say others should do it too, or they're being unfair
options.then: She bristles. Nobody likes being told they're the problem.

steps.why: Explaining it simply, in terms of the group, invites her in without pressure.

steps.prompt: The teacher praises the group's teamwork in front of everyone and looks at you. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and say everyone shaped it
options.then: The teacher smiles, and a few teammates sit up straighter.

options.text: Accept the praise as the one who started it
options.then: The teacher notes your name. Teammates exchange looks.

options.text: Shake your head and say it was nothing
options.then: The teacher moves on. The group's effort goes unnamed.

options.text: Point out who didn't pull their weight
options.then: The room tenses. The praise is gone, and so is the mood.

steps.why: Sharing the praise keeps the focus on the norm, not on you.

scenarios.debrief: Real example is steady; you needn't defend it or chase credit.
scenarios.relearn: Leading by example is steady and low-key; the point is the norm shifts, not the credit.

scenarios.hook: Friends say backing the girls' team makes you one of them, not a real bro.

steps.prompt: They repeat it in front of the whole squad. What do you do?

options.text: Keep backing the team and say it's just fair
options.then: A few boys roll their eyes. Two others quietly say they watched the match too.

options.text: Back off so the boys still see you as loyal
options.then: The jokes stop. You skip the girls' next match and it feels odd.

options.text: Say it was a one-off and won't happen again
options.then: They relax. The next girls' match has one fewer cheering voice.

options.text: Argue loudly that they're all sexist
options.then: They turn defensive. The squad splits and you're called preachy.

steps.why: Standing steady shows that backing fairness is strength, not a side against boys.

steps.prompt: The boys' captain asks if you'll help plan a joint practice day with the girls' team. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes and ask the girls' captain to plan it with you
options.then: The two captains sit down together. The schedule works for both teams.

options.text: Say yes, but let the boys' captain decide everything
options.then: It gets planned fast. The girls' team hears the time after it's fixed.

options.text: Say no, to keep the peace with your squad
options.then: The captain shrugs and the joint day is dropped.

options.text: Say yes if the girls bring the snacks
options.then: The captain laughs. Some of the girls aren't amused.

steps.why: Planning with the girls' captain treats both teams as equals.

steps.prompt: A younger boy wants to cheer at the girls' final but fears being teased. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll sit with him and cheer together
options.then: He grins. By the second half, three more boys have joined you.

options.text: Tell him to ignore the teasing
options.then: He nods, then sits at the back alone.

options.text: Tell him to wait till he's older
options.then: He shrugs and stays away. The stands are quieter.

options.text: Say he can cheer if his friends do
options.then: He waits for his friends. They never decide.

steps.why: Sitting beside him shows that strength looks like showing up.

steps.prompt: The school asks which team should get the new practice ground first. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest taking turns on a timetable
options.then: The coach nods. A timetable goes up on the notice board.

options.text: Say the boys' team should, since it's bigger
options.then: The coach shrugs. The girls' team practises on the old ground.

options.text: Say whichever team wins next gets it
options.then: The coach likes the idea. The teams don't start from the same place.

options.text: Say you don't mind either way
options.then: The coach picks one. Nobody asks the girls' captain.

steps.why: A schedule everyone can see treats both teams as equals.

scenarios.debrief: Leading on equality isn't a side against boys; it's strength, and frees boys too.
scenarios.relearn: A boy leading on fairness is showing maturity and strength, not betraying 'his side'.

scenarios.hook: You're made captain, and the boys expect an all-boys side for the big match.

steps.prompt: The team list is due today. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the strongest players and say why
options.then: Some boys grumble. Then they see the trial scores and can't argue.

options.text: Pick all boys to keep the team happy
options.then: The boys cheer. Two strong girls watch from the boundary.

options.text: Add a couple of girls to look fair
options.then: A couple of girls are named, but the strongest are left out. Everyone can tell, and it stings.

options.text: Let the coach decide so you aren't blamed
options.then: The coach picks quickly. You captain a side you didn't shape.

steps.why: Choosing on skill, openly, gives a team that everyone accepts as fair.

steps.prompt: Before the match, a boy demands to bat first, though another player scored higher in practice. What do you do?

options.text: Say the order follows practice scores
options.then: He frowns, reads the numbers, and takes his place.

options.text: Let him bat first to avoid a scene
options.then: He swaggers out. The better scorer waits, padded up, for a turn.

options.text: Offer a coin toss for the spot
options.then: He agrees. The toss is fair luck, but it ignores the practice scores.

options.text: Tell him to bat where told or sit out
options.then: He sulks and the dressing room goes tense.

steps.why: A clear rule, applied to everyone, settles it without a fight.

steps.prompt: You lose by a few runs, and a boy blames the selection. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's a team loss, then ask what to fix
options.then: A few nod. Someone suggests a new bowling plan.

options.text: Say nothing and take the blame quietly
options.then: The comment hangs. You wonder if you should have picked differently.

options.text: Agree it was a gamble and promise to play it safe
options.then: The boys relax. Next selection, you pick only the familiar names.

options.text: Point at the boy who dropped a catch
options.then: He scowls. The team drifts into blaming each other.

steps.why: Judging the team on what it did, not who was in it, keeps the standard fair.

scenarios.debrief: Choosing players by skill, openly, shows fairness and a strong team go together.
scenarios.relearn: Picking a mixed, skill-based team yourself models that ability, not gender, decides who plays.

scenarios.hook: You repeat a careless gendered comment, then catch yourself with friends watching.

steps.prompt: A friend raises an eyebrow at you. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "That came out wrong. I don't think that."
options.then: He nods. "Okay, fair. Thanks for saying so."

options.text: Pretend you didn't say it
options.then: Someone changes the subject. Your friend keeps looking at you.

options.text: Say you were only joking and they're too sensitive
options.then: He laughs awkwardly. The comment stays in the air.

options.text: Apologise again and again for ten minutes
options.then: The group gets uncomfortable and ends up reassuring you.

steps.why: A short, honest correction keeps your example trustworthy.

steps.prompt: A week later, the same friend makes a similar comment about girls. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "I slipped like that once. It's off."
options.then: He frowns. "Yeah. Didn't think about it."

options.text: Say nothing, because you slipped on it yourself
options.then: He carries on, sure it's fine. The group laughs.

options.text: Laugh, then change the subject
options.then: He moves on. The comment passes unchallenged.

options.text: Tell him off in front of the group
options.then: He stiffens and gets defensive. The group goes quiet.

steps.why: Admitting your own slip makes it a gentle call-in, not a call-out.

steps.prompt: A classmate says you still slip sometimes, though you're trying. What do you say?

options.text: Thank her and ask her to say so next time
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. I will, and you do the same for me."

options.text: Say you're only human, so it will happen
options.then: She nods. The pattern carries on, unnoticed.

options.text: Say she's being too strict
options.then: She stops raising it with you.

options.text: Promise you'll never slip again
options.then: She smiles politely. She knows promises like that don't last.

steps.why: Inviting feedback keeps you honest and shows that learning is normal.

scenarios.debrief: Leading by example isn't never slipping; it's owning slips and correcting course.
scenarios.relearn: One slip doesn't end your example; owning and correcting it keeps the example trustworthy.

scenarios.hook: At a relative's home, the boys are served first while the girls keep working.

steps.prompt: Your plate arrives while the girls are still in the kitchen. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to help, and wait so all eat together
options.then: Your aunt protests, then smiles. The girls sit down with you.

options.text: Eat first, since you're the guest
options.then: You eat. The girls carry on serving.

options.text: Say loudly that the girls should sit down too
options.then: The room goes quiet. Your aunt looks embarrassed in front of guests.

options.text: Whisper to your cousin that it's unfair
options.then: She shrugs and says that's how it is, then goes back to work.

steps.why: Pitching in and waiting leads without shaming anyone's home.

steps.prompt: After the meal, an uncle says guests shouldn't touch the dishes. What do you do?

options.text: Smile and carry a few plates to the sink
options.then: He waves a hand but doesn't stop you. A cousin follows with more.

options.text: Sit back down so you don't offend him
options.then: The dishes go to the girls again.

options.text: Tell him that rule is old-fashioned
options.then: He bristles, and the visit turns stiff.

options.text: Offer once, then give up when he insists
options.then: He nods, satisfied. You watch the girls clear up.

steps.why: A warm, simple offer respects elders and still shifts the habit.

steps.prompt: On the way home, your younger brother says the girls didn't mind. What do you say?

options.text: Say they looked tired, and you'll help next time
options.then: He thinks for a moment. "I didn't really look."

options.text: Tell him he's wrong and drop it
options.then: He rolls his eyes and puts in his earphones.

options.text: Agree that's just how that house is
options.then: He nods. Neither of you thinks about it again.

options.text: Tell him he must speak up on the next visit too
options.then: He winces. He doesn't want a fight with relatives.

steps.why: Sharing what you noticed, without blame, invites him to see it himself.

steps.prompt: On your next visit, your aunt hands you your plate first, smiling. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her warmly and ask to serve too
options.then: She laughs. "Come, then." You and your cousin serve together.

options.text: Take the plate and eat quickly
options.then: You finish first. The girls are still on their feet.

options.text: Refuse the plate and explain why
options.then: She looks hurt. "We only wanted to welcome you."

options.text: Take it and tell your cousin to hurry
options.then: She rushes to serve. Her face stays tight.

steps.why: Warm thanks plus an offer to serve shifts the habit without any speech.

scenarios.debrief: Pitching in and waiting so all eat together leads without shaming anyone's home.
scenarios.relearn: Pitching in, rather than waiting to be served, leads at home without shaming anyone.

scenarios.hook: A demeaning meme about girls is forwarded in your class group and people are laughing.

steps.prompt: The meme lands on your phone. What do you do?

options.text: Don't forward it. Reply, "Not this one. Let's not."
options.then: Two people send a thumbs up. The laughing slows down.

options.text: React with a laughing emoji and say nothing
options.then: Your emoji joins the pile. It reads as a yes.

options.text: Don't forward it, but say nothing in the group
options.then: The meme keeps circulating. Nobody knows you opted out.

options.text: Post a long message calling everyone sexist
options.then: Replies turn defensive. Two people leave the group.

steps.why: Not forwarding, and saying so lightly, lets others opt out too.

steps.prompt: A girl in the class goes quiet in the group for days. What do you do?

options.text: Message her privately and say you noticed
options.then: She replies after a while. "Thanks. It did sting."

options.text: Ask in the group why she's gone quiet
options.then: She doesn't reply. Others jump in with guesses.

options.text: Assume she's busy and wait
options.then: Days pass and she stays silent.

options.text: Tell her not to be so sensitive about it
options.then: She sends a thumbs up, then mutes the chat.

steps.why: A private, caring message tells her someone noticed, without putting her on show.

steps.prompt: The group admin asks whether the chat needs a rule about what gets posted. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest a simple rule: nothing that puts anyone down
options.then: The admin agrees and posts it. Two others add a thumbs up.

options.text: Say rules ruin the fun of a group
options.then: The admin shrugs. The chat stays as it was.

options.text: Say the admin should remove whoever posted the meme
options.then: The admin removes him. The group tenses and he blames you.

options.text: Say you don't mind either way and the admin can decide
options.then: The admin sighs and puts it off. Nobody decides anything.

steps.why: A simple shared rule sets the group's norm without singling anyone out.

steps.prompt: A friend sends a new meme that mocks girls and calls it harmless. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "That didn't sit right with me. Can we not?"
options.then: He pauses. "Okay, fair. I didn't think about it like that."

options.text: Laugh and say it's harmless
options.then: He grins. The next one is worse.

options.text: Skip it and send him a different meme
options.then: He laughs. "Okay, that one's better." He never hears why you skipped the first.

options.text: Say you'll stop talking to him if it happens again
options.then: He scoffs. "Okay, drama." The two of you get awkward.

steps.why: A light, private "can we not" names the problem without a fight, so he can listen.

scenarios.debrief: Not forwarding, and saying so lightly, models the group norm you want online.
scenarios.relearn: Not forwarding a demeaning meme, and saying lightly why, models better group behaviour online.

scenarios.hook: In the class council, boys talk over the girls and the teacher assumes a boy will lead.

steps.prompt: The discussion starts and you have a point ready. What do you do?

options.text: Speak up calmly and finish your point
options.then: A boy starts to cut in, but you carry on. The teacher writes it down.

options.text: Wait for a gap that never comes
options.then: The boys keep talking. The discussion moves on without you.

options.text: Stay quiet so you don't seem pushy
options.then: The council takes a vote. Your point never reaches the table.

options.text: Raise your voice and talk over them back
options.then: The room gets louder. The teacher claps for order and your point is lost.

steps.why: Speaking in your own steady voice claims your space without a fight.

steps.prompt: Priya has a point too but looks down, waiting to be asked. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Let's hear Priya. She had a point."
options.then: Priya looks up and shares. Two boys listen and take notes.

options.text: Say her point yourself so she needn't
options.then: The council likes it. Priya smiles, but stays small.

options.text: Hope someone else invites her
options.then: Nobody does, and the council moves to the next item.

options.text: Tell Priya to speak up for herself
options.then: Priya flushes and stays quiet, now feeling watched.

steps.why: Passing her the floor makes room for her voice without speaking for her.

steps.prompt: The teacher asks the council to name a chair, and a boy is proposed straight away. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest anyone interested says why, then vote
options.then: The teacher agrees. Three people speak, and two of them are girls.

options.text: Accept the boy since he's already proposed
options.then: It's settled with a nod. The vote is over in a minute.

options.text: Propose a girl without asking her first
options.then: She's caught off guard and says she isn't sure.

options.text: Say the teacher should just pick someone
options.then: The teacher picks the boy she had in mind from the start.

steps.why: An open process lets interest and readiness decide, not assumptions.

scenarios.debrief: Using your voice and pulling quieter peers in models leadership, not just for boys.
scenarios.relearn: Speaking in your own calm voice, and inviting quieter peers in, models leadership isn't 'a man's role'.

scenarios.hook: Your sister does the dishes and also tracks everyone's medicines and school forms.

steps.prompt: A form deadline clashes with her exams and she looks stressed. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what she tracks and take over the forms
options.then: She hands you a list. It's longer than you expected.

options.text: Do extra dishes so it feels fair
options.then: She thanks you. The forms and medicine chart stay on her list.

options.text: Tell her to ask Mum for help
options.then: She sighs. Mum is already doing her own share.

options.text: Say she's good at it, so she should carry on
options.then: She smiles tightly and goes back to her list.

steps.why: Asking what she tracks shows the hidden work so you can truly share it.

steps.prompt: One evening, Mum says the family should divide who handles what. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest a shared list so everyone has a task
options.then: Mum pauses, then reaches for a pen. Dad finds he has two tasks.

options.text: Say your sister already knows what to do
options.then: Mum nods. Nothing changes.

options.text: Offer to do more chores, with no list
options.then: You do a few chores that week, and the planning still sits with her.

options.text: Say the family already works fine as it is
options.then: Your sister looks at the table, and nobody says more.

steps.why: A shared list makes the hidden work visible and spreads it across everyone.

steps.prompt: A friend overhears you talking about your sister's workload and says boys don't do this stuff. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's fair to share, and you're learning
options.then: He shrugs, then asks how you split things at home.

options.text: Laugh along and say you only help a little
options.then: He grins. You stop mentioning it in front of him.

options.text: Say he's behind the times
options.then: He rolls his eyes. The chat turns into a joke fight.

options.text: Change the subject to the match
options.then: He lets it drop. He still thinks it's funny.

steps.why: Treating it as a normal skill, not a joke, invites a friend to try it.

steps.prompt: Her exams are over, and your sister says she wants one day off from every chore. What do you do?

options.text: Take her whole list for the day
options.then: She sleeps in. The medicines and forms are handled, too.

options.text: Say she can take it next week
options.then: She sighs. The day off keeps slipping away.

options.text: Do the visible chores and skip the rest
options.then: The kitchen is clean. The forms and medicines go unchecked.

options.text: Say everyone does their own chores, even her
options.then: She stiffens. A day off feels like a favour you won't grant.

steps.why: Taking over the whole list shows you can carry the load too.

scenarios.debrief: Real example shares the invisible planning too, not just the chores people can see.
scenarios.relearn: Sharing the 'invisible' errands, not just the visible ones, makes your example complete.

scenarios.hook: Friends dare you to rate girls walking past and call it just fun.

steps.prompt: A group of girls is passing now, and the dare is on. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Not my thing," and change the subject
options.then: They groan, but one asks about the match and the group drifts to that.

options.text: Play along a little so they don't mock you
options.then: You say a number. The girls glance back and you wish you hadn't.

options.text: Say you'll rate them if someone else goes first
options.then: Someone goes first, laughing. You're still part of it.

options.text: Tell them it's disgusting
options.then: The boys mock you for it. The teasing turns on you.

steps.why: A relaxed, brief no makes opting out look normal.

steps.prompt: A friend whispers that he thought it was a bit much too. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's easier if two of you say no
options.then: He grins. "Okay. Next time, both of us."

options.text: Say it's not worth bringing up
options.then: He shrugs. You both go along next time.

options.text: Say he should tell the others himself
options.then: He shakes his head. He doesn't want to be the odd one.

options.text: Say you'll tell the others he said so
options.then: He looks alarmed. "Please don't."

steps.why: A second voice makes saying no easier for both of you.

steps.prompt: Next week, the same friends start it near the school gate, where a girl looks upset. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Enough, let's go." Then tell a teacher about the girl
options.then: Some follow. The girl hurries inside, and the teacher goes to check on her.

options.text: Check on the girl, but say nothing to the boys
options.then: She thanks you quietly. The boys carry on at the next gate.

options.text: Stay out of it, since it's not your fight
options.then: They carry on. The girl's face stays with you.

options.text: Shout at them in front of everyone
options.then: They shout back. A teacher arrives and sends everyone off.

steps.why: Walking away and telling a teacher gets her help, and none of it is her fault.

scenarios.debrief: A relaxed, brief refusal models a standard others can follow without drama.
scenarios.relearn: Holding your standard calmly under peer pressure is what makes an example worth following.

scenarios.hook: A few boys keep joking with a wrong name for a classmate who corrected them.

steps.prompt: They do it again as the classmate walks in. What do you do?

options.text: Use the name they asked for, every time
options.then: They glance at you. A couple of the boys start using it too.

options.text: Use the wrong name too when they're around
options.then: The boys grin. The classmate's face closes.

options.text: Say nothing and avoid using any name
options.then: You steer clear of it. The joke carries on without you.

options.text: Tell the boys they're cruel in front of the class
options.then: The boys snort. The classmate looks mortified at being the focus.

steps.why: Using the name they asked for, every time, models simple respect.

steps.prompt: Later, a boy says the name thing is only a joke and tells you to lighten up. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's their name and you'd like to use it
options.then: He rolls his eyes but stops pressing. "Whatever."

options.text: Laugh and say you'll lighten up
options.then: He grins. The others still get the name wrong.

options.text: Say it's not your business what they call people
options.then: He shrugs. The jokes carry on, and the classmate hears them.

options.text: Tell him he's a bully
options.then: He bristles. "Now who's being rude?"

steps.why: Calmly stating a simple fact keeps it about respect, not an argument.

steps.prompt: The classmate sits near you at lunch, unsure whether you're on their side. What do you do?

options.text: Chat normally, then ask if they'd like a teacher to know
options.then: They relax. "Maybe," they say. "Thanks for asking." Soon they're telling you about their weekend.

options.text: Say loudly that you're on their side
options.then: Heads turn. They shrink a little in their seat.

options.text: Ask them to explain everything about their name
options.then: They go quiet. Not everyone wants to be the teacher.

options.text: Say you'd rather not get involved
options.then: They nod and shift their tray away.

steps.why: Steady respect plus an offer of adult help makes them feel safe, and none of this is their fault.

scenarios.debrief: Using the name someone asked for models the respect that sets the norm.
scenarios.relearn: Using a classmate's correct name, consistently, models simple respect that sets a norm.

scenarios.hook: You find a junior's lost answer sheet, and no one saw you pick it up.

steps.prompt: Her name and a good score are on it. What do you do?

options.text: Return it to her quietly, with no fuss
options.then: She blinks, then says thank you. You're already walking away.

options.text: Keep it, since no one will ever know
options.then: It sits in your bag. You think of it more than you expected.

options.text: Leave it on a desk and hope she finds it
options.then: A cleaner sweeps it up before she looks.

options.text: Return it and tell everyone you did
options.then: People pat your back. The praise feels odd.

steps.why: Doing the fair thing with no audience is the truest test of your example.

steps.prompt: Next week, a friend offers to share a leaked answer key for the test. What do you do?

options.text: Say no thanks and don't pass the key on
options.then: He shrugs and pockets his phone. It's a small moment.

options.text: Take a quick look, just once
options.then: You scroll it. The test feels less like yours.

options.text: Say no, but pass it to a friend who needs it
options.then: She takes it gladly. The key spreads.

options.text: Report him to the teacher in front of the class
options.then: He's furious, and the room goes silent.

steps.why: Declining quietly and not passing it on keeps you the same when unobserved.

steps.prompt: At term end, you rate your group members privately, and no one will see your answers. What do you do?

options.text: Rate everyone fairly, whoever they are
options.then: You think each rating through. It takes longer than expected.

options.text: Give your friends top marks to keep things easy
options.then: They'll never know. Neither will the quieter ones who did more.

options.text: Give the one you dislike the lowest marks
options.then: It feels satisfying for a day. Then it doesn't.

options.text: Skip the form, since no one will check
options.then: The teacher gets fewer answers than she needed.

steps.why: Fair ratings given in private are integrity with no audience at all.

scenarios.debrief: Integrity is doing the fair thing when no one's watching and there's no reward.
scenarios.relearn: Doing the fair thing when there's no audience or reward is the truest test of leading by example.

scenarios.hook: A friend loves coding but is told girls don't do tech, and she may drop it.

steps.prompt: The elective forms are due on Friday. What do you do?

options.text: Take the elective with her, matter-of-factly
options.then: She laughs, relieved. You sit together at the first class.

options.text: Agree she should pick something more suitable
options.then: She nods slowly and writes a different choice. She keeps coding at home.

options.text: Say it's her choice and stay out of it
options.then: She thanks you. She picks alone, with that line still in her ear.

options.text: Argue with the person who said it
options.then: He shrugs it off. She is embarrassed and still unsure.

steps.why: Joining her, matter-of-factly, makes the stereotype look silly.

steps.prompt: At the school tech fair, your friend shows the app she built. A boy says girls usually do the design, not the code. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "She wrote the code. Ask her about it."
options.then: He looks at her. She explains the code, and he listens.

options.text: Say nothing and let her handle it
options.then: She shrugs it off, but you can see it landed.

options.text: Tell the boy to go away
options.then: He leaves muttering. The mood at the stall sours.

options.text: Say her design work is great too
options.then: He nods and moves on. Her code goes unmentioned.

steps.why: Pointing to her work, calmly, shows that interest and skill decide, not gender.

steps.prompt: She asks if she should enter a coding contest. Her parents seem unsure. What do you say?

options.text: Offer to help her explain it to her parents
options.then: She brightens. Her father reads the rules and asks questions.

options.text: Say it's up to her parents
options.then: She nods and the form stays on her desk.

options.text: Say she should enter without telling them
options.then: She worries about hiding it. The excitement fades.

options.text: Say she'd need to be the best to win
options.then: She gets nervous and hesitates to start.

steps.why: Helping her explain it respects her family and backs her interest.

scenarios.debrief: Backing a friend toward a 'not for girls' subject shows interest decides, not gender.
scenarios.relearn: Backing a friend toward a 'boys' subject, and staying with it, models that interest beats stereotype.

scenarios.hook: You realise a joke you made last week stung a classmate.

steps.prompt: You see the classmate alone in the corridor. What do you do?

options.text: Apologise simply and directly, with no excuses
options.then: They look surprised, then nod. "Thanks for saying so."

options.text: Say, "I was only joking. Relax."
options.then: Their face closes. They walk off.

options.text: Ask a friend to tell them you're sorry
options.then: Your friend mumbles it. The classmate shrugs and walks on.

options.text: Wait and hope it blows over
options.then: The week goes by. The classmate avoids your eye.

steps.why: A plain apology takes responsibility for the hurt, whatever you meant.

steps.prompt: A week later, others tease the classmate about the same joke. What do you do?

options.text: Say the joke was yours and it wasn't fair
options.then: The group goes quiet. One of them says, "Yeah. Sorry."

options.text: Stay out of it, since the joke is old news now
options.then: The teasing continues until the bell.

options.text: Laugh nervously and hope it ends
options.then: It doesn't end. The classmate sees you laughing.

options.text: Tell them off and call them bullies
options.then: They snap back, and now the argument is about you.

steps.why: Owning your part shows others that taking responsibility is normal.

steps.prompt: A few days on, the classmate still keeps their distance. What do you do?

options.text: Give them space and stay friendly when you meet
options.then: One day they nod back. A small thaw begins.

options.text: Ask them every day if they've forgiven you
options.then: They feel pressured and avoid you more.

options.text: Tell others the classmate is overreacting
options.then: It gets back to them. Things get worse.

options.text: Stop talking to them altogether
options.then: The distance grows into a habit.

steps.why: Trust returns through steady respect, not by demanding forgiveness.

steps.prompt: A friend admits he made a similar joke last year and never apologised. What do you do?

options.text: Share your own slip-up and say it isn't too late
options.then: He thinks about it. "Maybe I'll message her today."

options.text: Tell him it's too late now
options.then: He nods. The old joke stays unaddressed.

options.text: Tell him to keep quiet and avoid it
options.then: He relaxes. The hurt stays where it is.

options.text: Tell him to apologise to her in front of everyone
options.then: He tries it in the canteen. Everyone turns to stare at her, and she looks away.

steps.why: Sharing your own slip-up, calmly, shows him it isn't too late to put it right.

scenarios.debrief: A plain apology, no excuses, models the accountability that makes an example trustworthy.
scenarios.relearn: Apologising plainly when your behaviour hurt someone models accountability others learn from.

scenarios.hook: Relatives ask you about your career but only ask your sister when she'll marry.

steps.prompt: An uncle starts the same questions again at a family function. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "She's aiming for engineering. Ask her."
options.then: Your uncle blinks, then turns to her. "Engineering? Tell me."

options.text: Answer about yourself and let her question slide
options.then: Your uncle nods happily. Your sister keeps her smile fixed.

options.text: Tell your uncle he shouldn't ask about marriage
options.then: He looks offended. An aunt hushes you and the mood sours.

options.text: Whisper to your sister to just ignore it
options.then: She nods tightly. The relatives carry on.

steps.why: Turning the question to her goals respects elders and treats her future seriously.

steps.prompt: Your sister says she's tired of explaining herself and asks what to do. What do you say?

options.text: Ask what she'd like said, and say exactly that
options.then: She thinks. "Say I'm preparing for entrance exams."

options.text: Say you'll handle every question from now on
options.then: She's relieved, but her own voice is still missing from the room.

options.text: Say it's easier to give them a date
options.then: She goes quiet. A date she doesn't mean feels heavier.

options.text: Say she has to answer them herself
options.then: She frowns. She isn't ready and feels left alone with it.

steps.why: Asking what she wants keeps her in charge of her own story.

steps.prompt: Your parents say the relatives mean well and ask you not to upset them. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll stay polite and steer to her plans
options.then: Mum nods slowly. "That we can live with."

options.text: Agree and promise to stay quiet in future
options.then: Your parents relax. The questions at the next function are the same.

options.text: Say relatives need to be told they're wrong
options.then: Mum winces. The next function begins with tension.

options.text: Say it's their problem, not yours
options.then: Dad looks tired. The talk ends there.

steps.why: Staying polite while redirecting changes a habit without a family fight.

steps.prompt: Your parents ask you to help your sister prepare for her entrance exam. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and offer to cover some of her chores
options.then: Mum smiles. Your sister gets two hours a day back.

options.text: Say she should study on her own
options.then: Your parents exchange a look. Her chores stay the same.

options.text: Say you'll help only if she asks
options.then: She doesn't ask. She doesn't like to.

options.text: Say you have your own exams to think about
options.then: Dad nods. Your sister finds a way, alone.

steps.why: Taking over some of her chores gives her time, which is real support.

scenarios.debrief: Steering attention to her goals shows equal seriousness, respecting elders.
scenarios.relearn: Treating your sister's goals as seriously as your own, openly, leads change inside the family.

scenarios.hook: Your friends start spreading an unkind rumour about a girl who isn't there.

steps.prompt: One friend is typing it into the group chat. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "That's not true. Please don't send it."
options.then: He pauses over the keys. "Okay, fair." He deletes it, though a couple of others already saw.

options.text: Add a detail to seem in the know
options.then: They love it. The rumour is now longer and meaner.

options.text: Say nothing and mute the chat
options.then: The rumour spreads by evening. You see it in a screenshot.

options.text: Warn her privately but say nothing to them
options.then: She thanks you, upset. The rumour still spreads.

steps.why: Defending someone who isn't there models the respect you'd want shown to you.

steps.prompt: The next day, the girl walks in looking tense, and a few classmates glance her way and murmur. What do you do?

options.text: Say hello and stay with her at break
options.then: She relaxes a little. "Thanks. I was dreading today."

options.text: Tell them off loudly for gossiping
options.then: They go quiet, then start up again once you leave.

options.text: Pretend not to notice
options.then: She walks past alone.

options.text: Ask her if what people say is true
options.then: She stiffens. Now she has to defend herself to you.

steps.why: Standing with her tells her she isn't alone, without asking anything of her.

steps.prompt: A teacher notices the murmuring and asks if something is going on. What do you do?

options.text: Say a rumour hurts her, and ask for help
options.then: The teacher thanks you and speaks to the class without naming her.

options.text: Say it's nothing and it'll blow over
options.then: The teacher nods. The whispering goes on.

options.text: Blame your friend out loud, in front of everyone
options.then: He glares at you across the room. Your friend group splits.

options.text: Say you'd rather not get involved
options.then: The teacher lets it go. The girl keeps walking past alone.

steps.why: A trusted adult can stop a rumour, and none of it is her fault.

scenarios.debrief: Standing up for someone not in the room models the fairness you'd want shown to you.
scenarios.relearn: Defending an absent friend's reputation models the respect you'd want shown to you.

scenarios.hook: You feel inspired to be a better ally but haven't done anything concrete yet.

steps.prompt: A friend asks what you plan to do about it. What do you say?

options.text: Say you'll pick one small thing this week
options.then: She smiles. "Like what?" You say sharing a chore, and mean it.

options.text: Say you'll post that you support equality
options.then: She likes the post. Nothing in your week changes.

options.text: Say you'll make a big plan first
options.then: You start a long list. The week ends with nothing begun.

options.text: Say it's not really your job
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. You change the subject.

steps.why: One small, specific act you really do beats a big promise you never start.

steps.prompt: At home that evening, dinner is over and the dishes are waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Pick up the plates and wash them unasked
options.then: Mum looks up, surprised. She sits down for the first time today.

options.text: Offer to help, then leave when someone says it's fine
options.then: You walk off. The dishes stay with Mum.

options.text: Wait for someone to ask you
options.then: Nobody does. Mum starts the dishes alone.

options.text: Tell your brother he should do them
options.then: He groans and pushes back. Nobody does any.

steps.why: Doing it unasked and visibly leads better than telling others to.

steps.prompt: A week later, the same friend asks how the ally thing is going. What do you say?

options.text: Say how it went, and name a next step
options.then: She nods. "Okay, I'll try one too."

options.text: Say it's going great and leave it there
options.then: She smiles. Neither of you knows what has changed.

options.text: Say you're done, since you did your bit
options.then: She shrugs. You tell yourself you've done enough.

options.text: Post about it online for everyone to see
options.then: Your phone fills with likes. The next chore is still waiting.

steps.why: A next small step turns allyship into a habit, not a moment.

steps.prompt: A month on, your younger brother asks what all this equality talk at home is about. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's fair to share, and invite him
options.then: He grumbles, then picks the smallest chore. "Fine."

options.text: Say it's just a phase
options.then: He shrugs. He assumes it will pass.

options.text: Say it's none of his business
options.then: He frowns. He feels shut out.

options.text: Tell him he's lazy for not doing any
options.then: He bristles. "You're not my boss."

steps.why: A plain reason plus an invitation makes it easy for him to join.

steps.prompt: At school, a teacher asks the class what small changes they've made for equality. What do you say?

options.text: Share honestly what you've tried so far, even if small
options.then: The teacher nods. Two classmates say they'll try it.

options.text: Say you support equality
options.then: The teacher nods. Nobody learns anything.

options.text: Describe a big campaign you'd like to run
options.then: It sounds grand. It doesn't start.

options.text: Say you'll start something soon
options.then: The teacher smiles politely. The week passes.

steps.why: Saying honestly what you have actually done beats a promise.

scenarios.debrief: Leading by example starts with one small, specific thing you actually do.
scenarios.relearn: One small, specific fair act you actually do beats a big promise you never start.

scenarios.hook: Your friends mock another boy for crying at a sad film and call him weak.

steps.prompt: He's wiping his eyes while they laugh. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Crying's normal," and sit next to him
options.then: He glances up. The laughing thins out.

options.text: Join the teasing so they don't turn on you
options.then: They cheer. He stares at the floor.

options.text: Say nothing and look at your phone
options.then: The mocking runs its course. He leaves early.

options.text: Tell the boys to grow up
options.then: They sneer. "Grow up? You're upset too?" The room tenses.

steps.why: Treating his feelings as normal helps every boy, and none of this is his fault.

steps.prompt: Later, he says he'd rather skip the next film night. What do you do?

options.text: Say you want him there, and sit with him
options.then: He thinks about it. "Okay. Maybe."

options.text: Tell him to toughen up
options.then: He nods stiffly and doesn't come.

options.text: Say you'll skip it too so it's equal
options.then: Neither of you goes. The others keep their habit.

options.text: Say the boys will forget in a week
options.then: He shrugs. He's still not sure he wants to come.

steps.why: Saying plainly that you want him there matters more than a speech.

steps.prompt: At the next film night you go to, a sad scene starts and everyone goes quiet. What do you do?

options.text: Let yourself feel it, without hiding it
options.then: A second boy sniffs. Nobody laughs. The scene plays on.

options.text: Crack a joke to break the mood
options.then: A few laugh. The moment passes and the feeling stays unspoken.

options.text: Keep your face blank until it's over
options.then: You hold it in. Around you, the other boys do the same.

options.text: Go for snacks until the scene ends
options.then: You miss it. When you return, everyone is dry-eyed and quiet.

steps.why: Showing your own feelings, without fuss, tells every boy he's allowed.

scenarios.debrief: Treating a boy's feelings as normal models that respect, and emotion, aren't gendered.
scenarios.relearn: Refusing to police a friend's 'unmanly' feelings models that respect isn't gendered.

scenarios.hook: Your team wins a prize, and as the loudest member you could take the credit.

steps.prompt: The teacher hands you the prize in front of the school. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and name what each teammate did
options.then: Teammates grin as their names are read out. One mouths a thank you.

options.text: Accept it with a quick thank you
options.then: The applause is for you. Your teammates clap from the side.

options.text: Say you led it, and the others helped
options.then: The teacher smiles at you. Teammates stand a step behind, unnamed.

options.text: Hand the prize to the quietest teammate
options.then: She's startled and doesn't know what to do. The room goes awkward.

steps.why: Naming what each person did makes the credit fair and visible.

steps.prompt: The prize comes with a voucher the team must share. What do you suggest?

options.text: Split it evenly, and name each person's part
options.then: Everyone agrees. Nobody feels counted out.

options.text: Take the biggest share, since you spoke the most
options.then: Teammates glance at each other. Nobody speaks, and the mood shifts.

options.text: Give it to whoever needs it most
options.then: People disagree about who that is. The talk turns uncomfortable.

options.text: Draw lots so there's no argument

steps.prompt: A year later, the school picks one student to represent it, and the teacher asks who from your team. What do you say?

scenarios.hook: A teammate's idea was ignored, then repeated by someone louder and praised.
scenarios.setup: You decide to set the credit straight.

steps.prompt: The teacher says: "Great idea, Rohan. We'll go with that."

options.text: "Glad we're going with it. That was Asha's idea."
options.then: The teacher turns to Asha. "Oh? Asha, say more."

options.text: "Rohan always has good ideas. We should hear him."
options.then: "He does," she says, writing it down.

options.text: "Sounds fine. Let's get started on the plan."
options.then: The teacher nods. "Good. Rohan, lead us."

options.text: "Rohan, admit it was Asha's idea. Everyone knows."
options.then: Rohan flushes. "I didn't copy it! Why accuse me?"

steps.why: A light, specific credit puts the idea back with its owner.

steps.prompt: Rohan says quietly after class: "I think Asha said that first. I didn't mean to take it. I got excited."

options.text: "I believe you. Next time, credit the person."
options.then: Rohan nods. "Yeah. I will."

options.text: "It's fine. Forget it. It's no big deal."
options.then: "Okay," he says, relieved. Nothing changes.

options.text: "You always do this. Everyone has noticed."
options.then: He folds his arms. "That's not fair."

options.text: "Sort it out with Asha yourself."
options.then: Rohan nods. He doesn't know where to begin.

steps.why: Assuming good faith and naming the habit helps him change.

steps.prompt: Asha stops you in the corridor and says: "About my idea. Please let me decide how it's raised."

options.text: "Okay. How would you like me to back you?"
options.then: She thinks. "Ask me to share. I'll do the rest."

options.text: "I'm only trying to help. Don't be ungrateful."

options.text: "You'd never have spoken up yourself."

steps.why: Asking how to back her respects her say in how she's supported.

scenarios.relearn: Modelling fair credit out loud, lightly, leads a group better than letting it slide.

scenarios.hook: After a family meal, the women clear the plates while the men stay seated.
scenarios.setup: Your uncle looks at you as you stand.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Sit, beta. That's not for boys."

options.text: "I'd like to. It's nobody's job."
options.then: Your uncle raises an eyebrow, then shrugs. "Hm. Your choice."

options.text: "Okay, Uncle. I'll sit."
options.then: "Good boy." You hover by your chair as the women carry the plates.

options.text: "I'll just take my own plate, then."
options.then: Uncle nods. "That's enough." The rest stays the same.

options.text: "That's so old-fashioned, Uncle."
options.then: He frowns. "Is that what they teach you?"

steps.why: A light, friendly line lets you act without shaming your elders.

steps.prompt: Your aunt passes with a stack of plates and says: "Don't worry about it, beta. We're used to it."

options.text: "Let me, Aunty. It goes faster with two."
options.then: She smiles, a little surprised. "Then take the glasses."

options.text: "Okay, Aunty. Thank you."
options.then: She nods and carries on. You stay by your chair as the plates go past.

options.text: "You shouldn't have to do all this."
options.then: She sighs. "Beta, don't start trouble."

options.text: "Then I'll ask Uncle to help too."
options.then: Her eyes widen. "No, no. Please don't."

steps.prompt: Your cousin says: "Why do you care? Nobody else does."

options.text: "It's a lot for them. Come on, grab some."

steps.prompt: Your uncle says gruffly: "Whatever they teach you, beta, this is how it has always been done."

options.text: "You're being stubborn."

options.text: "Then I'll tell Aunty not to serve you."
options.then: He stares. "You'll do no such thing."

scenarios.hook: Your juniors at the coaching centre look up to you, and a first-gen boy is too shy to ask doubts.

steps.prompt: He sits at the back during doubt time again. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with him after class and go over doubts
options.then: He starts asking, softly at first. His notes fill with answers.

options.text: Let him figure it out like you had to
options.then: He keeps quiet. His notes fill with question marks.

options.text: Tell him to ask the teacher during class
options.then: He nods. He doesn't ask, and the class moves on.

options.text: Give him your notes and leave it there
options.then: He reads them, but the doubts stay.

steps.why: Sitting with him gives a safe place to ask, which notes alone don't.

steps.prompt: He admits he's embarrassed because his English isn't strong. What do you say?

options.text: Say you struggled too, and use his language
options.then: He smiles with relief. "Yes, that's how I understand."

options.text: Tell him English will come with time
options.then: He nods. He still feels behind today.

options.text: Say he should do an English class first
options.then: He looks down. It sounds like another hurdle.

options.text: Say he doesn't need to worry about that
options.then: He nods, unconvinced.

steps.why: Sharing your own struggle and using his language makes asking feel safe.

steps.prompt: He asks you to teach him free after hours, and your own exams are close. What do you do?

options.text: Offer one weekly slot and a small study group
options.then: He's thrilled, and a classmate joins. Your exam time stays intact.

options.text: Say yes to everything and drop your own prep
options.then: You teach him daily. Your own revision slides.

options.text: Say you're too busy to help at all
options.then: He nods politely and stops asking.

options.text: Say he should pay for a tutor
options.then: He goes quiet. A tutor is out of reach for his family.

steps.why: A fixed slot and a small group let you keep helping without burning out.

steps.prompt: A term later, he tops a test, and a classmate says he must have cheated. What do you do?

options.text: Say he worked hard for it, and show his notebook
options.then: The classmate reads through it. "Okay. That's a lot of notes."

options.text: Ignore it and hope it passes
options.then: The remark sticks. He hears about it later.

options.text: Tell the classmate to shut up
options.then: He flares. The two of you are now in a fight.

options.text: Ask the teacher to check his answers
options.then: The teacher agrees. He feels more under suspicion than before.

steps.why: Standing by his work with plain facts protects him without a quarrel.

scenarios.debrief: Spending time on a shy junior's doubts is real, quiet leadership.

scenarios.hook: In the class committee, your friend's plan is ignored. Then a louder boy says it and gets clapped.

steps.prompt: The chair moves on to the next item. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Good. That's what Asha proposed earlier."
options.then: The chair turns to Asha. "Right. Asha, tell us more."

options.text: Let it slide to keep the peace
options.then: The next item starts. Asha looks at her notes.

options.text: Clap along, then tell Asha it's unfair
options.then: She agrees, but nothing changes in the room.

options.text: Ask the chair to throw out the louder boy's idea
options.then: The chair frowns. The meeting stalls and the room is irritated.

steps.why: Naming whose idea it was is a simple, powerful lift.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, Asha says she's annoyed but doesn't want a fuss. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what she'd like, and back her either way
options.then: She thinks. "Just keep naming me when it happens."

options.text: Say she should drop it, since it's only a committee
options.then: She nods and goes quiet.

options.text: Say you'll take it to the teacher for her
options.then: She flinches. "Please don't. Not yet."

options.text: Tell her to stand up to him next time
options.then: She smiles thinly. It's easier said than done.

steps.why: Asking what she wants keeps her in charge of how it's handled.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, a boy starts talking over her new plan. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Hold on. Let Asha finish."
options.then: The boy stops. Asha completes her point and the chair writes it down.

options.text: Wait for her to handle it
options.then: She stops mid-sentence. The chair moves on.

options.text: Restate her plan in your own words
options.then: The chair nods at you. Asha's name isn't mentioned.

options.text: Tell him he's being rude
options.then: He rolls his eyes. The meeting derails.

steps.why: Asking for her to finish keeps the floor hers, and the credit.

scenarios.hook: A talented girl in your group thinks stage anchor isn't for girls and won't try.

steps.prompt: Auditions for the anchor close tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Encourage her and rehearse with her

options.text: Suggest a boy who has already volunteered
options.then: He is first on the list, but the slot stays open until the meeting. She says she didn't want it anyway.

options.text: Put her name down without asking first
options.then: She finds out and panics. "I didn't say yes!"

options.text: Say she'd be good, but it's up to her
options.then: She smiles. The deadline passes while she thinks, but the committee keeps the slot open.

steps.prompt: At the planning meeting, the anchor choice is still open, and a senior says a girl anchoring would look odd to the guests. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll check with the principal first

options.text: Agree the guests may think so

options.text: Tell him he's being sexist

options.text: Offer to take over if it's too much
options.then: She hesitates, doubting herself even more.

options.text: Say the guests won't notice mistakes
options.then: She nods. Her hands are still shaking.

scenarios.hook: Your project tops the class, and the teacher assumes you did it alone and praises only you.

options.text: Enjoy the spotlight quietly

options.text: Share it only with your closest friends

scenarios.hook: A free seat at a district leadership camp is offered to you, and a quieter classmate would gain more.

steps.prompt: The coordinator wants your answer by tomorrow. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest your classmate, and say why
options.then: The coordinator notes her name. "Tell me more about her."

options.text: Take the seat, since you were asked first
options.then: You go. Your classmate never hears there was a seat.

options.text: Take the seat and promise to share your notes
options.then: You go. She reads your notes, but it isn't the same.

options.text: Tell your classmate to take your seat quietly

steps.prompt: A friend says leadership is a race, and giving chances away makes you lose. What do you say?

options.text: Say leaders are measured by who rises with them

options.text: Say he may be right, but you're not sure
options.then: He nods. You still feel unsettled.

options.text: Say what others do isn't your problem
options.then: He shrugs. The talk ends there.

options.text: Agree, and say you'll take the next one yourself
options.then: He nods. The next one keeps turning up for you.

steps.why: Real leadership shows in who rises with you, not who you pass.

options.text: Suggest open sign-ups and rotating seats
options.then: The principal writes it down. "Draft it for me."

options.text: Suggest only the top students be sent
options.then: The principal nods. The same names get chosen.

options.text: Suggest teachers pick who goes
options.then: Teachers choose their favourites. A few new names appear.

options.text: Say it's fine as it is
options.then: The principal nods. Nothing changes.

steps.why: Open sign-ups and rotation turn one gesture into a fairer system.

scenarios.debrief: Deliberately passing on an opportunity is exactly how gaps close.

scenarios.hook: A new girl joins mid-term, knows no one, and eats lunch alone every day.

steps.prompt: It's lunchtime again, and she's alone at a corner table. What do you do?

options.then: She picks up her lunch box. "Thanks. I wasn't sure."

options.text: Assume she prefers being alone
options.then: She stays in her corner. Days pass.

options.text: Smile at her from across the room
options.then: She smiles back, then returns to her lunch box.

options.text: Leave it to a teacher to arrange something
options.then: You go back to your own table. She is still in her corner.

steps.prompt: A friend says the group should stay small this term. What do you say?

options.text: Say there's room, and a new face is welcome

options.text: Agree the group should stay small
options.then: Nothing changes for the new girl.

options.text: Say she can join if she fits in

options.text: Say you'll hang out with her separately

options.text: Say the school should handle it
options.then: Your friend sighs, and nobody goes over. The new student sits alone.

options.text: Say they'll find their own group in time

options.text: Say you'll invite them if the others do

options.text: Write it yourself from your own memory
options.then: It's tidy. It misses what scared newcomers most.

options.text: Copy last year's guide with new dates

options.text: Leave it to the teacher

options.text: Quietly agree it's a long shot

options.text: Say you'll help, but keep your name off it

scenarios.hook: You've found a study method that helps you ace exams, and a classmate keeps failing the same way.

options.text: Keep your edge to yourself

options.text: Say only close friends can learn it

scenarios.hook: At home, your younger sister tries to give her opinion on a family decision.
