options.text: "I haven't really thought about it."
options.then: Dinesh raises an eyebrow. The question hangs there.

steps.why: Lifting someone doesn't take anything away from you.

steps.prompt: Dinesh says: "Okay, can you help me with algebra too? Don't tell anyone."

options.text: "Sure. Let's study together, openly. No secret needed."
options.then: He hesitates, then nods. "Okay. Fine, I'll come."

options.text: "Sure, but only if nobody finds out."
options.then: Dinesh grins. The tutoring happens, hidden, and the teasing stays unchallenged.

options.text: "Not unless you stop teasing people first."
options.then: Dinesh scowls. "Forget it. I'll ask someone else."

options.text: "Sorry. I'm too busy with my own prep right now."
options.then: Dinesh shrugs. "Okay." He goes back to struggling alone.

steps.why: Welcoming him in the open shows that learning together is normal.

scenarios.relearn: Naming that helping others is strength shuts down the 'weak' jibe.

scenarios.hook: Arman, a small-town student, is thinking about running for the student council.
scenarios.setup: He mumbles it as the nomination sheet goes round.

steps.prompt: Arman says: "Council kids are all from big English-medium schools. I don't belong."

options.text: "You'd be great. I'll back you if you go for it."
options.then: Arman looks up. "You'd actually back me?"

options.text: "Maybe it's not for you, honestly."
options.then: Arman nods. "Yeah. That's what I figured."

options.text: "Council is mostly about being popular anyway."
options.then: Arman winces. "Then I definitely don't have a chance."

options.text: "Then just apply and see what happens, okay?"
options.then: Arman shrugs. "Easy for you to say."

steps.why: Honest belief plus an offer of backing helps him step up.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Arman asks: "If I stand, what would I even say in the speech?"

options.text: "Say what you'd fix. Let's write three lines now."
options.then: He grabs a pen. Ten minutes later, he reads his lines aloud.

options.text: "Just copy last year's winning speech word for word."
options.then: Arman frowns. "That's not really me, though."

options.text: "I'll write it for you tonight."
options.then: He nods, relieved. Then he wonders whose speech it will be.

options.text: "Don't worry. Speeches never matter anyway."
options.then: Arman laughs. "Then why do people practise them?"

steps.why: Helping him find his own words keeps the message his.

steps.prompt: Arman says: "Someone told me I'd only be running to prove a point."

options.text: "You're running because you'd do it well."
options.then: He lets out a breath. "Okay. I needed to hear that."

options.text: "Then prove them wrong by winning."
options.then: Arman nods, but now every poster feels like a test.

options.text: "Ignore them. They're just jealous."
options.then: He shrugs. "Maybe. It still stung."

options.text: "Maybe wait a year so you don't seem pushy."
options.then: Arman looks down. "So I shouldn't run?"

steps.why: Grounding his reasons in his own strengths keeps his confidence steady.

scenarios.relearn: Genuine encouragement plus backing helps someone step up.

scenarios.hook: Your group's project went well, but Reha did the hardest part and stayed silent.
scenarios.setup: The class is clapping as the teacher moves on.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Thank you, whole group. Nice teamwork."

options.text: "Sir, Reha worked out the hardest part."
options.then: The teacher turns. "Is that right, Reha? Thank you."

options.text: "Thanks, sir. We all did our bit."
options.then: The teacher nods and moves on. Reha says nothing.

options.text: "Yes, sir. Reha can tell you the details later."
options.then: The teacher shrugs and opens his register. Nobody asks Reha.

options.text: "Thanks, sir. I'll tell Reha you said so."
options.then: The teacher smiles and says to pass it on. Reha hears the thanks only second-hand.

steps.why: Naming Reha in front of the teacher gives her credit where it counts.

steps.prompt: The teacher says: "Who will present this at assembly?"

options.text: "Reha knows it best. I'd like her to present."
options.then: The teacher pauses. "Reha, would you?"

options.text: "I'll do it. I'm used to speaking."
options.then: The teacher agrees. Reha leans back in her chair.

options.text: "Let's ask the group who feels like presenting."
options.then: Two loud voices volunteer. Reha says nothing.

options.text: "Whoever. Reha won't want to, I think."
options.then: The teacher nods. Reha doesn't get asked.

steps.why: Offering her the stage, and not assuming she'd refuse, gives her a real chance.

steps.prompt: Reha says: "People always give credit to the loud ones."

options.text: "Then let's make sure quiet ones get named."
options.then: Reha smiles. "Okay. I'd like that."

options.text: "Maybe you should speak up more."
options.then: Reha looks away. "I know. It isn't that easy."

options.text: "That's just how it works."
options.then: Reha shrugs. She isn't surprised.

options.text: "I'll try to speak for you from now on."
options.then: Reha hesitates. "I'd rather speak for myself, sometimes."

steps.why: Pledging to name quiet contributors changes the habit, not the person.

scenarios.relearn: Naming the quiet person whose work went unseen is how you lift, not just thank.

scenarios.hook: On the fest committee, Sana is always handed the decorations, never the lead.
scenarios.setup: The coordinator is sharing out the stage events.

steps.prompt: The coordinator says: "Sana, you'll do decorations again, right?"

options.text: "Sana should lead the stage show. She's earned it."
options.then: The coordinator blinks. "Sana? How would you feel about that?"

options.text: "Sure. Decorations are her strength."
options.then: The coordinator ticks the list. Sana nods and says nothing.

options.text: "Let's give Sana a break from decorations."
options.then: The coordinator moves her to registration. It's another background job.

options.text: "Whoever's free can lead. I'll leave it."
options.then: Two committee members raise their hands. Sana does not.

steps.why: Naming her for the lead role breaks a limiting pattern.

steps.prompt: Sana says quietly: "I'm not sure the others would listen to me if I led."

options.text: "I'll back you up in the first meeting."
options.then: Sana lifts her head. "Okay. That would help."

options.text: "Then I'll just tell them what to do for you."
options.then: Sana nods. If you do all the talking, the team may never hear her.

options.text: "They will. Just be firm."
options.then: Sana nods. She doesn't say how firm she can be.

options.text: "Maybe lead something smaller first."
options.then: Sana nods. Smaller is where she's been all year.

steps.why: Backing her visibly gives the team a reason to listen.

steps.prompt: Later, the coordinator reopens the stage list. A committee member says: "Sana isn't experienced enough to lead stage."

options.text: "She ran the whole decoration plan. That's leading."
options.then: He pauses. "Hm. I hadn't counted that."

options.text: "Okay. Maybe we should wait."
options.then: Nobody pushes back. Sana's name stays off the stage list.

options.text: "You're only saying that because she's a girl."
options.then: He bristles. "That's not fair. I just think she's new."

options.text: "Let the coordinator decide who's experienced."
options.then: The coordinator says she'll think about it. Nothing is decided.

steps.why: Pointing to what she has already led answers the doubt with facts.

scenarios.relearn: Offering someone a bigger role breaks a limiting pattern.

scenarios.hook: In the class group chat, Divya's suggestion is ignored. Then a boy repeats it and gets thanked.
scenarios.setup: The chat is still scrolling.

steps.prompt: Rahul types: "Idea! Let's run a quiz stall at the fest!"

options.text: "Yes, that was Divya's idea above. Good call, Divya."
options.then: Rahul replies: "Oh, I missed her message. Sorry, Divya!"

options.text: "Great idea, Rahul. Let's go with that one then."
options.then: Fifteen thumbs-ups land on Rahul's message. Divya's is still buried.

options.text: "Didn't someone say that earlier already, though?"
options.then: Rahul sends a shrug. Nobody works out who.

options.text: "Rahul, stop copying Divya's ideas all the time."
options.then: The chat goes silent, and then argues about Rahul instead.

steps.why: Naming Divya right in the chat puts credit where it belongs.

steps.prompt: A teacher in the chat asks: "Who proposed the quiz stall?"

options.text: "Divya did. Here's her message from earlier."
options.then: The teacher replies: "Thank you, Divya. Good idea."

options.text: "We all did, sir. It came up in the chat."
options.then: The teacher says okay. Divya says nothing.

options.text: "Rahul posted it, but it felt like a group thing."
options.then: The teacher thanks Rahul. Divya sends a sad face to you.

options.text: "Not sure, sir. Maybe ask Divya if she remembers."
options.then: The teacher sends a question mark. Nobody answers.

steps.why: Showing who proposed it, with proof, gets the credit right.

steps.prompt: Rahul types: "Let's sort the stall plan. Who wants to lead it?"

options.text: "Divya came up with it. She should lead."
options.then: Rahul replies: "Sure. Divya, tell me what you need."

options.text: "Rahul can lead the plan."
options.then: Rahul sends a thumbs-up. Divya's reply is just a dot.

options.text: "Let's just vote on who leads the plan."
options.then: The vote splits, and the louder members win.

options.text: "Rahul can lead, as long as Divya is credited on it."
options.then: Rahul says fine. Divya is still helping, not leading.

steps.why: Handing the lead to the person who had the idea completes the credit.

scenarios.relearn: Crediting the first author in the chat amplifies the right person.

scenarios.hook: A junior, Naina, is about to skip a poetry contest she would do well in.
scenarios.setup: She's folding the entry form into her bag.

steps.prompt: Naina says: "I'll probably lose, so what's the point?"

options.text: "Trying teaches you loads. I'll help you prep."
options.then: Naina looks up. "You'd help? Okay. Maybe I will."

options.text: "Maybe sit this one out if you're unsure."
options.then: Naina nods and tucks the form away. "Yeah. Maybe."

options.text: "You'll definitely win. I've heard your poems."
options.then: Naina laughs, but looks a little pressured instead.

options.text: "Then just enter and don't expect much."
options.then: Naina shrugs. "That's not very exciting."

steps.why: Naming what trying gives and offering help lifts her in.

steps.prompt: Naina says: "I don't have time to practise with exams coming."

options.text: "Fifteen minutes after school, twice a week?"
options.then: Naina counts on her fingers. "That could work."

options.text: "Skip it this year. Exams matter more."
options.then: Naina nods. The form stays in her bag.

options.text: "Then don't practise. Just wing it."
options.then: She frowns. "That sounds scary."

options.text: "Just practise whenever you can find the time."
options.then: Naina agrees. No time is ever found.

steps.why: A small fixed slot makes practice possible even in exam season.

steps.prompt: Naina says: "A senior told me juniors never win these."

options.text: "Let's read last year's winners and see how."
options.then: Naina leans in. "Okay. Let's look."

options.text: "Seniors know best. Maybe wait a year."
options.then: Naina nods. A year feels like a long way off.

options.text: "Prove her wrong. Win, whatever it takes."
options.then: Naina swallows. Now she has something to lose.

options.text: "She's just trying to scare you off."
options.then: Naina frowns. "Why would she do that?"

steps.why: Looking at real winners turns a rumour into something she can learn from.

scenarios.relearn: Encouraging her to try, with an offer to help, lifts her in.

scenarios.hook: After the family dinner, your mother starts the cleanup alone again.
scenarios.setup: The relatives are chatting in the next room.

steps.prompt: Your mother says: "You go and sit with everyone. I'll finish up here."

options.text: "Sit, Ma. I've got the dishes. Others can clear."
options.then: She pauses. "Arre, okay." She sits, looking surprised.

options.text: "Okay, Ma. Call me if you need help."
options.then: She smiles. You go to the living room. She does it all.

options.text: "Cousins, come help! Ma is doing it all again!"
options.then: The cousins groan, and your mother looks embarrassed.

options.text: "Sure, Ma. I'll just grab some water first."
options.then: She nods. By the time you come back, she's done.

steps.why: Taking the work yourself, unasked, shows sharing instead of telling.

steps.prompt: At the next dinner, your aunt says, smiling: "Arre, kitchen work is for the women of the house."

options.text: "Ma cooked for hours, Aunty. We all clear up."
options.then: Your aunt laughs, a little awkward. "Hm. I hadn't thought of that."

options.text: "Haha, true. Maybe I should go and sit."
options.then: Your aunt smiles, pleased. The women of the house clear the plates.

options.text: "That's such an old-fashioned thing to say."
options.then: Your aunt stiffens. The table goes quiet.

options.text: "Aunty, please don't say that in front of Ma."
options.then: Your aunt waves a hand. "I'm only joking." Nobody mentions it again.

steps.why: A warm, plain line holds the norm without shaming anyone.

steps.prompt: After the next dinner, your mother says: "Beta, I'm used to doing it all. It's fine."

options.text: "I know, Ma. But I'd like to. It's our home."
options.then: She smiles, softer. "Then at least let me dry."

options.text: "Okay. I'll only help when you ask."
options.then: She nods. She seldom asks.

options.text: "It's not fair that you do it all, Ma."
options.then: She looks uncomfortable. "It's how we do it, beta."

options.text: "Then Papa should do it instead of you, Ma."
options.then: She laughs. "Ask him that yourself." Nobody does.

steps.why: Saying why you help makes it a habit, not a one-off favour.

scenarios.relearn: Taking the load yourself, unasked, lifts and models sharing.

scenarios.hook: A junior, Anjali, has her first interviews coming up and looks to you.
scenarios.setup: She catches you at the library door.

steps.prompt: Anjali says: "Could you show me how you prep? I'm terrified."

options.text: "Of course. Let's do a practice round Saturday."
options.then: Anjali's shoulders drop. "Saturday works. Thank you!"

options.text: "I'm pretty busy. Just look it up online."
options.then: Anjali nods quickly. "Okay. Sorry to ask."

options.text: "Sure. I'll send you my notes sometime."
options.then: She thanks you. The notes never quite arrive.

options.text: "Ask the career counsellor. They run sessions often."
options.then: Anjali says okay. The counsellor's sessions are full for weeks.

steps.why: A real time and a practice round make mentoring concrete.

steps.prompt: Anjali finds you again before her interviews and says: "I'm worried I'll freeze when they ask about my weaknesses."

options.text: "Let's draft an honest answer together, then rehearse it."
options.then: Anjali writes a line. "That actually sounds like me."

options.text: "Just tell them you work too hard."
options.then: Anjali frowns. "They'll know that's a cliché."

options.text: "Don't worry. Nobody really freezes in the real thing."
options.then: Anjali looks unsure. "I think I might."

options.text: "Just say you don't have any weaknesses."
options.then: Anjali laughs nervously. "That can't be true."

steps.why: Writing an honest answer together gives her something solid to say.

steps.prompt: Anjali says: "A friend wants help too, but I didn't think you'd have time."

options.text: "Bring her along. There's room for her too."
options.then: Anjali brightens. "Really? She'll be so happy."

options.text: "Yeah, I'm quite busy. Maybe not this time."
options.then: Anjali nods. Her friend stays unprepared.

options.text: "Give her a printed list of common questions instead."
options.then: Anjali nods. Her friend gets the list without the practice.

options.text: "Only if she's serious. Not everyone is."
options.then: Anjali frowns. "She is. I think."

steps.why: Making room for another junior grows the circle of help.

scenarios.relearn: Saying yes to mentoring, with a real time, is a true lift.

scenarios.hook: You and your friend Sana co-designed a poster for the class.
scenarios.setup: She holds it up in front of the class.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Wonderful poster. All your own work, I hear?"

options.text: "Thank you. Sana co-designed it. The layout was hers."
options.then: The teacher turns to Sana. "Sana? It's lovely work, then."

options.text: "Thank you, ma'am. I'm glad you like it so much."
options.then: The teacher beams. Sana studies her shoes.

options.text: "Thanks. Sana helped a little with the colours."
options.then: The teacher nods. Sana's real part is shrunk to a footnote.

options.text: "Thank you. Can we talk about it after class?"
options.then: The teacher says of course, and looks around for where to display it.

steps.why: Naming Sana right away keeps the credit fair.

steps.prompt: The teacher says: "Lovely. Shall I put it on the main notice board? I'll need a name for the card."

options.text: "Please put both our names. We made it together."
options.then: The teacher writes both names on a card and smiles.

options.text: "Yes, please. Just my name is fine."
options.then: The teacher pins it up with one name. Sana walks by it daily.

options.text: "Maybe. Sana may not mind either way, though."
options.then: The teacher shrugs and uses only your name.

options.text: "Put it up. I'll sort out names later."
options.then: The poster goes up. "Later" never comes round.

steps.why: Putting both names on display makes the credit lasting.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "I didn't want to make a fuss about the poster."

options.text: "It isn't a fuss. Your work should have your name."
options.then: Sana smiles. "Okay. Thanks for saying it."

options.text: "Right. Let's just forget about it, then."
options.then: Sana nods. She looks relieved, then a little sad.

options.text: "You should have said something earlier, then."
options.then: Sana flushes. "I didn't know how to."

options.text: "I'll just give you credit next time instead."
options.then: Sana nods. "Okay." Next time is far away.

steps.why: Saying credit isn't a fuss helps her feel entitled to it.

scenarios.relearn: Naming a co-creator when you're over-credited keeps it fair.

scenarios.hook: A capable girl, Ishita, is talked over when she volunteers to captain the team.
scenarios.setup: Your coach is asking for volunteers.

steps.prompt: Your coach says: "Imran says he'll captain. Anyone else?"

options.text: "Ishita volunteered first. Let's hear her plan."
options.then: The coach pauses. "Ishita? Go ahead."

options.text: "No, Imran's fine. Let's get on with it."
options.then: The coach nods. Ishita's hand stays half-raised, then drops.

options.text: "Ishita, go on. You need to speak up louder."
options.then: Ishita goes red and says, "Never mind." The coach moves on.

options.text: "Maybe ask the team to vote quietly, coach."
options.then: The coach shrugs. The vote starts, and Imran has the louder friends.

steps.why: Naming Ishita and asking to hear her plan gives her the floor.

steps.prompt: Imran whispers: "Come on. A girl captain? The guys won't listen."

options.text: "They'll listen to a good plan. Let's hear it."
options.then: Imran hesitates. "Fine. Let's hear it."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Let's not risk it yet."
options.then: Imran grins. Ishita notices and goes quiet.

options.text: "That's so sexist, Imran. Shame on you."
options.then: Imran snaps, "Don't say that. I was just being real."

options.text: "Let the team decide. I won't take any sides."
options.then: Imran nods. The loudest voices decide the day.

steps.why: Asking him to judge her plan, not her gender, moves the talk to facts.

steps.prompt: Ishita tells you: "If I'm picked, I'm worried the team will test me."

options.text: "They might. I'll back your calls in front of them."
options.then: Ishita nods slowly. "That helps a lot. Thank you."

options.text: "Then don't take it if you're worried."
options.then: Ishita looks away. "Maybe you're right."

options.text: "Just ignore them. Captains don't get tested."
options.then: Ishita smiles, but doesn't believe it.

options.text: "I'll make sure nobody tests you. Don't worry."
options.then: Ishita laughs. "You can't promise that."

steps.why: Backing her calls in public builds the team's trust in her.

scenarios.relearn: Saying out loud that she's capable backs her into the role.

scenarios.hook: A scholarship form lands on your desk. It fits a friend's situation far better than yours.
scenarios.setup: Your friend Farhan sits down next to you.

steps.prompt: Farhan says: "Is that the scholarship form? I wish I'd known."

options.text: "It suits you more than me. Want help applying?"
options.then: Farhan looks stunned. "Really? For me? Okay. Yes."

options.text: "Yes, and I'm applying for it. Sorry, Farhan."
options.then: Farhan nods. "Of course. I get it." He asks if he can still get a copy to try.

options.text: "I'll tell you the details if I don't get it."
options.then: Farhan nods. By then the deadline will be near.

options.text: "It's due soon. Just check the notice board."
options.then: Farhan thanks you. He doesn't know where to start.

steps.why: Passing the chance on with real help opens the door.

steps.prompt: Farhan asks: "What if I don't qualify after all?"

options.text: "Let's read the criteria together and check."
options.then: You go through the page, line by line. Farhan relaxes.

options.text: "You will. I'm sure you qualify, Farhan."
options.then: Farhan smiles. He still hasn't checked the criteria.

options.text: "Then forget it. Don't waste your time on it."
options.then: Farhan slumps. "Right. Why bother."

options.text: "Ask the teacher. They'll know about it all."
options.then: Farhan nods and puts it off. The teacher is away this week.

steps.why: Checking the criteria together turns doubt into a plan.

steps.prompt: Farhan says: "My parents think we shouldn't take charity."

options.text: "It's a scholarship you qualify for, not charity. Want me to explain?"
options.then: Farhan thinks. "Maybe. They'd listen to you."

options.text: "Then maybe don't tell them about it."
options.then: Farhan frowns. "I can't hide that from them."

options.text: "Your parents just don't understand how it works."
options.then: Farhan stiffens. "They understand more than you think."

options.text: "Then skip it, since they feel that way."
options.then: Farhan nods slowly. The form goes back in the folder.

steps.why: Explaining respectfully lets his family decide with the facts.

scenarios.relearn: Passing on a chance that suits someone better, and helping them take it, opens a door.

scenarios.hook: You helped a junior, Yash, get through his exams, and he has come to thank you.
scenarios.setup: He hands you a thank-you note.

steps.prompt: Yash says: "I got through because of you. How can I ever repay you?"

options.text: "Pay it forward. Help the next person."
options.then: Yash grins. "Okay. I can do that."

options.text: "Just remember it was me who helped you."
options.then: Yash nods, a little deflated. "Of course. I will."

options.text: "A treat at the canteen would be nice."
options.then: Yash laughs and buys you a samosa. The favour is square.

options.text: "No need. It was nothing, really."
options.then: Yash smiles. He still feels he owes something.

steps.why: Asking him to help the next person multiplies the lift.

steps.prompt: A week later, Yash says: "I keep wondering how to give back. Who could I help? I don't know who needs it."

options.text: "Look for someone struggling. Offer a little time."
options.then: Yash thinks. "There's a classmate who sits alone. I'll try."

options.text: "Wait until you're a topper. Then help."
options.then: Yash laughs, unsure. "That could take years."

options.text: "Pick someone popular. They'll spread the word."
options.then: Yash nods. The popular kid doesn't need him.

options.text: "Leave it to me. I'll pick someone for you."
options.then: Yash shrugs. "Okay." He waits, then picks a classmate himself.

steps.why: Pointing him to someone nearby makes the first step easy.

steps.prompt: Days later, Yash says: "I went ahead and offered help to a classmate, but he says he doesn't need it."

options.text: "Say the offer is open. Some people take time."
options.then: Yash nods. "Okay. I'll check in once, lightly."

options.text: "Then don't bother. Not everyone wants help."
options.then: Yash shrugs. He drops the idea for good.

options.text: "Insist. He'll thank you later."
options.then: Yash winces. "That feels pushy."

options.text: "Tell the teacher he's refusing help."
options.then: Yash frowns. "That would just embarrass him."

steps.why: Leaving the door open respects his pace and keeps help available.

scenarios.relearn: Asking a mentee to help the next person multiplies the lift.

scenarios.hook: At a family dinner, your uncle has strong views on women and work.
scenarios.setup: Plates are being passed when he says it.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "There's no pay gap. Women pick easy jobs."

options.text: "Women often earn less for the same work, Uncle."
options.then: He frowns. "Same work? Who told you that?"

options.text: "You may be right, Uncle. I haven't checked."
options.then: He nods, pleased. "Exactly. Glad someone agrees."

options.text: "Whatever. Can we please just eat dinner now?"
options.then: He sighs and passes the dal. The claim stands.

options.text: "That's the most ignorant thing I've heard today."
options.then: He bristles. "Is that how you speak to elders?"

steps.why: A short, plain fact opens the talk without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says: "Besides, women quit jobs for families anyway."

options.text: "Often because home care falls on them, not always by choice."
options.then: He pauses. "Hm. So it's not that they want less?"

options.text: "True. So it makes sense that they earn less."
options.then: He smiles, satisfied. Your cousin looks at you, startled.

options.text: "That's only an excuse you tell yourself, Uncle."
options.then: His face hardens. "I don't have to listen to this."

options.text: "I don't really know. Let's drop it for tonight."
options.then: He shrugs and takes a second helping.

steps.why: Naming the care load shows it's a structural cause, not simply women's choice.

steps.prompt: Later, your aunt catches you in the kitchen and says quietly: "Beta, your uncle is set in his ways. Will you bring this up with him again?"

options.text: "I do respect him, Aunty. I'd just like to share what I read."
options.then: She softens. "Hm. As long as you stay polite."

options.text: "You're right, Aunty. I'll leave it there."
options.then: She nods, relieved. "Good. Let's keep dinners peaceful."

options.text: "He may mean well, Aunty, but it's still a myth."
options.then: She gasps. "Don't say that about your uncle!" She hurries back to the others.

options.text: "I'll take it up with him on WhatsApp later."
options.then: She shrugs. Nobody reads that chat anyway.

steps.why: Saying it politely respects her worry and keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: Your uncle says later: "Why do you even care about all this?"

options.text: "It affects women I care about. That's why."
options.then: He's quiet. "I never thought of it that way."

options.text: "No reason, Uncle. I just like a good argument."
options.then: He laughs. "You get that from your father."

options.text: "Because everyone is posting about it online lately."
options.then: He sniffs. "Online. That explains it."

options.text: "Because someone at this table needed correcting."
options.then: He stiffens and walks off. The talk is over.

steps.why: Making it personal and warm shows why fairness matters.

scenarios.relearn: Women earn less for the same work; it's mostly bias and the care load.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Aman is in a grumpy mood in the group chat.
scenarios.setup: He's complaining about his mother nagging him.

steps.prompt: Aman writes: "Housework isn't real work, yaar. Mum's always home."

options.text: "It's hours of real work daily. It's just unpaid."
options.then: He sends a thinking face. "Hours? Really?"

options.text: "Haha. I guess so. Never thought about it much."
options.then: He sends a laugh. The chat moves on.

options.text: "Anyway. Has anyone sorted the trip plan yet?"
options.then: Someone replies about trains. Aman's remark sits there.

options.text: "Your mum would be so hurt to hear that."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Why are you making it about my mum?"

steps.why: Naming the hours makes invisible work visible.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Aman writes: "Mum was sick yesterday. I had to cook. It's hard."

options.text: "Hope she's better. Now you know it's real work."
options.then: He replies: "Yeah. I burned the rice twice."

options.text: "Told you. I was right about everything."
options.then: He sends a flat "ok". The mood in the chat drops.

options.text: "Haha. Welcome to the kitchen, chef. Enjoy."
options.then: He sends a laughing face. The point passes him by.

options.text: "It's just once. Don't make it a big deal."
options.then: He shrugs. "Right. Just once."

steps.why: Linking his own experience to the point lets him see it for himself.

steps.prompt: The next day, Aman asks: "How do I start helping at home without making it weird?"

options.text: "Pick one regular job. Do it without being asked."
options.then: He types: "Dishes after dinner. Okay."

options.text: "Just tell her you'll help whenever she asks."
options.then: He sends a thumbs-up. She'll have to ask every time.

options.text: "Make a big announcement so she notices."
options.then: He cringes. "That's so awkward."

options.text: "Do everything for one day, then stop."
options.then: He groans. "That sounds exhausting. And pointless."

steps.why: A steady, unasked job shares the load for real.

steps.prompt: Aman says: "My dad says men don't do that stuff."

options.text: "Maybe not before. Show him by quietly doing it."
options.then: He smiles. "People change when they watch. I'll try."

options.text: "Then don't, so you stay out of trouble."
options.then: He nods. The dishes go back to his mother.

options.text: "Tell him he's old-fashioned."
options.then: He winces. "I can't say that to my father."

options.text: "Do it secretly so he doesn't see."
options.then: He frowns. "Then nobody learns anything."

steps.why: Quiet example persuades family without a fight.

scenarios.relearn: Housework is hours of real, daily labour, just unpaid and uncounted.

scenarios.hook: You have started speaking up for equal lab turns, and a friend has noticed.
scenarios.setup: He catches you after practical class.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "You're always taking the girls' side now."

options.text: "It's not sides. Fairness helps everyone."
options.then: He pauses. "Everyone? Even us?"

options.text: "Fine. I'll stay out of it from now on."
options.then: He grins. "Good. Back to normal."

options.text: "You're right. Maybe I'm overdoing it."
options.then: He claps your shoulder. The lab turns stay as unequal as before.

options.text: "Better than taking the side of whoever shouts loudest."
options.then: His face tightens. "Wow. Okay."

steps.why: Naming fairness calmly shows that standing for it isn't a side.

steps.prompt: Another friend says: "Bro, boys should stick together."

options.text: "Sticking together is fine. So is being fair."
options.then: He shrugs. "I guess both can be true."

options.text: "True. We should stick together."
options.then: He nods, pleased. The girls' side of the lab goes quiet again.

options.text: "You're all being unfair right now."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Yaar, relax."

options.text: "Whatever. I'll do what I want."
options.then: He shrugs. The group turns to a game.

steps.why: Holding both loyalties shows fairness isn't disloyalty.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your friend asks: "Why does it even matter to you?"

options.text: "Equality is good for all of us, including you."
options.then: He thinks. "Including me? How?"

options.text: "It doesn't. I'm just copying someone."
options.then: He laughs. "Knew it."

options.text: "Because I'm better at this than you."
options.then: He scoffs. "Sure you are."

options.text: "I don't know. Forget it."
options.then: He nods. The question stays open.

steps.why: Saying that equality helps everyone is a strong, honest reason.

steps.prompt: A classmate, Sana, says: "We can speak for ourselves, you know."

options.text: "Of course. I'll amplify you, not speak over you."
options.then: Sana nods. "That's what I wanted. Thanks."

options.text: "Fine. I'll stay out of your way."
options.then: Sana shrugs. Her points are still talked over.

options.text: "Then you should speak up more."
options.then: Sana's jaw tightens. "I do. They don't hear it."

options.text: "I'm only helping, so you should be grateful."
options.then: Sana's face closes. "I didn't ask for gratitude."

steps.why: Amplifying without speaking over lets her lead her own cause.

scenarios.relearn: Backing fairness isn't picking a side; it helps everyone and it's just decent.

scenarios.hook: In a debate-club warm-up, a peer picks a topic on women in politics.
scenarios.setup: You're asked to respond to him.

steps.prompt: Your peer says: "Reserving seats for women is just reverse unfairness."

options.text: "It fixes a long shortfall of women in power."
options.then: He tilts his head. "A shortfall? Since when?"

options.text: "Maybe. I haven't really decided on that yet."
options.then: He smirks. "So you agree with me."

options.text: "Let's not argue about politics, yaar."
options.then: He shrugs. "Fine, but I still want your answer."

options.text: "Only someone sexist would say a thing like that."
options.then: He glares. "Wow. So I can't even ask a question?"

steps.why: Naming the long shortfall frames seats as balance, not unfairness.

steps.prompt: Your peer asks: "Honestly, shouldn't the best candidates just win?"

options.text: "Yes. But talent is everywhere. Seats open doors."
options.then: He hesitates. "Hm. Door first, then merit?"

options.text: "Absolutely. Merit is all that matters."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. The question about who gets heard is dropped.

options.text: "Women are simply better candidates than men overall."
options.then: He laughs. "Now you're just being silly."

options.text: "I'm not sure. Ask someone older about it."
options.then: He shrugs. The question hangs in the room.

steps.why: Seats widen who gets a fair chance to show merit.

steps.prompt: Another peer says: "Won't it just put politicians' wives in the seats?"

options.text: "Fair worry. Many women lead on their own, and we should watch."
options.then: She nods. "So it's the next step, not the end."

options.text: "No. That never happens."
options.then: She raises her eyebrows. "Never? Really?"

options.text: "Probably. So it's all pointless anyway."
options.then: She smiles. "Exactly. Why bother?"

options.text: "I won't talk about family politics, sorry."
options.then: She shrugs. Nobody answers her worry.

steps.why: Admitting a real worry builds trust and keeps the point.

steps.prompt: Your coach asks: "What would you actually do about it?"

options.text: "Back women candidates, ask questions, and vote."
options.then: She nods. "Concrete. I like that."

options.text: "Nothing really. It's up to the politicians."
options.then: She sighs. "Hm. Anyone else?"

options.text: "Rant online until everything changes somehow."
options.then: She smiles thinly. "Rants rarely change much."

options.text: "Wait for the next generation to sort it all out."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "And what do they wait for?"

steps.why: A concrete, doable action is what turns an opinion into leadership.

scenarios.relearn: Reserved seats balance a long shortfall of women in power; that's repair, not unfairness.

scenarios.hook: Your group has a quieter member, Mitali, who rarely gets to present.
scenarios.setup: You're planning the project presentation together.

steps.prompt: Your teammate says: "If you help her present, you'll look less good."

options.text: "Lifting her makes the whole team stronger."
options.then: He frowns. "Stronger? Not for you."

options.text: "Hmm. Maybe I should just do it all myself."
options.then: He nods, satisfied. Mitali's turn is left hanging.

options.text: "Yeah. Good point. Let's pick whoever presents best."
options.then: He grins. "Smart." The best talkers get the slots, and Mitali is not one.

options.text: "Don't tell me how to spend my own time."
options.then: He scowls. "Fine. Don't say I didn't warn you."

steps.why: Helping a teammate shine strengthens the whole team's work.

steps.prompt: The next day, Mitali says: "I'd like to present too, but I'm worried about the slides."

options.text: "Let's build them together. Then you present."
options.then: Mitali relaxes. "Together. Okay, yes."

options.text: "I'll do the slides. You just read them."
options.then: She nods, relieved. The slides aren't hers.

options.text: "Just wing it. You'll be fine on the day."
options.then: She goes pale. "Wing it? I can't."

options.text: "Maybe the teacher can pick someone else."
options.then: She nods quietly. Her turn is gone.

steps.why: Building the slides together makes her presentation her own.

steps.prompt: Your teammate says: "The teacher is grading each of us. Share less credit."

options.text: "Credit isn't a fixed pie. We all gain."
options.then: He pauses. "Hm. If the team does better, maybe so do we."

options.text: "True. I'll keep the best parts for myself."
options.then: He smiles. Mitali gets the leftover slides.

options.text: "We'll see what the teacher says."
options.then: He shrugs. The question goes unanswered.

options.text: "Fine. I'll mention her name only once."
options.then: He nods. Mitali's work shrinks to one mention.

steps.why: Credit isn't a fixed pie, and teams gain when all are seen.

steps.prompt: Your teacher asks: "Whose names should I credit for this project?"

options.text: "Mitali's name belongs there too. Credit her, ma'am."
options.then: She writes down Mitali's name. "Thank you. Noted."

options.text: "We did it together. Credit the group."
options.then: She nods, ticking the box. Nobody is named.

options.text: "Me, ma'am. I organised the team and the work."
options.then: She writes your name. Mitali looks at her notes.

options.text: "Whoever the others say, ma'am."
options.then: She waits. Nobody speaks, so she moves on.

steps.why: Naming the real contributor passes credit on to the person who earned it.

scenarios.relearn: Lifting a teammate makes the whole team stronger; it's not a loss for you.

scenarios.hook: A relative questions your late-night studying for boards.
scenarios.setup: She stops you in the hallway at a family function.

steps.prompt: Your relative says: "Why study so hard? You'll just get married."

options.text: "My education is mine, whatever else comes."
options.then: She blinks. "Hm. I didn't think you'd say it so calmly."

options.text: "Maybe I'm studying too hard for nothing."
options.then: She nods, pleased. You feel your chest tighten.

options.text: "I don't know, Aunty. You might be right."
options.then: She pats your arm and nods, as if the matter is nearly settled.

options.text: "That's such an outdated thing to say, Aunty."
options.then: She stiffens. "Is that how you speak to your elders?"

steps.why: Calmly claiming your education keeps respect and your own values.

steps.prompt: Your relative says: "Boys need careers. Girls need good matches."

options.text: "Girls need careers too. I'm building mine."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "Careers too? You're ambitious."

options.text: "Maybe. Let's not talk about it now."
options.then: She nods, and the topic stays alive in her mind.

options.text: "That's what's wrong with this family."
options.then: The room goes silent. Your mother looks mortified.

options.text: "Everyone says that. I'll stop mentioning it."
options.then: She smiles. Your plans go back into your bag.

steps.why: Claiming your career calmly respects her without arguing.

steps.prompt: Your mother says quietly: "Beta, I heard the relatives. What do you want to do about your studies?"

options.text: "I want to keep going. Can I explain my plan, Ma?"
options.then: She sighs, then nods. "Okay. Tell me."

options.text: "Nothing, Ma. I'll stop talking about studies."
options.then: She smiles, relieved. The plan goes quiet.

options.text: "Tell the relatives to stop asking me."
options.then: Your mother's face closes. "I can't tell them that."

options.text: "I'll just do it behind their backs."
options.then: She looks worried. "That will only cause more trouble."

steps.why: Showing your plan brings your mother in as an ally.

steps.prompt: Your counsellor asks: "What's your plan after boards?"

options.text: "Apply to the college I want, and share my plan with my parents."
options.then: He nods. "Then let's work out the steps."

options.text: "Wait and see what my family decides."
options.then: He tilts his head. "And what do you want?"

options.text: "Do whatever my cousins do."
options.then: He smiles gently. "Their path may not be yours."

options.text: "Keep it vague so nobody argues."
options.then: He sighs. "Vague plans rarely get you anywhere."

steps.why: A concrete plan, shared with family, keeps your goal and your bonds together.

scenarios.relearn: A girl's education is hers to keep; she leads best from her own values.

scenarios.hook: You're a boy who keeps raising fairness at home and school.
scenarios.setup: Your friend corners you, genuinely puzzled.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Equality is women's business. Why do you care?"

options.text: "It's everyone's business. Boys speaking up matters."
options.then: He blinks. "Boys? Why would that matter?"

options.text: "True. It's not really my thing."
options.then: He nods. "Right? Glad you see it."

options.text: "My sister made me, that's all."
options.then: He laughs. "Tell your sister to fight her own battles."

options.text: "Because someone has to teach you boys."
options.then: He rolls his eyes. "Wow. Thanks, professor."

steps.why: Saying it's everyone's business makes allyship normal.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend says: "Honestly, don't boys lose out if girls get more?"

options.text: "Not really. Equal roles free boys too."
options.then: He considers it. "Free? Like how?"

options.text: "Maybe. That's why I keep quiet sometimes."
options.then: He nods. The worry stays right where it was.

options.text: "Boys have it easy anyway. They can handle it."
options.then: He scoffs. "Easy? You don't know my life."

options.text: "I don't know. Let's drop it."
options.then: He shrugs. The question sits there.

steps.why: Naming how equality helps boys too answers the fear behind it.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "Other boys will think you're weak for this."

options.text: "Speaking up for fairness takes guts. I'm fine."
options.then: He pauses. "Fine. Maybe it does."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll tone it down."
options.then: He nods. You say less after that.

options.text: "Let them think what they like. I'll show them."
options.then: He sighs. "Chill. I'm only telling you."

options.text: "Nobody notices what I do anyway."
options.then: He shrugs. "Maybe." You wonder whether it matters at all.

steps.why: Standing up for fairness shows strength, not weakness.

steps.prompt: A week later, your friend says: "Suppose I did want to help. What would I even do?"

options.text: "Start small. Share a chore and skip the jokes."
options.then: He nods slowly. "Chores. I can do that."

options.text: "Post about it every day, so everyone sees."
options.then: He grimaces. "I'm not doing that."

options.text: "Just agree with whatever girls say."
options.then: He frowns. "That's not fair either."

options.text: "Nothing. Just think about it for now."
options.then: He nods. Thinking alone changes nothing yet.

steps.why: Small, steady actions are how allies begin.

scenarios.relearn: Equality is everyone's business; boys speaking up is one of the strongest levers.

scenarios.hook: You suggest sharing chores fairly at home.
scenarios.setup: You're both washing up after lunch.

steps.prompt: Your sibling says: "One person can't change anything anyway."

options.text: "One person living it shifts the room."
options.then: They roll their eyes. "Sure. Let's see."

options.text: "Yeah. You're probably right. Why bother?"
options.then: They nod. "See? Easier that way."

options.text: "Maybe I'm just being dramatic about chores."
options.then: They shrug. The chores stay as they are.

options.text: "Then I'll wait until someone important does it."
options.then: They snort. "That could be forever."

steps.why: One person modelling the change shifts everyone around them.

steps.prompt: At dinner, your father asks: "Who will lay the table today?"

options.text: "I'll do it today. Let's do a rota from tomorrow."
options.then: Your father blinks. "A rota? Hm. Okay, try it."

options.text: "Not me. I did it last time."
options.then: He sighs and gets up himself. Nobody else moves.

options.text: "Ask Ma. She always does it."
options.then: Your mother half-rises, then sighs and does it.

options.text: "Let's wait for someone to volunteer."
options.then: Silence. The food gets cold.

steps.why: Doing it now and offering a fair rota turns a moment into a habit.

steps.prompt: Your sibling says: "Chore plans never last in our house."

options.text: "Maybe. Let's try one week and see what we learn."
options.then: They shrug. "One week. Fine."

options.text: "You're right. Let's not bother."
options.then: They smile. The idea quietly dies.

options.text: "They will if I nag everyone every day."
options.then: They groan. "Nobody wants a nagging rota."

options.text: "Then you do it all, since you know best."
options.then: They scowl. "That's not fair either."

steps.why: A short trial week keeps trying simple and low-stakes.

steps.prompt: Your friend says: "I want to share chores at home too. How do I start?"

options.text: "Pick one job and do it unasked. Others may follow."
options.then: She nods. "One job. I'll start with dinner."

options.text: "Make a big speech first, then they'll follow."
options.then: She winces. "My family would just laugh."

options.text: "Wait for the right moment. It'll come."
options.then: She nods. Months pass, and the moment doesn't.

options.text: "Only start if everyone agrees to it first."
options.then: She sighs. "Nobody will agree. So I won't start."

steps.why: One unasked job is how you show, not tell, the change.

scenarios.relearn: One person living the change shifts the room; starting beats waiting.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that DENY the real, measured gaps.

scene.text: Women carry far more unpaid care at home
"There's honestly no pay gap left"
Boards and benches are still mostly men
"Women just aren't built to lead"
A law now reserves seats for women

scenarios.why: Both flagged lines deny measured facts: the pay gap is real, and the leadership gap is barriers, not biology.
scenarios.relearn: The gaps are measured; flat denials like these are the myth.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that blame women for the gaps instead of the system.

scene.text: Bias makes hiring mothers harder
"They just don't try hard enough"
The care load eats women's work hours
"It's pure laziness, nothing else"
Steering girls from STEM narrows careers

scenarios.why: The flagged lines pin the gap on women's effort; the real causes are bias, care load and steering.
scenarios.relearn: The gaps are structural; 'they don't try' is victim-blaming, not a cause.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that frame equality as men losing out.

scene.text: Sharing care frees boys from rigid roles
"Equality just means men suffer"
Fairer homes make families stronger
"Every gain for her is a loss for me"
Equality lifts everyone, men included

scenarios.why: The flagged lines treat equality as zero-sum; in truth it's not a loss for men, it lifts everyone.
scenarios.relearn: Equality isn't men losing out; it lifts everyone, men included.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that wave away unpaid care as 'not work.'

scene.text: Cooking and cleaning is hours of daily labour
"Housework isn't really work"
Care work holds families and the economy up
"She just sits at home all day"
Unpaid care is invisible in GDP but real

scenarios.why: The flagged lines dismiss real, exhausting labour; unpaid care is huge, essential work women mostly do.
scenarios.relearn: Unpaid care is real, essential work, not 'just sitting at home.'

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that treat leading on equality as weakness or betrayal.

scene.text: Backing equality shows real strength
"A guy who supports this is weak"
It's everyone's job, not a side to pick
"You're betraying the boys by helping"
Standing for fairness is just maturity

scenarios.why: The flagged lines paint male allyship as weakness or betrayal; leading on equality is strength and maturity.
scenarios.relearn: Leading on equality is strength, not weakness or betrayal, for boys and men.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that fake-blame women's 'choices' for the pay gap.

scene.text: Women earn less even for the same work
"They just pick the easy, low-pay jobs"
Bias slows women's promotions
"No one's stopping them, it's all choice"
The care load limits hours for paid work

scenarios.why: The flagged lines blame 'choice'; much of the pay gap is bias and the unpaid-care load.
scenarios.relearn: Much of the pay gap is bias and care load, not women's free 'choice.'

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that spread fatalism about the gaps.

scene.text: The gaps close when people and policy act
"One person can't change anything"
Progress so far came from real effort
"It's hopeless, just leave it alone"
Lifting one person can shift a room

scenarios.why: The flagged lines preach helplessness; the gaps are fixable and one person genuinely shifts a room.
scenarios.relearn: The gaps are fixable through action; fatalism is the myth, not the truth.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that claim the gaps are already fully closed.

scene.text: Gaps have shrunk but clearly remain
"It's all completely equal now"
Women are still scarce in top roles
"There's nothing left to fix"
Surveys still measure a real care gap

scenarios.why: The flagged lines declare equality finished; measured gaps in pay, leadership and care still remain.
scenarios.relearn: Real gaps remain; 'it's all equal now' is a comforting myth, not fact.

scenarios.hook: In your group project, the boys keep presenting and the girls keep taking notes.

steps.prompt: The next presentation is coming up and the pattern is repeating. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest splitting roles by skill and interest
options.then: The group pauses. Someone says, "Okay. Who's actually best at what?"

options.text: Say nothing, since it's not your problem
options.then: The pattern repeats. The same voices go unheard.

options.text: Loudly call the boys sexist in front of the class
options.then: The boys get defensive and the point is lost in the noise.

options.text: Offer to present, and leave the others as they are
options.then: You present well. The notes stay with the same people.

steps.why: Roles by skill and interest, said calmly, change the pattern.

steps.prompt: At the next meeting, Rohit says boys just speak better, so it's easier this way. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest everyone tries one slide and the group judges
options.then: Rohit shrugs. "Fine. One slide each, then."

options.text: Agree it's easier and drop the subject
options.then: Rohit smiles. The roles stay exactly as they are.

options.text: Tell him that's a sexist excuse and nothing else
options.then: Rohit goes cold. The meeting turns into an argument.

options.text: Offer to write the notes if he presents
options.then: Rohit nods happily. You've taken the notes role yourself.

steps.why: A fair trial lets skill, not habit, decide.

steps.prompt: Anika, who has taken notes all term, says she'd like to present but hasn't wanted to push. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her to just speak up at the meeting herself

options.text: Tell the group she must present next, no discussion

options.text: Tell her notes matter just as much as presenting
options.then: Anika shrugs. "I know. I'd still like a turn."

steps.why: Backing her to try gives her a real chance, at her pace.

steps.prompt: A boy from another group jokes that boys always present best. What do you say?

options.text: Say "Whoever prepares best presents best," and move on
options.then: He shrugs. A couple of people nod.

options.text: Laugh along so you fit in
options.then: He grins. Anika's face closes as she walks past.

options.text: Argue with him until he backs down
options.then: He digs in and raises his voice. A small crowd gathers.

options.text: Tell him he's backward and walk away
options.then: He mutters to his friends. Nothing changes.

steps.why: A light, steady line sets the norm without making a scene.

scenarios.debrief: Assigning roles by skill, said calmly, leads the room without shaming.
scenarios.relearn: Roles by skill and interest, not gender, is leadership by example.

scenarios.hook: After dinner, the clean-up always lands on your sister while you relax.

steps.prompt: She starts clearing the plates again. What do you do?

options.text: Get up and share the clean-up, unasked
options.then: She looks surprised, and a cousin starts stacking plates too.

options.text: Promise to help next time
options.then: She nods. She carries it again tonight.

options.text: Announce how progressive you're being as you clear a plate
options.then: Everyone smiles, and your sister rolls her eyes at the speech.

options.text: Ask her if she needs any help
options.then: "No, it's fine," she says. She does it herself.

steps.why: Sharing the load yourself, unasked, shifts the home norm.

steps.prompt: Your father says from the sofa: "Let her do it. She's quick at it." What do you do?

options.text: Say "Let's all do a bit. I'll start," and start
options.then: Your father chuckles and, after a moment, picks up a glass.

options.text: Laugh and stay on the sofa
options.then: Your sister keeps going. Nobody speaks.

options.text: Tell him loudly that he should help too

options.text: Tell your sister to say no next time
