options.text: Tell yourself that thinking about fairness is enough
options.then: It feels like progress. Nobody's day changes.

steps.why: Keeping it small keeps it alive when life gets busy.

steps.prompt: A cousin laughs that small steps change nothing. What do you do?

options.text: Say small steps add up, and you mean to try one
options.then: He shrugs. A week later he asks how it's going.

options.text: Agree that small steps are pointless and drop it
options.then: He nods, satisfied. Your idea quietly stops.

options.text: Argue with him until he stops answering you
options.then: He backs off, annoyed. You feel less sure.

options.text: Stop telling anyone what you're doing anymore
options.then: It feels safer. You also miss a chance to bring someone along.

steps.why: Steady, small action shows its worth without a debate.

scenarios.debrief: A concrete small step is how leadership actually begins.
scenarios.relearn: A real plan is one small, specific action you'll do this week.

scenarios.hook: In your study group, the same girl, Rina, always ends up taking the notes.

steps.prompt: The group is dividing roles for a new unit. What do you do?

options.text: Propose rotating roles by interest, not gender
options.then: Most agree. Rina smiles. "Can I try presenting?" One boy looks unsure.

options.text: Say nothing, since it's not your business
options.then: Rina is handed the notebook again.

options.text: Offer to take notes this time yourself
options.then: It helps today. By next week, Rina is back on notes.

options.text: Tell Rina she should refuse to take notes
options.then: Rina shrugs. "Then who will?" She keeps the notebook.

steps.why: Proposing a fair rotation changes the habit for everyone.

steps.prompt: A week later Rina asks for a turn at presenting. A boy says swapping roles wastes time. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest a two-week trial, then check
options.then: He sighs. "Okay. Two weeks."

options.text: Drop the idea to keep the peace in the group
options.then: Rina takes the notes again. The boy looks pleased.

options.text: Tell him he's just lazy
options.then: He bristles. The group goes tense.

options.text: Ask the teacher to make a rule for the whole group
options.then: The teacher says, "Settle it yourselves." The boy rolls his eyes.

steps.why: A short trial makes it easy to say yes.

steps.prompt: Two weeks later, the group meets to talk about who does what. What do you do?

options.text: Ask everyone what they like and let people choose
options.then: Rina says she likes notes, but wants to present once a month.

options.text: Call it settled and keep roles as they are
options.then: It runs on, but two people quietly dislike their role.

options.text: Let whoever speaks first decide
options.then: The loudest voices pick, and nobody else gets a say.

options.text: Make a strict rule that everyone tries every role weekly
options.then: The rule feels heavy. Two people stop turning up.

steps.why: Choosing by skill and interest keeps it fair and keeps it working.

scenarios.debrief: Assigning roles by skill and interest, and modelling it, is real leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by assigning roles by skill and interest, not by gender.

scenarios.hook: Your capable friend Asha keeps ducking the class-rep role.

steps.prompt: Nominations close on Friday and Asha says it's not for her. What do you do?

options.text: Name what she's good at and offer to back her
options.then: Asha blinks. "You noticed that? Let me think."

options.text: Apply yourself and move on
options.then: Your nomination goes in. Asha doesn't mention hers.

options.text: Nominate her without telling her
options.then: Her name is read out. She's furious and embarrassed.

options.text: Say "No worries, it's a lot of work anyway"
options.then: Asha nods, relieved. She doesn't apply.

steps.why: Naming her strengths and offering support lifts her toward the chance.

steps.prompt: Asha says she fears speaking in front of the class. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to practise speaking up with her
options.then: You practise in the corridor. Her voice steadies.

options.text: Tell her nobody will care how she speaks
options.then: Asha frowns. "Then why does everyone judge so loudly?"

options.text: Offer to write her speech for her
options.then: The speech sounds smooth, but it doesn't sound like Asha.

options.text: Tell her to just be confident
options.then: Asha sighs. "If it were that easy."

steps.why: Practising with her builds her own confidence.

steps.prompt: On speech day, a boy says loudly that a girl won't make a good class rep. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Let's judge by who speaks best" and move on
options.then: A few nod. The boy grumbles but sits down.

options.text: Laugh it off as banter
options.then: Asha hears it from the next row and goes quiet.

options.text: Argue with him in front of everyone
options.then: It turns into a scene. Asha wants to vanish.

options.text: Tell Asha to ignore him
options.then: Asha nods. She still looks smaller.

steps.why: A calm, fair standard answers him without a scene.

steps.prompt: After the vote, a younger girl asks how to run next year. What do you do?

options.text: Encourage her and offer to back her run
options.then: She grins. "I'll start thinking about it."

options.text: Say it's a lot of stress and not worth it
options.then: She shrugs. "Maybe not, then."

options.text: Tell her to ask a teacher instead
options.then: She nods politely and doesn't ask anyone.

options.text: Tell her to wait until she's older
options.then: She nods. The idea fades.

steps.why: Passing encouragement on is how the circle grows.

scenarios.debrief: Encouraging capable, overlooked people is exactly what lifting others means.
scenarios.relearn: Mentor and back capable-but-overlooked people toward chances they'd skip.

scenarios.hook: At a club meeting, your idea is ignored until a boy repeats it as his own.

steps.prompt: Everyone praises him and nods. What do you do?

options.text: Say, "Glad it caught on. That was my point."
options.then: He blinks. "Oh, right. Sorry, I built on yours."

options.text: Let it slide to avoid an awkward moment
options.then: The notes carry his name. Your voice feels smaller.

options.text: Say loudly that he stole it from you
options.then: The room freezes. People rush to his side.

options.text: Whisper to a friend that he always does this
options.then: She nods. Nobody else hears, and nothing changes.

steps.why: A calm, plain correction puts the credit back without a fight.

steps.prompt: After the meeting, he comes over and says: "Can we talk about the idea from today?"

options.text: Thank him for asking, and ask him to credit people next time
options.then: He nods. "Fair. I will."

options.text: Say it's totally fine and to forget it
options.then: He grins, relieved. It happens again at the next meeting.

options.text: Tell him he should apologise to the whole club
options.then: He bristles. "That would be so embarrassing."

options.text: Say you'll tell the teacher about it
options.then: He pales. "It was one time. Please."

steps.why: Hearing him out and naming what you need keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: The club's next meeting is about to start and you have a new idea. What do you do?

options.text: Write it down first, then speak up
options.then: It sits in the group notes with your name. People refer to it.

options.text: Hold it back in case it gets taken again
options.then: The idea never comes up. A boy suggests something similar later.

options.text: Give it to a friend to say for you
options.then: She says it well. But now it's hers.

options.text: Say it louder than anyone else
options.then: You win the room. The mood turns tense.

steps.why: Writing it down makes the source clear and keeps the peace.

steps.prompt: A newer girl says she stopped sharing ideas because the same thing happens to her. What do you do?

options.text: Share your own story and offer to credit each other
options.then: She smiles. "I'd like that. I'll start again."

options.text: Tell her to toughen up and speak louder
options.then: She nods slowly and says nothing more.

options.text: Say it's just how meetings go
options.then: She shrugs. Her ideas stay in her notebook.

options.text: Tell her to report the boys to the teacher right away
options.then: She shakes her head. "I don't want trouble."

steps.why: Sharing the habit with a peer spreads the norm.

scenarios.debrief: Amplifying, crediting whose idea it really was, is core to lifting others.
scenarios.relearn: Amplify: credit the person whose idea it was when it's ignored then repeated.

scenarios.hook: You're choosing where to put your leadership energy this term.

steps.prompt: A teacher asks what you want to improve this term. What do you say?

options.text: Something in my own friend group or class
options.then: She writes it down. "Start with the people you know."

options.text: Wait until a school-wide stage opens up
options.then: Weeks pass. The stage never arrives.

options.text: The biggest problem in the whole city
options.then: It's about the whole city. You can't tell where to begin.

options.text: I'll see what everyone else picks first
options.then: The others pick. You follow, and none of it is yours.

steps.why: Starting with the people around you is where change starts.

steps.prompt: In your friend group, a quiet girl is never asked where to eat. What do you do?

options.text: Ask her where she'd like to go
options.then: She lights up. "Really? There's a place near my home."

options.text: Tell the group they're leaving her out
options.then: The group goes defensive. She shrinks into her seat.

options.text: Carry on, since she never says anything
options.then: The usual place wins again. She goes along.

options.text: Wait for someone else to notice
options.then: Nobody does. She stays silent through lunch.

steps.why: A small question makes space for a voice that's usually missed.

steps.prompt: A teacher notices your group works well and asks you to help the class. What do you do?

options.text: Agree and bring friends in to share it
options.then: The class tries your method. Three others lead parts.

options.text: Refuse, since that's the teacher's job
options.then: She nods. The class stays as it was.

options.text: Agree, and run the whole thing alone
options.then: It works, but you're exhausted and nobody else learns it.

options.text: Agree, then drop it as soon as it gets hard
options.then: The idea fades. The teacher stops asking.

steps.why: Sharing leadership makes it last and spreads it.

scenarios.debrief: Your everyday circles are where your leadership is most real.
scenarios.relearn: Lead where you already have influence: home, group, class.

scenarios.hook: A boy in your group jokes that leading is a girl's hobby now.

steps.prompt: The others glance at you. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Fairness is everyone's job. I'm in"
options.then: A girl nearby smiles. The boy shrugs. "Okay, okay."

options.text: Laugh along so it blows over
options.then: The joke gets a laugh. You feel a little smaller.

options.text: Tell him he's a fool for saying that
options.then: He snaps back. The others split into sides.

options.text: Say you don't care either way
options.then: He nods. "Fair enough." Nothing shifts.

steps.why: Saying plainly that you're in shows leading on equality takes strength.

steps.prompt: Another boy says you're only doing it to impress the girls. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's about what's fair, and keep going
options.then: He rolls his eyes, but the teasing runs out of steam.

options.text: Say you don't really care about it, just joking
options.then: He grins. A girl in the group looks away.

options.text: Tell him he's only jealous of the attention
options.then: He bristles and the teasing gets sharper.

options.text: Tag every girl you know in a post about equality
options.then: Likes arrive. Nothing about the group changes.

steps.why: Steady, plain answers show it comes from your values, not from showing off.

steps.prompt: A girl in the group says she's tired of boys trying to save her. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what kind of support she'd actually want
options.then: She thinks. "Just let me finish my point and credit me."

options.text: Tell her not every boy is like that
options.then: She sighs. "I know. That's not what I said."

options.text: Say sorry and stay out of it from now on
options.then: She shrugs. You sit out the next three meetings.

options.text: Offer to take over her tasks to make things easier
options.then: She frowns. "I didn't ask you to do mine."

steps.why: Asking what helps keeps her in charge and still supported.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, a boy asks you quietly how to get involved. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him what you do and invite him to the next one
options.then: He nods, nervous. "Okay. Can I sit next to you?"

options.text: Send him a long reading list first
options.then: He glances at the list and never starts.

options.text: Tell him to keep it secret from the group
options.then: He agrees. Joining feels like something to hide.

options.text: Say it's not for everyone
options.then: He shrugs. He doesn't ask again.

steps.why: A personal invitation brings another boy in.

scenarios.debrief: Boys leading on equality is one of the most powerful moves this game asks for.
scenarios.relearn: Leading on equality as a boy is strength, and it's needed.

scenarios.hook: At home you notice your sister Kavya does all the cleanup after dinner.

steps.prompt: Dinner ends and she starts stacking the plates. What do you do?

options.text: Start sharing the cleanup, unasked, every night
options.then: Kavya looks surprised. "You don't have to." You carry on.

options.text: Say chores should be shared, then go to your room
options.then: Papa nods. You scroll your phone while Kavya cleans.

options.text: Help once to make a point
options.then: Kavya says thanks. Next night she is alone again.

options.text: Tell her to ask for help next time
options.then: Kavya says she shouldn't have to ask.

steps.why: Quiet, steady help shows what fair looks like better than words.

steps.prompt: Another night, Amma says cleanup is Kavya's job and you should rest. What do you do?

options.text: Say politely you'd like to help, and do it
options.then: Amma sighs, but lets you. Kavya gives you a small smile.

options.text: Say okay and leave it to Kavya, to keep things calm
options.then: Kavya keeps doing it alone.

options.text: Tell her she's being old-fashioned
options.then: Amma's face closes. "Don't talk to me like that."

options.text: Help only when Amma is out of the house
options.then: It works. Kavya notices, but the house doesn't.

steps.why: Respectful persistence shifts the norm without a fight.

steps.prompt: Your younger brother asks why chores are such a big deal at home. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Everyone eats, so everyone helps"
options.then: He rolls his eyes. You hand him a cloth and he dries a few plates.

options.text: Tell him to mind his own business
options.then: He stomps off, and nothing changes for him.

options.text: Say it's just a rule you have to follow
options.then: He nods. It sounds like a chore, not a choice.

options.text: Give him a long lecture about gender roles
options.then: His eyes glaze over. He leaves halfway through.

steps.why: A simple line and a task invite him in without a lecture.

steps.prompt: A friend visits, sees the washing up and asks who usually does it. What do you do?

options.text: Say your home is learning to share it
options.then: He laughs. You hand him a cloth. "Fine, I'll dry."

options.text: Say it's Kavya's job, not yours
options.then: He nods. Kavya hears it, and says nothing.

options.text: Change the subject quickly
options.then: He gives you a curious look. Kavya looks away.

options.text: Joke that you only help to please your parents
options.then: He grins. Kavya hears it and looks down.

steps.why: Owning the habit calmly shows it as normal.

scenarios.debrief: Sharing the unequal load yourself, visibly and unasked, leads by example.
scenarios.relearn: Share the unequal load yourself, visibly and unasked; example beats telling.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Aman keeps making the same demeaning joke about women, and you want it to stop kindly.

steps.prompt: He tells it again at the bus stop. What do you do?

options.text: Message him later: "That didn't sit right. Can we drop it?"
options.then: Aman replies after a while. "Huh. It's just a joke, though."

options.text: Mock him about the joke in front of the whole group chat
options.then: Aman gets defensive. The group splits.

options.text: Say "Oh no, not that one again" and laugh it off
options.then: Aman laughs too. "You love it."

options.text: Say nothing, since everyone has heard the joke before
options.then: He tells it to a new person next week.

steps.why: A private, good-faith message changes minds better than a public fight.

steps.prompt: A few days later Aman tells the joke again. You don't laugh, and he says: "Don't be so sensitive. It's just a joke." What do you do?

options.text: Say you're not angry. You just won't laugh at it
options.then: He pauses. "Okay. I hear you."

options.text: Say sorry and tell him it was nothing at all
options.then: Aman grins, relieved. The joke is back by Friday.

options.text: Tell him he's the one with the real problem here
options.then: He crosses his arms. "Wow."

options.text: Ask your friends to back you up and tell him he's wrong
options.then: Aman feels ganged up on. The group goes tense.

steps.why: Staying calm and plain keeps the talk about the joke, not about him.

steps.prompt: A week later Aman starts the joke and a new boy laughs along. What do you do?

options.text: Stay calm and ask Aman to pick a different joke
options.then: Aman hesitates, then switches to cricket.

options.text: Laugh a little to avoid a fight
options.then: The new boy sees you laugh. He tells it to his friends.

options.text: Tell the new boy off for laughing along
options.then: The new boy stiffens. Aman shifts, uneasy.

options.text: Leave the group without saying a word to anyone
options.then: They wonder where you went. The joke gets told anyway.

steps.why: A calm request in the moment holds the line and keeps people in the room.

steps.prompt: A month later, a quiet friend says the joke still bothers her. What do you do?

options.text: Ask how she'd like it raised with Aman
options.then: She says, "Please don't name me. Just keep it calm."

options.text: Tell her it's only a joke and he means no harm
options.then: She nods. She stops mentioning it.

options.text: Tell her to say it to Aman herself instead
options.then: She winces. "That's why I told you."

options.text: Say you already tried once, so it's done
options.then: She nods quietly. The joke keeps coming.

steps.why: Listening, asking what she wants and then acting keeps her in charge.

scenarios.debrief: A respectful, private call-in changes minds better than a shaming call-out.
scenarios.relearn: A respectful, private call-in changes minds better than public shaming.

scenarios.hook: You've finished the game and want it to change something real.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks if the game was any use. What do you say?

options.text: I'll name one action and one person to lift
options.then: Your cousin nods. "Who's the person?" You think of a classmate.

options.text: It was fun, and that's it
options.then: He shrugs. The game fades from your mind.

options.text: I'm going to fix the whole school
options.then: He laughs kindly. The plan has no first step.

options.text: I'll tell everyone what they're doing wrong
options.then: He groans. "Please don't start with me."

steps.why: One action and one person lifted turns learning into change.

steps.prompt: You notice an often overlooked classmate eating lunch alone. What do you do?

options.text: Sit with her and ask what she's good at
options.then: She mentions she draws. Her eyes light up.

options.text: Wave from across the room
options.then: She waves back. The distance stays.

options.text: Send her a thumbs-up emoji later
options.then: She replies with one. Nothing else changes.

options.text: Tell her what she should do with her life
options.then: She goes quiet, then says, "Maybe. I'll think about it."

steps.why: Sitting with her and asking shows real interest.

steps.prompt: A week later, you think back over what you have done so far. What do you do?

options.text: Note what worked and plan the next small step
options.then: You jot it down. The next step is easier to see.

options.text: Stop, since you've done it already
options.then: The week ends. The habit never starts.

options.text: Tell everyone what you've achieved
options.then: People roll their eyes. She looks embarrassed.

options.text: Double everything at once to make up for lost time
options.then: It's too much. By Wednesday you drop it.

steps.why: Reviewing and planning the next small step keeps it going.

steps.prompt: Days later, the classmate from lunch comes over and asks why you bothered with her. What do you say?

options.text: It's what I'm trying to do this term. Want to lift someone too?
options.then: She smiles. "I'd like that. I know who."

options.text: It's nothing
options.then: She nods. The moment passes.

options.text: I just wanted to feel good about myself
options.then: She stiffens a little. "Oh."

options.text: I thought you could help me with homework
options.then: She goes quiet. It feels like a missed chance.

steps.why: Naming what you're doing and inviting her in spreads it.

scenarios.debrief: A concrete commitment is what turns a game into real leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Commit to one action and one person to lift; make it real.

scenarios.hook: A teammate, Ishan, gets an idea wrong in front of the class, and you want to lead without embarrassing him.

steps.prompt: Heads turn toward you. What do you do?

options.text: Add to his idea and credit what he got right
options.then: Ishan relaxes. "Right, the second part. Thanks."

options.text: Point out the mistake in front of the whole class
options.then: A few snicker. Ishan goes red.

options.text: Stay silent and let the teacher correct him
options.then: She corrects him bluntly. Ishan shrinks.

options.text: Whisper the answer so he can say it
options.then: He repeats it shakily. The class can tell.

steps.why: Building on what's right keeps his dignity and fixes the idea.

steps.prompt: After class, Ishan says he felt silly. What do you do?

options.text: Name what he got right and offer to help
options.then: He smiles a little. "Okay. Tonight?"

options.text: Tell him everyone has already forgotten about it
options.then: He doesn't believe it. He still feels silly.

options.text: Joke about it to lighten the mood a little
options.then: He laughs weakly. The sting stays.

options.text: Say he should have checked the answer first
options.then: He nods and looks at his shoes.

steps.why: Naming strengths and offering help repairs the sting.

steps.prompt: For the next project, Ishan is nervous to speak first. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to rehearse his part with him
options.then: He rehearses. His voice is steadier on the day.

options.text: Tell him to just let you do the speaking
options.then: He nods, relieved. His part gets smaller.

options.text: Say nobody will remember if he slips up
options.then: He half smiles. He still dreads it.

options.text: Tell him to pick a smaller role instead
options.then: He switches to slides. His idea goes unheard.

steps.why: Practising with him builds his own confidence and keeps his voice in the room.

scenarios.debrief: Leading keeps people's dignity: build on them rather than expose them.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by building on people and keeping their dignity, not exposing them.

scenarios.hook: You're nervous to lead anything because you might get it wrong.

steps.prompt: A friend asks you to lead the poster team for the school fair. What do you do?

options.text: Take one small part and treat slip-ups as learning
options.then: You take the colour scheme. It's small enough to try.

options.text: Say no until you're sure you won't fail
options.then: She asks someone else. You watch the posters go up without you.

options.text: Say yes, then plan every detail for weeks
options.then: The plan grows and grows. Nothing starts.

options.text: Say yes and do every part yourself to avoid mistakes
options.then: You finish it all. You're worn out by Wednesday.

steps.why: Starting small lets you learn without the fear of getting it all wrong.

steps.prompt: A week later, you try something small in class and it flops. What do you do?

options.text: Note one change and try again
options.then: A classmate admits she would have panicked. You write down one change.

options.text: Decide you're just not a leader
options.then: The flop feels like proof. You stop volunteering.

options.text: Blame the others for not helping
options.then: They look hurt. Next time fewer people offer.

options.text: Pretend it never happened
options.then: Nobody mentions it. You also don't learn from it.

steps.why: Treating a slip as information keeps you moving.

steps.prompt: A younger friend says she is scared to try leading too. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her you were scared too, and start small together
options.then: She laughs, surprised. "You? Really?" Her shoulders drop.

options.text: Tell her to wait until she feels completely sure
options.then: She nods. The wait has no end.

options.text: Tell her it's easy and she'll be fine
options.then: She goes quiet. If she slips, she'll feel she's the only one.

options.text: Tell her leading isn't for everyone
options.then: She nods and drops the idea.

steps.why: Sharing your own nerves makes it safe for her to start.

scenarios.debrief: You don't need to be flawless to lead: starting and learning is the way.
scenarios.relearn: You needn't be flawless to lead; start small and learn as you go.

scenarios.hook: You have an idea for a fairer class duty rota, but you can't run it alone.

steps.prompt: The class monitor asks who can run a new duty rota. What do you do?

options.text: Offer to lead it, and invite a friend in
options.then: Your friend Ritu says yes. "Two is better."

options.text: Push it through on your own, without asking anyone
options.then: You make the chart alone. Nobody feels it's theirs.

options.text: Hand the idea to the monitor and step back
options.then: She likes it but doesn't know the details. It stalls.

options.text: Drop it until someone else suggests it
options.then: Nobody else suggests it. The old rota limps on and people grumble.

steps.why: Inviting one person to lead with you makes it easier and more likely to last.

steps.prompt: Soon after, the class asks how a fairer rota would actually work. What do you do?

options.text: Share a simple draft and ask for changes
options.then: People suggest swaps. The draft gets better.

options.text: Announce the final rota with no changes allowed
options.then: People grumble. The rota feels like an order.

options.text: Say you'll explain later when it's ready
options.then: The questions pile up. People lose interest.

options.text: Let the loudest voices decide it
options.then: A few friends shape it. The rest feel left out.

steps.why: Asking for input makes the plan theirs too.

steps.prompt: A boy complains that some rota duties are for girls. What do you do?

options.text: Say duties go by turn, and ask him to try it
options.then: He grumbles. "Okay. One week."

options.text: Change the rota quietly to keep him happy
options.then: The rota quietly goes back to the old split.

options.text: Tell him he's being unfair and narrow-minded
options.then: He bristles. A few friends side with him.

options.text: Say the monitor will deal with it later
options.then: The monitor says to settle it yourselves. The complaint hangs.

steps.why: A short trial lets people see fairness in practice.

steps.prompt: A month on, two classmates keep skipping their rota duties. What do you do?

options.text: Ask them what's getting in the way
options.then: One has a clash with tuition. You fix the timing together.

options.text: Do their duties yourself and say nothing
options.then: It works for a week. You're tired and it isn't fair on you.

options.text: Put their names on the board for everyone
options.then: They feel shamed. One stops talking to you.

options.text: Scrap the rota and go back to the old way
options.then: The old way returns. Nobody is happier.

steps.why: Asking why, with others, solves the cause and keeps trust.

scenarios.debrief: Inviting others in turns your idea into shared, lasting leadership.
scenarios.relearn: Inviting others to lead with you multiplies the effect.

scenarios.hook: Ravi, a junior, keeps getting talked over in your club, and you have some standing there.

steps.prompt: Ravi starts to speak and two seniors cut in. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Let's hear Ravi finish"
options.then: The room settles. Ravi continues, a little surprised.

options.text: Keep your standing for your own ideas
options.then: You put forward your plan. Ravi doesn't speak again.

options.text: Tell the seniors off for interrupting
options.then: They get annoyed. Ravi wishes you hadn't.

options.text: Hope someone else steps in
options.then: Nobody does. Ravi gives up mid-sentence.

steps.why: Using your standing to make space is what lifting looks like.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, Ravi says he's thinking of leaving the club. What do you do?

options.text: Ask what would make it easier to stay
options.then: He says he'd like a set time to speak. You note it.

options.text: Tell him to just speak louder next time
options.then: Ravi sighs. "I try. They don't stop."

options.text: Tell him he can't leave now
options.then: He looks uneasy. He feels pushed, not heard.

options.text: Say you'll make the seniors apologise
options.then: Ravi winces. "Please don't. That'd be worse."

steps.why: Listening first finds what he actually needs.

steps.prompt: The club plans an event, and the seniors pick the speakers. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest speakers sign up and take turns
options.then: The seniors agree. Ravi signs up and so do others.

options.text: Suggest Ravi by name and say no more
options.then: Ravi is on the list. He looks nervous but pleased.

options.text: Let the seniors pick as they always do
options.then: The usual names are called. Ravi isn't among them.

options.text: Say you'll speak so Ravi doesn't have to
options.then: You speak. Ravi stays in the audience.

steps.why: A fair sign-up opens the stage to everyone, not just Ravi.

steps.prompt: At a later session, Ravi gets a short turn to speak, and a senior mocks his nervous voice afterwards. What do you do?

options.text: Tell the senior privately it wasn't fair
options.then: The senior mutters, then shrugs. Later you tell Ravi what landed well.

options.text: Laugh along since it's only teasing
options.then: Ravi sees you laugh. He avoids the next meeting.

options.text: Announce what the senior said to the whole club
options.then: The senior turns red. People pick sides.

options.text: Tell Ravi to toughen up
options.then: He nods and stops smiling.

steps.why: A private word and real feedback protect his dignity and his place.

scenarios.debrief: Using your standing to make space for others is the heart of lifting.
scenarios.relearn: Spend your standing to make space for quieter voices; that's lifting.

scenarios.hook: Your teacher praises you for a project that your friends Aisha and Dev mostly carried.

steps.prompt: The whole class claps. What do you do?

options.text: Say "Aisha and Dev did the heavy lifting"
options.then: The teacher turns to them. "I didn't know. Thank you both."

options.text: Accept it quietly and hope they understand
options.then: Aisha looks at the floor. Dev stays quiet.

options.text: Say "It was a team effort" and smile politely
options.then: The teacher smiles. She still writes only your name.

options.text: Thank the whole class and your teachers instead
options.then: The clapping goes on. Nobody learns who did the work.

steps.why: Naming who did the work shares the credit and builds trust.

steps.prompt: At lunch, Aisha says she doesn't mind who gets the credit. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her, then check the marks sheet has all three names
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. Fine by me."

options.text: Take her word for it and drop the whole thing
options.then: She nods. The matter ends there.

options.text: Tell her she should really mind more than that
options.then: She frowns. "Please don't tell me how to feel."

options.text: Offer to buy her lunch to make up for it
options.then: She smiles and takes the samosa. The record stays as it was.

steps.why: You can respect how she feels and still keep the record true.

steps.prompt: The next project starts and the teacher asks who wants to lead. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll co-lead and share credit up front
options.then: The teacher nods. Aisha and Dev look relieved.

options.text: Take the lead again, since you got the praise
options.then: The teacher notes your name. Aisha shrugs.

options.text: Offer Aisha's name without asking her
options.then: Aisha is put on the spot. She looks anxious.

options.text: Stay silent so nobody notices you
options.then: Nobody leads. The teacher picks a name at random.

steps.why: Setting out shared credit at the start prevents the same gap again.

scenarios.debrief: Sharing credit lifts the people who earned it, and marks you as a leader.
scenarios.relearn: Share credit with the people who earned it; it builds trust and teams.

scenarios.hook: You want to lead, but worry your family will see it as showing off.

steps.prompt: You're asked to lead the school's cultural committee. What do you do?

options.text: Accept, and plan to lead by quiet example
options.then: You agree. At home you mention it simply, without fuss.

options.text: Turn it down so nobody thinks you're showing off
options.then: The role goes to someone else. You feel a small tug of regret.

options.text: Accept, and tell everyone at home how important you now are
options.then: Your father raises an eyebrow. Your mother's smile tightens.

options.text: Accept, but hide it from your family
options.then: It feels like a secret. Your mother hears it from a neighbour.

steps.why: Quiet example lets you lead and keeps your family close.

steps.prompt: At a family dinner, an uncle warns that leaders get too proud. What do you do?

options.text: Smile and ask for his advice on leading with care
options.then: He softens. "Be humble and you'll do fine."

options.text: Tell him he's old-fashioned about these things
options.then: The table goes quiet. Your mother looks away.

options.text: Argue with him that real leaders are never proud
options.then: He raises his voice. The dinner ends early.

options.text: Agree with him and say you'll stay out of leading
options.then: He nods. You feel leading slipping away.

steps.why: Respectful listening keeps the family on your side.

steps.prompt: Your cousin asks how to lead without being called a show-off. What do you say?

options.text: Let your work and kind words do the talking
options.then: She nods. "That feels doable."

options.text: Don't bother, because people will always talk
options.then: She shrugs. She decides not to try.

options.text: Copy the style of a famous leader you admire
options.then: She tries it. It feels fake and she stops.

options.text: Ignore what your family thinks about it all
options.then: She frowns. "I can't. They matter to me."

steps.why: Quiet example and kind words respect family and still lead.

steps.prompt: A month later, your grandmother says she's heard good things about you. What do you do?

options.text: Thank her and say your friends and teachers deserve credit too
options.then: She smiles. "Good. Keep your people close."

options.text: Say it was nothing
options.then: She tilts her head. "Don't be shy."

options.text: Tell her you're the best leader the school has had
options.then: Her smile fades. "We'll see."

options.text: Change the subject quickly
options.then: She senses you're uneasy. The moment passes.

steps.why: Sharing the credit shows the kind of leader you are.

scenarios.debrief: Leading by example and call-in respects family while still shifting the norm.
scenarios.relearn: Lead by quiet example; it respects family and still shifts the norm.

scenarios.hook: Outside school, a heated row between two older boys is turning rough.

steps.prompt: They are shoving each other near the gate and a crowd is forming. What do you do?

options.text: Stay back and find a teacher or trusted adult at once
options.then: A teacher heads to the gate straight away. You keep clear of the crowd.

options.text: Step between them to take the lead
options.then: The shoving swings your way and the crowd gets louder.

options.text: Film it on your phone so there is proof
options.then: The boys notice the camera and get angrier.

options.text: Walk past and tell yourself it's none of your business
options.then: The shouting grows louder behind you.

steps.why: Bringing in an adult keeps everyone, including you, safer.

steps.prompt: Later, a teacher asks anyone who saw the gate row to come and see her. What do you do?

options.text: See her after class and tell her calmly what you saw
options.then: She listens and thanks you. She says she'll speak to both boys.

options.text: Say you saw nothing so you stay out of it
options.then: She nods and moves on, saying her door is open if you remember anything.

options.text: Name everyone you think was involved
options.then: Some of the names were just bystanders. They get called in.

options.text: Post what you saw in the class chat first
options.then: The post spreads. The boys and their friends are furious.

steps.why: A private, factual word helps the adults act without adding to the row.

steps.prompt: The next day, a boy from the row hears you were at the gate and tells you to mind your own business. What do you do?

options.text: Walk away and tell a teacher or your parents
options.then: You walk off with a friend. A teacher takes note.

options.text: Answer him back loudly in front of the corridor crowd
options.then: A crowd gathers. The boy steps closer.

options.text: Ask your friends to scare him into leaving you alone
options.then: It turns into a standoff. A teacher spots the group.

options.text: Post about him in the class chat for everyone to see
options.then: The post spreads. Tempers rise on both sides.

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult is the safe way to handle a threat.

steps.prompt: A younger student asks what to do if a row like that starts again. What do you say?

options.text: Stay back and get a teacher, or call 112
options.then: They nod. "Stay back and get an adult. Got it."

options.text: Step in and try to calm everyone down
options.then: They look unsure but remember it as the brave way.

options.text: Just ignore it and walk away from it
options.then: They shrug. They're not sure when it's serious.

options.text: Film it and share it with friends
options.then: They nod. The idea of filming sticks.

steps.why: Staying clear and getting help is the plan to share.

steps.prompt: The school asks students for ideas to keep the gate safer. What do you do?

options.text: Suggest a teacher at the gate at closing time
options.then: The teacher writes it down and asks how students could report worries.

options.text: Suggest senior students patrol the gate each day
options.then: A teacher frowns. Students shouldn't have to handle that.

options.text: Suggest banning the boys involved from the gate
options.then: A teacher notes it down, then asks where the boys would go instead.

options.text: Say nothing, because it's the school's job
options.then: The ideas come from others, and the teacher writes those down.

steps.why: Simple adult supervision keeps the gate safe for everyone.

scenarios.debrief: Real leadership puts safety first: when it's unsafe, bring in a trusted adult, and it is never your fault if others fight or threaten you.
scenarios.relearn: When it's unsafe, bring in a trusted adult or 112, never confront alone.

scenarios.hook: Your plan to lead fizzled last month and you're tempted to give up.

steps.prompt: A friend asks how your plan is going. What do you say?

options.text: It fizzled, so I'm shrinking it to one tiny action
options.then: She nods. "That sounds doable. What's the action?"

options.text: It's going great
options.then: She smiles. You feel like a fraud.

options.text: Leading isn't really for me
options.then: She looks surprised. "Even one tiny try?" You say you'll think about it.

options.text: I'll restart when I feel motivated again
options.then: She nods. The motivation doesn't turn up that week.

steps.why: Being honest and shrinking the step gets you moving again.

steps.prompt: A week later you give it a real try, and by day three you've forgotten what you meant to do. What do you do?

options.text: Do it now and set a small reminder
options.then: You do it in five minutes. The reminder works the next day.

options.text: Take it as proof you can't stick to things
options.then: The thought sticks. You stop trying that evening.

options.text: Skip the week and start again on Monday
options.then: Monday comes. So does a new reason to wait.

options.text: Do three days' worth tonight
options.then: You're tired by the second one. The third doesn't happen.

steps.why: Doing it now and setting a reminder rebuilds the habit.

steps.prompt: A friend says she tried leading and quit too. What do you do?

options.text: Share your tiny action and invite her to try one
options.then: She smiles. "Okay. One thing, one week."

options.text: Tell her to push harder next time
options.then: She frowns. "That's what I did last time."

options.text: Agree that it's pointless
options.then: She sighs. You both feel flatter, but next morning you try one tiny thing anyway.

options.text: Tell her where she went wrong
options.then: She stiffens. "I didn't ask for a review."

steps.why: Sharing a small step lets both of you start again together.

steps.prompt: A month later, you've kept the action going on most days. What do you do?

options.text: Notice it, then add one small step
options.then: You write down the next step. It feels within reach.

options.text: Stop, since it's working now
options.then: The habit slips again within weeks.

options.text: Triple it overnight
options.then: It's too much. By Friday you drop it.

options.text: Tell the whole class how much you've changed
options.then: People roll their eyes. A few smile politely.

steps.why: Noticing progress and building on it keeps leading steady.

scenarios.debrief: One stumble isn't the end: shrink the step and begin again.
scenarios.relearn: One stumble isn't the end; shrink the step and begin again.

scenarios.hook: You're tempted to copy a famous person's leadership style.

steps.prompt: You're drafting how you'll lead the group project. What do you do?

options.text: Write down what you value and build from that
options.then: You list three values. They shape a plan that sounds like you.

options.text: Copy your favourite speaker's every move
options.then: You rehearse their gestures. It feels stiff.

options.text: Ask the group to pick a style for you
options.then: Everyone suggests something different. Nothing is decided.

options.text: Copy the loudest leader in your class
options.then: You try being loud. Your voice cracks on day one.

steps.why: Your own values give you a style you can keep up.

steps.prompt: The first meeting starts and the group looks to you. What do you do?

options.text: Speak plainly in your own words and ask for ideas
options.then: Someone says, "Finally, a clear start."

options.text: Use the dramatic speaking style you practised at home
options.then: People exchange glances. One tries not to laugh.

options.text: Say very little to avoid saying it wrong
options.then: The silence drags. Someone else starts talking.

options.text: Give orders so you look in charge
options.then: People comply, but nobody offers ideas.

steps.why: Plain words in your own voice help people join in.

steps.prompt: Weeks in, someone says your leadership style isn't what they'd expect. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's your own style and ask what would help
options.then: They think. "Fair. At least it sounds like you."

options.text: Switch to the style they expect
options.then: You try it. It feels borrowed again.

options.text: Defend yourself loudly
options.then: The room tenses. The point gets lost.

options.text: Copy their favourite leader after all
options.then: You imitate. You feel like you're acting.

steps.why: Staying true to your style and asking for feedback keeps it real.

scenarios.debrief: Leading from your own values is what makes your style sustainable.
scenarios.relearn: Build your style from your own values, not a copied one.

scenarios.hook: You want your friend Imran to help you lead a fairer group project.
scenarios.setup: You find him in the library.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Lead a project? Isn't that the teacher's job?"

options.text: "We can set the tone ourselves. It's better with two."
options.then: Imran considers it. "With you? Fine. Tell me more."

options.text: "True. I'll just handle the whole thing myself."
options.then: Imran shrugs. "Doing it all alone sounds exhausting, though."

options.text: "Fine. We'll leave it all to the teacher."
options.then: Imran nods. "The usual split is what we always get, though."

options.text: "If you won't, I'll just name you leader anyway."
options.then: Imran frowns. "Don't push me."

steps.why: Inviting a friend to share the lead makes it easier and more likely.

steps.prompt: Imran asks: "Okay, but what would 'fairer' even mean for the group?"

options.text: "Everyone tries each role, based on what they enjoy."
options.then: Imran nods. "That could work."

options.text: "Whatever the loudest person picks."
options.then: Imran snorts. "That's what we have now."

options.text: "Fairer means whatever you and I decide."
options.then: Imran frowns. "That's not fair either."

options.text: "No idea. Let's ask the teacher to write the rules."
options.then: Imran sighs. "Then it's not ours."

steps.why: Rotating by interest is simple and fair.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Some of the boys will think we're making a fuss."

options.text: "Maybe. We'll keep it light and let the results show."
options.then: Imran grins. "Okay. I can do light."

options.text: "Then we should tell them off."
options.then: Imran shakes his head. "They'll just dig in."

options.text: "Then let's not do it."
options.then: Imran looks half relieved, half let down. "Let me think about it."

options.text: "Then we'll go over their heads to the teacher."
options.then: Imran looks uneasy. "That'll make it worse."

steps.why: Light, steady action wins people over better than a fight.

steps.prompt: Imran says: "Okay, I'm in after all. Who goes first as leader?"

options.text: "We take turns. Flip a coin and swap every week."
options.then: Imran laughs. "Deal. Heads for me."

options.text: "Me. It was my idea, after all."
options.then: Imran nods slowly. You can tell he's left holding the notes.

options.text: "You. I'd rather not be the main face."
options.then: Imran blinks. "Wait, I'm doing it alone?"

options.text: "Whoever the group votes for at the end of term."
options.then: Imran looks puzzled. "So who leads till then?"

steps.why: Sharing the lead in turns keeps it fair for both of you.

scenarios.relearn: Inviting others to lead with you multiplies the effect.

scenarios.hook: Priya's idea was ignored, then Ankit repeated it and the group moved on.
scenarios.setup: You are sitting beside Priya at the group table.

steps.prompt: Your group leader says: "Ankit's idea is great. Let's go with it."

options.text: "That was Priya's idea earlier. Priya, want to add?"
options.then: The leader pauses. "Oh. Priya, go ahead."

options.text: "Anyway, let's keep moving. We're running late."
options.then: The group moves on. Priya stays quiet.

options.text: "Maybe Priya can help Ankit with his idea."
options.then: The leader nods. Priya is now an assistant on her own idea.

options.text: "Whoever said it first, let's just get going now."
options.then: The leader shrugs. "Fine." Ankit gets the credit.

steps.why: Naming whose idea it was and handing her the floor puts the credit back.

steps.prompt: Later, Priya tells Ankit the idea was hers. Ankit says to you: "I didn't mean to take it. It just came to me."

options.text: "That's okay. Just say whose it was next time."
options.then: Ankit nods. "Fair. I'll do that."

options.text: "You took Priya's idea and passed it off as yours."
options.then: Ankit flushes. "That's not fair."

options.text: "No problem at all. These things just happen."
options.then: Ankit relaxes. It happens again next week.

options.text: "Fine, but you now owe her something."
options.then: Ankit frowns. "What am I supposed to do?"

steps.why: Assuming good faith and naming what you need changes the habit.

steps.prompt: Priya says quietly: "About the other day. Next time I want to be the one to say it's my idea."

options.text: "Understood. Next time I'll point to you."
options.then: Priya smiles. "That works."

options.text: "I only wanted to help."
options.then: Priya sighs. "I know. That's the problem."

options.text: "Then you'll have to speak louder next time."
options.then: Priya frowns. "It's not about volume."

options.text: "Fine. I'll stay out of it from now on."
options.then: Priya shrugs. The next time, nobody speaks for her.

steps.why: Pointing to her and stepping back keeps the idea in her voice.

scenarios.relearn: Amplify by crediting whose idea it really was when it's repeated.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Leela keeps ducking the hockey team's captain role.
scenarios.setup: You're packing up after practice.

steps.prompt: Leela says: "I'm not captain material. Ask someone else."

options.text: "You'd be great at this. I've got your back."
options.then: Leela looks up. "You really mean that?"

options.text: "Eh, maybe it's not really your thing after all."
options.then: Leela nods. "Yeah. Probably."

options.text: "Okay. I'll just go and ask someone else, then."
options.then: Leela shrugs. "Coach hasn't picked yet, though. I keep wondering."

options.text: "Stop being silly. You're doing it. I've decided."
options.then: Leela frowns. "Don't decide for me."

steps.why: Telling her you believe in her and backing her gives her a reason to try.

steps.prompt: Leela says: "What if the team doesn't listen to me?"

options.text: "They already do. You sorted drills last week."
options.then: Leela thinks. "I did, didn't I?"

options.text: "Then shout louder until they finally listen."
options.then: Leela winces. "That's not me."

options.text: "They'll listen if you copy how Coach does it."
options.then: Leela frowns. "I'd feel like I'm acting."

options.text: "Then step down fast. It's really no big deal."
options.then: Leela nods slowly. "Maybe."

steps.why: Pointing to what she's already done shows she can.

steps.prompt: Leela says: "Coach says it's between me and Mohit. I'm worried."

options.text: "Tell Coach why you want it. I'll back you."
options.then: Leela breathes out. "Okay. I'll go tonight."

options.text: "Let Mohit have it. He probably wants it more."
options.then: Leela nods. She doesn't sound sure, but she puts her name in anyway.

options.text: "I'll go and tell Coach to pick you myself."
options.then: Leela frowns. "Please don't. I want it to be fair."

options.text: "Don't stress about it. It's only a role."
options.then: Leela half smiles. "It's not only a role to me."

steps.why: Helping her speak for herself while you back her up works best.

steps.prompt: Leela says: "Coach picked me as captain! What should I do first?"

options.text: "Try one small change. Ask each player what she needs."
options.then: Leela grins. "Okay. I'll start tomorrow."

options.text: "Rest now. We'll see."
options.then: Leela nods. The week passes without a plan.

options.text: "Make big changes straight away to show who's boss."
options.then: Leela winces. "That would shake everyone."

options.text: "Wait until the team asks you to do something."
options.then: Leela frowns. "They may never ask."

steps.why: A small, listening step builds trust with the team.

scenarios.relearn: Encourage and back capable people toward chances they'd otherwise skip.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Kunal keeps cracking the same demeaning joke about girls.
scenarios.setup: You catch him alone after school.

steps.prompt: Kunal says: "What's up? You look serious."

options.text: "That joke didn't sit right with me. Can we not?"
options.then: Kunal blinks. "My jokes? Which one?" You name it, and he winces.

options.text: "You're disgusting. Everyone should hear this."
options.then: Kunal snaps. "What is your problem?"

options.text: "Nothing at all. I'm just tired. Forget it."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. The joke is back by lunchtime.

options.text: "Everyone's saying you're a bit of a creep."
options.then: Kunal goes pale. "Who's saying that?"

steps.why: A private, calm line names the problem without an attack.

steps.prompt: The next day the joke gets a laugh in class, and Kunal catches you not laughing. He says: "It's only a joke, yaar. Don't be so sensitive."

options.text: "Even as a joke, it lands badly on girls."
options.then: Kunal pauses. "I didn't think about it that way."

options.text: "Fine, forget it. I'm just in a bad mood today."
options.then: Kunal grins. "See? Relax." Then he squints. "Still not laughing, though."

options.text: "You're not even funny and you never were."
options.then: Kunal flinches. "Wow. Thanks a lot."

options.text: "Then I'll ask someone else to tell you."
options.then: Kunal stiffens. "So you'll gang up on me?"

steps.why: Explaining the impact keeps it about the joke, not him.

steps.prompt: Kunal says: "Okay, but who are you to decide what's funny, anyway?"

options.text: "Nobody. I'm just asking you, as a friend."
options.then: Kunal's shoulders drop. "Okay. I hear you."

options.text: "Everyone. I'm the voice of reason here."
options.then: Kunal rolls his eyes. "Sure. Our great judge speaks."

options.text: "You're right. Say whatever you like."
options.then: Kunal smirks. Nothing has moved.

options.text: "Someone has to. You obviously can't."
options.then: Kunal scowls. "Wow. Okay."

steps.why: Staying humble and asking as a friend keeps him listening.

steps.prompt: Days later, Kunal says: "My cousins tell jokes like that too. At home it's normal."

options.text: "Maybe it is there. We can do it differently here."
options.then: Kunal shrugs. "Maybe. It's not that deep."

options.text: "Your family must be awful if that's normal there."
options.then: Kunal's face hardens. "Leave my family out of this."

options.text: "Okay, then. It's just your family's thing, I guess."
options.then: Kunal nods and the subject drops. He looks thoughtful, though.

options.text: "Then tell your cousins they're all wrong."
options.then: Kunal laughs. "As if I could."

steps.why: Respecting his family while still setting your own line keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: A week later Kunal says: "I almost told the joke again today. I stopped myself."

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. That takes effort."
options.then: Kunal grins, a little shy. "Yeah. Weird, but okay."

options.text: "Finally. It took you long enough."
options.then: Kunal's smile fades. "Right. Thanks."

options.text: "Great. Now tell everyone you're sorry."
options.then: Kunal groans. "One thing at a time."

options.text: "Don't make a big deal of it."
options.then: Kunal nods. He sounds a bit deflated.

steps.why: Noticing the effort helps the change last.

scenarios.relearn: A private, good-faith call-in changes minds better than public shaming.

scenarios.hook: You're a boy, and you spoke up for fairness in class today.
scenarios.setup: It's break time and a few others are listening.

steps.prompt: Your mate Deva says: "Oi, whose side are you on, the girls'?"

options.text: "No sides in fairness. Backing it takes strength."
options.then: Deva blinks. "Strong? Hmm. Okay, maybe."

options.text: "Fine, forget I said anything. I was only joking."
options.then: Deva grins. "Thought so."

options.text: "Ha, I'm a rebel now. Cool, huh? Join me."
options.then: Deva rolls his eyes. "Sure, rebel."

options.text: "Mind your own business, Deva, and let it go."
options.then: Deva's smile fades. "Whoa. Okay."

steps.why: Saying plainly that fairness has no sides shows strength.

steps.prompt: Deva says: "Real boys don't care about this stuff."

options.text: "I'm the same guy. I just care what's fair."
options.then: Deva shrugs. "You haven't changed that much."

options.text: "You're right. I won't bring it up again."
options.then: Deva nods. The topic closes.

options.text: "Real boys? You mean bullies?"
options.then: Deva bristles. "Say that again?"

options.text: "Whatever. Let's just play and forget it."
options.then: Deva tosses you the ball. Nothing has been said.

steps.why: Staying yourself while holding your value is steady strength.

steps.prompt: Deva says: "The others are still talking about it. Won't they make fun of you?"

options.text: "Maybe. I'd still rather be fair than popular."
options.then: Deva whistles. "That's a lot."

options.text: "Then it's not worth standing for. I'll drop it."
options.then: Deva nods. Something you cared about quietly goes.

options.text: "Let them laugh. I'll show them all up."
options.then: Deva laughs. "You're going to fight everyone?"

options.text: "Let's pretend I never said it, okay? Keep it quiet."
options.then: Deva smirks. "Everyone heard already. Weird, though."

steps.why: Being fair, even when it costs a little, is what makes it strength.

steps.prompt: Deva says quietly: "My sister stopped playing cricket. People talk."

options.text: "That's unfair. Want to bring her into our game?"
options.then: Deva's face opens up. "Really? She'd love that."

options.text: "Not my problem."
options.then: Deva looks away. "Right."

options.text: "Tell her to ignore the talk."
options.then: Deva sighs. "It's not that simple."

options.text: "Let's tell the whole school she's the best player."
options.then: Deva looks panicked. "No! She'd hate that."

steps.why: A simple, kind invitation helps without taking over.

scenarios.relearn: A boy leading on equality is strength; there are no 'sides' in fairness.

scenarios.hook: Your teammate Sana mostly drove your project, but praise lands on you.
scenarios.setup: The teacher is announcing the marks.

steps.prompt: Your teacher says: "Excellent work. You must be proud."

options.text: "Thanks, but Sana drove most of it. Credit her."
options.then: The teacher smiles. "Sana, I hadn't realised. Thank you."

options.text: "Yeah, honestly it was pretty much all me."
options.then: The teacher nods. Sana looks at her notebook.

options.text: "Thanks, ma'am. We all worked hard on it."
options.then: She smiles. She still writes only your name.

options.text: "Thank you, ma'am. I'm really glad it worked."
options.then: She nods. The class claps for you.

steps.why: Naming Sana gives the credit to the person who earned it.

steps.prompt: A week later your teacher says: "For the exhibition, who wants to present the project?"

options.text: "Sana led it. Sana, would you like to present? I'll help."
options.then: Sana looks surprised. "Me? Okay. If you'll help."

options.text: "I'll do it. I'm used to presenting anyway."
options.then: The teacher writes your name. Sana says nothing.

options.text: "Whoever you pick. I don't mind either way."
options.then: The teacher picks you. Sana looks away.

options.text: "Let's just decide it by tossing a coin."
options.then: The coin falls your way. Sana shrugs.

steps.why: Asking the person who led it keeps credit tied to the work.

steps.prompt: Sana says: "The exhibition is on Saturday. I'm nervous about my part at the stall. Can you stay close on the day?"

options.text: "Yes. I'll be right beside you."
options.then: Sana breathes out. "Thank you. That helps."

options.text: "You'll be fine. Just don't be nervous."
options.then: Sana forces a smile. The nerves stay.

options.text: "I'll do all the talking for you. It's easier."
options.then: Sana looks relieved, then flat. The idea was hers.

options.text: "I can't. I have my own things to do."
options.then: Sana nods. She goes quiet.

steps.why: Standing beside her supports her without taking over.

scenarios.relearn: Share credit with whoever earned it; it builds trust and teams.

scenarios.hook: Your quieter friend Zara sat out the club elections today.
scenarios.setup: You sit with her after school.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "I'm not loud. I don't think I can lead anything."

options.text: "You already lead: calm and fair. Try one small thing."
options.then: Zara looks up. "You really think so?"

options.text: "Yeah, leading's probably not for everyone, to be honest."
options.then: Zara nods quietly. "Probably."

options.text: "You just need to be a lot louder, honestly."
options.then: Zara winces. "That's the whole problem."

options.text: "Don't worry about it. I'll lead and you follow."
options.then: Zara smiles, but looks a little smaller.

steps.why: Naming what she already does well helps her believe in her style.

steps.prompt: Zara asks: "If I did try something small, what would it even be?"

options.text: "What do you care about? Start there."
options.then: Zara thinks. "I like reading. Quiet places."

options.text: "Anything. It doesn't matter much."
options.then: Zara frowns. "Then why bother?"

options.text: "Stand for school captain."
options.then: Zara pales. "That's not small."

options.text: "I'll pick something for you."
options.then: Zara shrugs. "Okay. But it won't be mine."

steps.why: Starting from her own values makes the step hers.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "I'd start a quiet reading corner. But people may laugh."

options.text: "They might. I'll set it up with you."
options.then: Zara laughs softly. "Okay. Two of us is better."

options.text: "If they laugh at it, just skip the whole thing."
options.then: Zara nods. The corner idea stays in her head.

options.text: "Make it a big event so they all notice."
options.then: Zara looks alarmed. "That's not what I meant."

options.text: "Ask the teacher to run the whole thing for you."
options.then: Zara sighs. "Then it wouldn't be mine."

steps.why: Offering to help while keeping it hers is real backing.

steps.prompt: Zara says: "A week on, I'm still wondering if I'm cut out for this."

options.text: "Doubt is normal. Let's find one small win."
options.then: Zara thinks. "Well, I told you about the reading corner. That counts."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. Try something else."
options.then: Zara nods slowly. Her shoulders sink.

options.text: "Don't think about it. Just push harder."
options.then: Zara frowns. "That's not how I work."

options.text: "Everyone has doubts. Just ignore yours."
options.then: Zara shrugs. The doubt doesn't go anywhere.

steps.why: Finding one small win turns doubt into a next step.
